- "Wrote spec", in Spec's colour, when it wrote or edited a file in the spec location, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../../../scope/project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) says, or under .claude/reference
- "Wrote code", in Code's colour, when it wrote or edited a file in the code location, the project config's codeRoot
- "Wrote files", in the theme's muted grey, when it wrote or edited a file in neither, outside the project's own data in .suspense
- "Answered", in Ask's colour, when it wrote or edited no file at all, or only files in .suspense, and gave a final summary, as a question almost always does
- "No changes", in the theme's muted grey, when it wrote or edited no such file and gave no final summary

So a run shows one or more of the first three, or exactly one of the last two. The spec location is the one the task was sent against, as its compiled prompt records, or for a run that doesn't record one, the project config's root; a project whose config gives no codeRoot has no code location, and nothing counts as code in it.
A file counts as written or edited when the run's tool calls report writing or editing it, with a file tool or a shell command, as the referenced spec works them out, a subagent's included; a file only read never counts. Each colour is its mode's, as the [PromptModesScope](../../../scope/prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it, including any colour chosen in the theme editor. The label is in the colour at full strength, on a faint tint of it, about a sixth of its strength, readable in light and dark mode.

##### Not While Running

While the run is under way, no tags are shown; they appear once it is over, however it ended, done, failed, or cancelled. A task or question restored from the history, among the previous tasks or answers, shows them as its record replays, worked out against the project it belongs to, the same as when it ran.

#### Tool Calls

##### Description

A tool call's Output cell shows its most telling argument. For Files, Edit, Command, Web, and Agent calls the tool's name is left out, since the badge already says what it is; any other tool's name comes first. Arguments other than commands are shown on a single line.

##### Paths

Any path inside the project directory is shown relative to it, and the project directory itself reads `.`.

##### Commands

A command is shown whole, as a syntax-highlighted bash block, and a long one is split across lines at `&&`, `||`, `|`, and `;`, one command per line with the chained ones indented. It never splits inside quotes, command substitutions, brackets, comments, or heredocs.

#### Streaming

##### Description

While the run is under way, the table ends in a waiting row for whatever the harness does next. As soon as a row's type is known, its badge is real, and as soon as its text or argument arrives, that is shown.

##### Raw Output

Until a row has something meaningful to show, its Type cell is a skeleton and its Output cell shows the last three lines of the harness's raw JSON output: muted, monospace, JSON syntax-highlighted, and always three lines tall so the row doesn't jump. Before any output has arrived it reads "Waiting for the harness…".

##### Skeletons

While the input of a Files, Edit, Command, Web, or Agent call is still arriving, its Output cell shows only a skeleton.
A skeleton stands in for a running row only while there is nothing meaningful to show for it. As soon as there is, no skeleton is shown for it at all.

#### Scrolling

##### Description

The table usually has its lock to the bottom, following the run's latest output. While the end of the table is scrolled out of view, raw output that would only change the waiting row redraws nothing. What a row shows that never changes once known, such as a command laid out across lines or a line of raw output highlighted, is worked out once.

#### Collapsed Steps

##### Description

A use can say its table collapses the steps leading up to the answer, once the run is finished, as the [TableScope](../table/TableScope.md#table-scope) collapses rows. The steps are every row up to and including the harness's last tool call; the answer is the rows after it.
A run with no tool calls, or with nothing after its last one, has nothing to collapse and shows whole. A run still under way shows its latest step as usual.

#### Sent

##### Description

A run can be sent more while it works. Each message sent to it is a row of its own, in order among what the harness did, where it was sent. Its Type is a "Sent" badge, and its Output the message's first line, the whole message as it was typed shown on hover. The rows after it are what the harness did in answer, until the next message. A Sent row has no status.
A Sent row is never collapsed among the steps leading up to an answer.

#### Notices

##### Description

A notice is something the application tells the run's reader about the run, rather than something the harness did or a failure: chiefly that it put back changes a task made where its mode may not change anything, a Code task in the spec or a Spec task in the code. It is passive. It is never shown as an error, never in the theme's error colour, and never fails the task, changes its status, or counts among the errors a run ended with.

##### Row

A notice is a row of its own, where it happened among the run's rows, its badge reading "Notice" with an info icon, in the muted grey of a badge that marks nothing wrong. Its output is a single line summing it up, muted, beside a right chevron, such as "Put back 3 spec files this Code task changed" or "Put back 1 code file this Spec task changed". It has no status.

##### Details

Clicking the line expands the notice's details in place, beneath it, and its chevron turns down; clicking it again collapses them. For changes put back, the details say that a task in its mode may not change that location, so what it changed there was put back as it was, and then list each file put back, one per line, by its path in the project. A notice starts collapsed, and each stays as it was left for as long as the application runs.

##### Kept

A notice is kept with its task, and shown the same wherever the task's output is, the latest task's table, a previous task opened, and a Freeform or Ask reply read as a chat, where it sits among the reply's steps as a muted line that expands the same way, never at the reply's end with its errors.

#### Legibility

The output from a realtime agent should be readable and meaningful.

#### Narrow Widths

However narrow the table is drawn, the Output column keeps most of its width. The Type and Status columns are no wider than their widest label needs, and the space inside the cells and around the table tightens as the table narrows, so the output is never squeezed into a sliver between padding and empty space.

#### Resending

A prompt sent before can be sent again, from a Resend button: a small ghost button with a rotating-arrow icon, whose tooltip says it sends the prompt again as it was sent. The prompt resent stays where it is. A prompt whose mode isn't known, saved before modes were, is resent from the chat input's selected tab. What is being written in the chat input, and attached to it, is left alone, and so is the Slice toggle.

#### Cancelling

A task under way can be cancelled, from a Cancel button: a small ghost button with a stop icon, whose tooltip says "Cancel this task", at the right of the latest task's header, beside its Resend button, shown only while the task is building, compiling, or running. With a task running in each lane, the one that isn't the latest task shows among the previous tasks as Running, with the same Cancel button at the right of its heading, beside its Resend button, and clicking it never opens or closes the item. A task is cancelled straight away, whatever the harness is in the middle of: a build or compile under way is abandoned before the task is run, and a run is stopped, the harness's process ended, not left to finish its turn.
A cancelled task keeps the output it had so far, and its status reads "Cancelled", as the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list) shows, in the history as much as in its header. It adds no commit note, and any change the harness had already made to files is left as it is. Its lane's queue carries on after it, as it does after a task that fails, sending the next prompt waiting in it, and the next task carries on the same conversation. The task in the other lane, and questions, are not cancelled with it.

It sits wherever Resend does for a task, at the right of the latest task's header and of the heading of each previous task, and clicking it never opens or closes the item. Tasks sent in Chain, questions, and prompts whose mode isn't known don't offer it.

# Message List

## How To Build

A MessageList should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A MessageList should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The task view of prompt mode: the tasks sent to the harness and their output as the harness works on them.

### Shape

#### Description

Shows tasks and their output, not a conversation. Prompts aren't shown on the right with responses on the left, and tool calls aren't gathered into groups. Freeform is the exception: a Freeform task is shown as a regular chat, as its freeform says.

#### Sent Prompt

##### Description

A task's header shows the compiled markdown that was actually sent to the harness, rendered as markdown, once it has compiled, along with the name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from.

#### Status

##### Description

A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green, "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and dark mode.

#### Output Table

##### Description

A task's output is a [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope), whose rows are what the harness did for the task. While the task is under way, its table ends in the waiting row for whatever the harness does next. Tasks never collapse their steps, since their whole chain is of interest.

#### Links

##### Description

Links in the compiled prompt and in reply text are clickable. A link to a file opens it, as the [OpenFileScope](../../open-file/index.md#open-file-scope) says, and a web link opens in the browser. The file path on a Read, Edit, Write, or MultiEdit row is shown as a link and opens that file the same way.

#### Backgrounds

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The task view of prompt mode: the tasks sent to the harness and their output as the harness works on them.

### Shape

#### Description

Shows tasks and their output, not a conversation. Prompts aren't shown on the right with responses on the left, and tool calls aren't gathered into groups. Freeform is the exception: a Freeform task is shown as a regular chat, as its freeform says.

#### Sent Prompt

##### Description

A task's header shows the compiled markdown that was actually sent to the harness, rendered as markdown, once it has compiled, along with the name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from.

#### Status

##### Description

A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green, "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and dark mode.

#### Output Table

##### Description

A task's output is a [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope), whose rows are what the harness did for the task. While the task is under way, its table ends in the waiting row for whatever the harness does next. Tasks never collapse their steps, since their whole chain is of interest.

#### Links

##### Description

Links in the compiled prompt and in reply text are clickable. A link to a file opens it, as the [OpenFileScope](../../open-file/index.md#open-file-scope) says, and a web link opens in the browser. The file path on a Read, Edit, Write, or MultiEdit row is shown as a link and opens that file the same way.

use /lib
use /ui
use /ui/components/sidebar/Panel
from .. import RightSidebarScope
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope

export panel SubagentsPanel:
    title: Subagents
    counted: false
    height: fit
    scrolls: true
    scrollbar: overflowing

    concept: {SubagentsConcept}

concept SubagentsConcept:
    pitch:
        The bottom panel of the @{RightSidebarScope}, beneath the referenced
        files and the understanding: the subagents the harness started for
        the running task, each shown in the colour of the mode that started
        it.

    shape: {SubagentsShape}

shape SubagentsShape:
    description:
        It lists only subagents, the agents the harness started, never the
        other background tasks a run starts, such as shell commands run in the
        background, which hold the run open, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, but aren't shown here.

        It is shown only once the run has started a subagent, and takes no
        room before. One row per subagent, in the order they started, each 24
        pixels tall, 8 pixels in from the panel's edges: a spinner while it is
        at work, then a tick, a cross, or a dash for how it ended, done,
        failed, or stopped, beside what it was started to do, in small text,
        cut off with an ellipsis, muted once it has ended. Its tooltip gives
        what it was started to do, and beneath, muted, its kind and what it
        is doing or how it ended. The panel is only as tall as its rows need,
        up to 30% of the sidebar's height, scrolling beyond that.

    byMode:
        Each subagent is shown according to the mode of the task that started
        it, as the @{PromptModesScope} colours modes: its row has a bar 2
        pixels wide down its left edge in that mode's colour, and its spinner
        and tick are drawn in it too, while a cross or dash keeps its own
        colour. A subagent's mode is the mode its task was sent in, and for a
        step of a chain, the step's own: the spec step and a spec follow-up
        are Spec's, and the code step is Code's, never Chain's purple. Its
        tooltip names the mode, "Started by the Code task", "Started by the
        Spec step", and so on. A task whose mode isn't known, as one from the
        history saved before modes were, has no bar and keeps its spinner and
        tick in their own colours, its tooltip reading "Started by the task".
        A Chain task on its own, before its code step has been sent, is the
        chain's spec step, so its subagents are Spec's and labelled "Spec".

        While a chain runs, the panel keeps the subagents of each of its
        steps, not only the step running: they are grouped by step, in the
        order the steps ran, each group headed by a small label in its mode's
        colour, "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", with the step running
        last. A task that isn't part of a chain has one group, and no label.
        Once the run is over, the sidebar slides back with them all, as it
        says.
----
use /lib

export shape MessageListStatusShape:
    description:
        A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in
        blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green,
        "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, and "Not recorded" in grey for
        a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are
        readable in both light and dark mode.

content.content:
with `--replay-user-messages`. A message taken in between turns is
        answered with a result of its own, and one taken while a turn is under
        way is answered within that turn, sharing its result.

        A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its
        turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the
        background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background
        task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its
        kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet
        ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started,
        and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended
        as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is
        matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run
        when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.

        A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is
        the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no
        background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while
        a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still
        going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays
        open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's
        input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the
        harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the
        state of that last result; until the process exits, the task keeps
        running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task
        as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its
        input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the
        background, since its whole process group is ended with it.

        Codex's `codex exec` and OpenCode's `opencode run` read a single prompt
        and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either
        takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.

        Questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes,
        commit messages, and prompt titles each take a single prompt, as ever.

        harness's process, and a run whose input is already closed, or whose
        harness can't be fed, can't stop one on its own.

use /lib
use /ui
use /ui/components/sidebar/Sidebar
from ./referenced-files import ReferencedFilesPanel
from ./subagents import SubagentsPanel
from ./understanding import UnderstandingPanel
from /scope/application/Body import BodyScope
from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope
from /ui/components/sidebar import SidebarScope

export sidebar RightSidebarScope:
    side: right

    panels:
        - @{ReferencedFilesPanel}
        - @{UnderstandingPanel}
        - @{SubagentsPanel}

    concept: {RightSidebarConcept}

concept RightSidebarConcept:
    pitch:
        A second @{SidebarScope}, at the right of the message list and the
        chat input beneath it, that lists
        the spec files the running task references, so it's clear what part of
        the spec the harness is working from, and the constraints it has taken
        from it for the task.

    shape: {RightSidebarShape}

shape RightSidebarShape:
    description:
        It runs the full height of the body, beside the body's tab bar, the
        message list or file beneath it, and the chat input beneath those, which stops at its left edge rather than
        running beneath it. It keeps the width it was dragged to while the
        application runs.

        Its panels sit one above the other, in this order: the referenced
        files at the top, the understanding beneath them, and the subagents
        last, along the bottom of the sidebar, beneath both. The referenced
        files are only as tall as their rows need, up to half the sidebar's
        height, scrolling beyond that; the subagents, once there are any, are
        only as tall as their rows need, up to 30% of the sidebar's height;
        and the understanding fills what is left between them, until they are
        resized. While the run has started no subagent, the understanding
        reaches the sidebar's bottom.

    resizingPanels:
        The panels themselves can be resized, as the sidebar can. The edge
        between one panel and the next, where the lower panel's header meets
        the body of the one above, is a handle: dragging it up or down moves
        that edge, the panel above growing as the one below shrinks, or the
        other way, their contents laid out anew at each height as it changes.
        Hovering the handle shows the resize cursor for up and down and a thin
        line along the edge in the theme's accent, which goes once the pointer
        leaves and the drag is over; otherwise no line is drawn there, the
        change of colour still being the edge.

        No panel can be dragged shorter than its header and one row of its
        contents, 32 pixels below its header, nor can one be pushed out of
        the sidebar. Once a panel has been dragged, it keeps its height rather
        than being only as tall as its rows need: the referenced files no
        longer fit their rows or stop at half the sidebar, and scroll once
        their rows are taller than the height they were given. The heights
        they were dragged to are kept while the application runs, the next
        time the sidebar slides out included, as its width is; when the
        sidebar's height changes, as when the window is resized, the
        referenced files and the subagents keep their heights and the
        understanding takes what is left, as far as the smallest heights
        allow. Double-clicking the handle puts
        both panels back as they start, the referenced files fitting their
        rows again.

    look:
        The sidebar's body is on the ribbon's command area colour, #222222 in
        dark mode. Each panel's header is 32 pixels tall, on the darkest
        surface, #111111 in dark mode, as the file tree is, its title in
        small semibold text, 8 pixels from the left, with no count beside it.
        There is no line anywhere in it, not between a header and its body,
        nor between one panel and the next: the change of colour is the edge.
        Each header has, along its bottom, the 1 pixel border in its panel
        body's colour that every panel header has, as the @{SidebarScope}
        says, which is no line, since it is the body's own colour.
        The only line is the one down its left edge, where it meets the
        message list and the chat input, which is the handle it is resized
        by, apart from the line that shows along the edge between two panels
        while it is hovered or dragged, as resizing the panels says. In light mode the
        same steps are taken, as the ribbon's are.

        Neither panel has a permanent scrollbar, since its column would break
        the 8 pixel inset: a panel shows its scrollbar only while its contents
        are taller than it, and none otherwise. When it shows, it is the
        same scrollbar as every other, as the @{ScrollbarScope} says.

        A panel whose contents fit doesn't scroll at all, not even by a
        pixel, at any display scale or window size: it counts as taller than
        its contents need only once they overflow it by a whole pixel or
        more, so what is left over from rounding to the display's pixels
        never counts, and while they fit, it stays scrolled to its top. So
        neither the wheel nor a drag moves rows that all fit, and no
        scrollbar shows for them.

    showing:
        It is only there while a task is running: from the moment a task is
        sent from the Code, Chain, or Spec tab until its run is over. Questions
        from the Ask tab never show it, even when one is sent from the queue.

        When a task starts, it slides out from the right edge of the message
        list and the chat input, growing from nothing to its width, its
        contents sliding into view from behind that edge as it does. When the
        run is over, it slides back the same way. The slide is quick and
        settles without bouncing. It pushes rather than covers: from the
        first frame of the slide to the last, the body's tab bar, the message
        list or open file beneath it, and the chat input end exactly at the
        sidebar's left edge, narrowing as it grows and widening as it
        shrinks, laid out again each frame, as the @{BodyScope} says. Nothing
        runs beneath the sliding sidebar, nothing is clipped by it, and
        nothing jumps to a new width once the slide settles.


export ReferencedFilesPanel
export UnderstandingPanel
export SubagentsPanel

cd /workspace; cat > /tmp/new.pi <<'EOF'
export panel SubagentsPanel:
    title: Subagents and commands
    counted: false
    height: fit
    scrolls: true
    scrollbar: overflowing

    concept: {SubagentsConcept}

concept SubagentsConcept:
    pitch:
        The bottom panel of the @{RightSidebarScope}, beneath the referenced
        files and the understanding: the subagents and background commands
        the harness started for the running task, each shown in the colour of
        the mode that started it, with how long it has been running, so one
        that seems stuck can be seen and stopped.

    shape: {SubagentsShape}

shape SubagentsShape:
    description:
        It lists the background tasks the harness started for the run, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} keeps them: its subagents, the agents it
        started, and its background commands, the shell commands it ran in the
        background, such as a long build. A background task of any other kind
        isn't shown.

        It is shown only once the run has started one, and takes no room
        before. One row per background task, in the order they started,
        subagents and commands together, each 24 pixels tall, 8 pixels in
        from the panel's edges: a spinner while it is at work, then a tick, a
        cross, or a dash for how it ended, done, failed, or stopped, beside a
        small icon for its kind, a robot for a subagent and a terminal for a
        command, in the theme's muted grey, then what it was started to do, in
        small text, cut off with an ellipsis, muted once it has ended. For a
        subagent that is its description, and for a command the command
        itself, on one line, in monospace. Its tooltip gives what it was
        started to do, and beneath, muted, its kind, "Subagent" or "Command",
        and what it is doing or how it ended. The panel is only as tall as its
        rows need, up to 30% of the sidebar's height, scrolling beyond that.

    elapsed:
        At the right of each row, 8 pixels in from the panel's edge, is how
        long it has been running, from when the harness said it started, in
        extra small muted tabular figures, as a task's elapsed time is written
        beside its status: "0:42", "12:05", "1:02:33". While it is at work it
        counts up every second; once it has ended it stops at how long it ran.
        What it was started to do is cut off before the time rather than
        running beneath it.

    stopping:
        A row at work can be stopped, from a Stop button: a small ghost button
        with a stop icon, 18 pixels square, which takes the place of its
        running time while the row is hovered, whose tooltip reads "Stop this
        subagent" or "Stop this command". Clicking it stops only that
        background task, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says: the task the
        run is for and every other background task carry on, and nothing else
        in the panel or the task's output changes. Once clicked, the button
        is disabled and the row's spinner stays until the harness notifies its
        end, when it shows a dash for stopped, as any stopped one does. A row
        that has ended has no Stop button, and neither does one whose run
        can't stop it on its own, as one whose input is already closed, where
        the task's own Cancel button stops everything still going.

    byMode:
        Each background task is shown according to the mode of the task that
        started it, as the @{PromptModesScope} colours modes: its row has a
        bar 2 pixels wide down its left edge in that mode's colour, and its
        spinner and tick are drawn in it too, while a cross or dash keeps its
        own colour. A background task's mode is the mode its task was sent
        in, and for a step of a chain, the step's own: the spec step and a
        spec follow-up are Spec's, and the code step is Code's, never Chain's
        purple. Its tooltip names the mode, "Started by the Code task",
        "Started by the Spec step", and so on. A task whose mode isn't known,
        as one from the history saved before modes were, has no bar and keeps
        its spinner and tick in their own colours, its tooltip reading
        "Started by the task". A Chain task on its own, before its code step
        has been sent, is the chain's spec step, so its background tasks are
        Spec's and labelled "Spec".

        While a chain runs, the panel keeps the background tasks of each of
        its steps, not only the step running: they are grouped by step, in
        the order the steps ran, each group headed by a small label in its
        mode's colour, "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", with the step
        running last. A task that isn't part of a chain has one group, and no
        label. Once the run is over, the sidebar slides back with them all,
        as it says.
EOF
f=spec/ui/components/right-sidebar/subagents/index.pi
head -6 $f > /tmp/h; cat /tmp/h /tmp/new.pi > $f; piton check 2>&1 | tail -15

content.text:
I've changed the spec only. `piton check` reports no problems, and `piton build` wrote 79 files without errors. I confirmed the new sections appear in the refreshed `.claude/reference`.

## What changed in the spec

**1. Subagents panel** (`.claude/reference/ui/components/right-sidebar/subagents/index.md`)
- **Title:** now "Subagents and commands".
- **What it lists (`#description`):** it now shows the run's background shell commands, such as a long build, as well as its subagents. Before, it explicitly left commands out. Subagents and commands share one list in the order they started.
- **Row layout:** each row has the spinner or end icon as before, then a small muted icon for its kind (a robot for a subagent, a terminal for a command), then what it was started to do. That is the description for a subagent, or the command itself in monospace on one line. The tooltip now names the kind, "Subagent" or "Command".
- **`#elapsed` (new):** at the right of each row is how long it has been running, counted from when the harness said it started. It uses the same format as the task time below and counts up every second. Once the row ends it stays at how long it ran, and the row's text is cut off before the time.
- **`#stopping` (new):** hovering a running row swaps its time for an 18px ghost Stop button with a stop icon. The tooltip reads "Stop this subagent" or "Stop this command".
  - Clicking it stops only that one. The main task and everything else keep going.
  - The button then turns disabled, and the spinner stays until the harness reports that it ended. The row then shows the dash for stopped.
  - There's no Stop button on rows that have ended, or when the run can no longer stop one on its own (its input is already closed). In that case the task's own Cancel button is the way to stop it.
- **`#by-mode`:** the existing mode colour bar and chain-step grouping are unchanged, and now cover commands too.

**2. Running background tasks** (`.claude/reference/scope/harness-integration/index.md#feeding`, new paragraph)
- **Kind:** each background task is a subagent (started by an Agent or Task tool call) or a command (a shell command run in the background). Its kind comes from what started it.
- **Start time:** recorded when the harness says it started.
- **Stopping one:** the harness is asked on the run's input to stop that task by its id. For Claude Code, that is its stream-json control request for stopping a task. The task then ends, as stopped, when the harness reports it, and the run carries on.
- **Never by killing the process:** stopping one task must not end the harness's process. A run whose input is closed, or whose harness can't take more input (Codex, OpenCode), can't stop a single task.

**3. How long the current task has run** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#elapsed`, under Status)
- **Where:** beside every task's status label, both in the latest task's header and in each previous task's heading. That includes a task running in the other lane.
- **What it counts:** time since the task was sent, building and compiling included. It uses small muted tabular figures, "0:42", "12:05", or "1:02:33" once past an hour.
- **When it stops:** it counts up every second while the task is under way, and stops at the total once the task is over.
- **History:** tasks from the history whose record has no start and end show no time. So the code should save each task's start and end times in its record.

**4. Right sidebar** (`.claude/reference/ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#description`): its wording now says the bottom panel holds subagents and background commands.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `SubagentsPanel`: `#description`, `#elapsed`, `#stopping`, `#by-mode`
- `HarnessIntegrationScope`: `#feeding`
- `MessageList`: `#status` / `#elapsed`
- `RightSidebarScope`: `#description`

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791107396-MonitorAndStopStuckAgents.understanding.md`.

The Claude Docs, Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Drive connectors need authorizing in your claude.ai connector settings before they can be used. None of them were needed here.

Claude Code's result reports `modelUsage` and `total_cost_usd` as running totals for the whole conversation, not for the run. A run that carries on a conversation includes every run before it in that conversation. Right now we add them up per run, so a project that cost about $2,000 at API prices shows as about $18,000. A run's own figures are how much its conversation's totals rose since that conversation's previous run. If the totals went down instead, the conversation started over, and the run counts in full.

The "This project" group should cover every run saved in the project's history and asks, not only those since it was opened, and keep updating as new runs report. Cost should be worked out from the tokens at each model's published API prices: input, output, cache read, and cache writes at the 5-minute or 1-hour rate, using the split the harness reports. Show the total, and how much of it was input, output, cache reads and cache writes, since caching is most of it. A model whose prices aren't known gets no cost, never a guess. Say that this is what the tokens would cost at API prices, not what a subscription charges.

<Ctrl+N> while in the chat input does just what pressing New conversation does, for the selected tab, and nothing while the button is disabled. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
Its tooltip says which conversation it resets, with its shortcut: "Start a new conversation for spec tasks (Ctrl+N)", "Start a new conversation for code tasks (Ctrl+N)", "Start a new conversation for spec and code tasks (Ctrl+N)", or "Start a new conversation for questions (Ctrl+N)", adding, while a run in it is under way, that the run finishes in the conversation left. It is disabled only while that conversation has nothing to carry on and no run in it is under way, its tooltip then saying the next task, or question, already starts a new conversation.
Both sit on the bar's bottom line, which runs beneath them as it does beneath the help text, and neither is cut off: the help text gives way to them when the bar is narrow.

##### Usage

Just right of the context figure, before New conversation, sits the agent's usage: how much of the harness picked, of the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope), has been used, as Claude Code's /usage shows it. Its summary is short and extra small, muted like the context figure: "Usage", then the share used of the plan limit nearest to running out, such as "Usage 42%", turning the theme's warning colour from 80% and its error colour once the limit is reached. When the harness reports no plan limits, the summary is the cost of this project's runs since it was opened, such as "Usage $1.24", or the tokens they used, as the context figure is written, when it reports no cost either. Until anything has been reported, it reads "Usage", with nothing after it.
Clicking the summary opens a popover above it with all the details, each group headed, and each figure labelled:
- Plan limits: each limit the harness reports, such as the current
  session's and the week's, with the share used as a bar and a
  percentage, and when it resets.
- Conversation: the context the selected tab's conversation holds,
  and its input, output, cache-read, and cache-written tokens, and
  its cost.
- This project: the same totals for every run in the project since
  it was opened, tasks and questions, and how many runs there were.
- The harness and model the figures came from, and when they were
  last reported.
A group, or a figure, the harness doesn't report is left out rather than shown as zero, and when nothing has been reported the popover says so. The figures come from what the harness reports as its runs go, never from running anything of its own to ask, and update in place while the popover is open, following each reply. Clicking outside the popover, or pressing Escape, closes it. The summary's tooltip says to click for the details. Like the context figure, it is never cut off: the help text gives way to it.

##### Slice

Just left of the context figure sits the Slice toggle: a small ghost button with a scissors icon, reading "Slice", which shows as selected while it is on. It starts off. Its tooltip says what the prompt is sent as: while off, the prompt written as a spec, its references linking to the spec they name; while on, the prompt with the `piton slice` of each spec it references. Clicking it turns it on or off, and it applies to every tab, Ask included. It stays as it is across sends, tab switches, and project switches, as the prompt being written does, and the help text gives way to it as it does to the session controls.

##### Colour

The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are not tinted: they stay the flat surface the description gives, whatever the mode, the mode showing in the tab labels' colours and the send button's. The send button's colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes, straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap around, so pressing <Ctrl+Tab> on Freeform fades grey straight to Code's red, and <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Freeform's grey; neither lights up Chain, Spec, or Ask on the way. A fade to or from Freeform's grey keeps the other tab's hue, only draining or filling its colour, so it never passes through another hue. Between Code and Spec it passes through Chain's colour, whatever colours they have been given in the theme editor.
The send button, both its halves, is a muted slate: the selected mode's colour, purple with Chain selected, mixed well down into the theme's base surface, so it reads as a quiet hint of the mode, about #3b4252 for Spec's blue in dark mode, standing apart from Queue and Preview without shouting. Its label and chevron are in the theme's text colour for a solid hue, and the line between its halves is only faintly darker or lighter than it, half as far as its hover, just enough to part them. Disabled, the button fades as a disabled button does, in the same colour, and the line fades with the half it borders, never staying solid across a faded button.

<Ctrl+N> while in the chat input does just what pressing New conversation does, for the selected tab, and nothing while the button is disabled. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
Its tooltip says which conversation it resets, with its shortcut: "Start a new conversation for spec tasks (Ctrl+N)", "Start a new conversation for code tasks (Ctrl+N)", "Start a new conversation for spec and code tasks (Ctrl+N)", or "Start a new conversation for questions (Ctrl+N)", adding, while a run in it is under way, that the run finishes in the conversation left. It is disabled only while that conversation has nothing to carry on and no run in it is under way, its tooltip then saying the next task, or question, already starts a new conversation.
Both sit on the bar's bottom line, which runs beneath them as it does beneath the help text, and neither is cut off: the help text gives way to them when the bar is narrow.

##### Usage

Just right of the context figure, before New conversation, sits the agent's usage: how much of the harness picked, of the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope), has been used, as Claude Code's /usage shows it. Its summary is short and extra small, muted like the context figure: "Usage", then the share used of the plan limit nearest to running out, such as "Usage 42%", turning the theme's warning colour from 80% and its error colour once the limit is reached. When the harness reports no plan limits, the summary is the cost of this project's runs since it was opened, such as "Usage $1.24", or the tokens they used, as the context figure is written, when it reports no cost either. Until anything has been reported, it reads "Usage", with nothing after it.
Clicking the summary opens a popover above it with all the details, each group headed, and each figure labelled:
- Plan limits: each limit the harness reports, such as the current
  session's and the week's, with the share used as a bar and a
  percentage, and when it resets.
- Conversation: the context the selected tab's conversation holds,
  and its input, output, cache-read, and cache-written tokens, and
  its cost.
- This project: the same totals for every run in the project since
  it was opened, tasks and questions, and how many runs there were.
- The harness and model the figures came from, and when they were
  last reported.
A group, or a figure, the harness doesn't report is left out rather than shown as zero, and when nothing has been reported the popover says so. The figures come from what the harness reports as its runs go, never from running anything of its own to ask, and update in place while the popover is open, following each reply. Clicking outside the popover, or pressing Escape, closes it. The summary's tooltip says to click for the details. Like the context figure, it is never cut off: the help text gives way to it.

##### Slice

Just left of the context figure sits the Slice toggle: a small ghost button with a scissors icon, reading "Slice", which shows as selected while it is on. It starts off. Its tooltip says what the prompt is sent as: while off, the prompt written as a spec, its references linking to the spec they name; while on, the prompt with the `piton slice` of each spec it references. Clicking it turns it on or off, and it applies to every tab, Ask included. It stays as it is across sends, tab switches, and project switches, as the prompt being written does, and the help text gives way to it as it does to the session controls.

##### Colour

The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are not tinted: they stay the flat surface the description gives, whatever the mode, the mode showing in the tab labels' colours and the send button's. The send button's colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes, straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap around, so pressing <Ctrl+Tab> on Freeform fades grey straight to Code's red, and <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Freeform's grey; neither lights up Chain, Spec, or Ask on the way. A fade to or from Freeform's grey keeps the other tab's hue, only draining or filling its colour, so it never passes through another hue. Between Code and Spec it passes through Chain's colour, whatever colours they have been given in the theme editor.
The send button, both its halves, is a muted slate: the selected mode's colour, purple with Chain selected, mixed well down into the theme's base surface, so it reads as a quiet hint of the mode, about #3b4252 for Spec's blue in dark mode, standing apart from Queue and Preview without shouting. Its label and chevron are in the theme's text colour for a solid hue, and the line between its halves is only faintly darker or lighter than it, half as far as its hover, just enough to part them. Disabled, the button fades as a disabled button does, in the same colour, and the line fades with the half it borders, never staying solid across a faded button.

content.content:
#### Contents

- `history/`: every task sent, as its hidden anchor's source, named by the second it was sent and the anchor's name, and beside it, once its run is over, a `.json` record of the same name holding the compiled userPrompt the harness received, the system prompt as it received it and the harness it went to, whether it has been marked done by hand for sending to the other mode, each line the harness printed, each message sent to the task while it ran, in its place among those lines, any error, and, in a git repository, the hashes of the two snapshots of the working tree taken as it started and ended, as the task snapshots below say
- `snapshot-index`: in a git repository, the private index the task snapshots are built with, as they say
- `images/`: every image attached to a task or question, saved when it is sent or queued, named by the second it was saved and a short hash of its content, with its own extension, so the same image attached twice is saved once
- `asks/`: every question asked from the Ask tab, saved the same way as a task but apart from them
- `queue/`: each queued prompt, as its hidden anchor's source, imports included, named so they list in the order they were queued, marked when each was queued rather than when it was saved, so prompts queued one straight after another keep their order however long each takes to save
- `divergence/`: each divergence report, a JSON file named by when it was made
- `system-prompts/`: each mode's system prompt template, a Markdown file named after its mode, code.md, combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md, and the spec-reading prompt injected into them, spec-reading.md
- `commit-notes.json`: the Git panel's commit notes
- `run.json`: the project's run targets, as the [RunTargetsScope](../run-targets/index.md#run-targets-scope) says
- `harness.json`: the last report the harness gave of the skills and agents it has
- `fluency.md`: the project's Piton fluency, as `piton agent --print-fluency` printed it at the last spec build, generated rather than edited, for the Spec and Chain prompts to point at, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says
- `conversations.json`: which conversation of each lane's tasks, the spec lane's and the code lane's, and of the questions, was last left for a new one, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, so it isn't carried on again once the project is reopened
- `sessions/`: the harness's sessions for each conversation run in a container, a folder per conversation, `spec` for the spec lane's and `questions` for the questions', each mounted into that conversation's runs only, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says, so a conversation carries on across runs, restarts, and moves of the project
- `Containerfile`: written by hand, when the project has one, built FROM the application's default image to add what the project's runs need, such as its toolchains, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says

            stand. Claude Code's result reports its `modelUsage` and
            `total_cost_usd` as running totals for the whole conversation, so a
            run that carries on a conversation includes every run before it in
            that conversation. A run's own figures are how much its
            conversation's totals rose since that conversation's previous run,

            saved in the history or have just reported, so every run is counted
            once and no run's figures are counted again in a later one's.

            and every question in its asks, not only those since it was

I rewrote the Usage section of the chat input spec to cover all three problems. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 79 files, and the new text appears in `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#usage`.

## What changed in the spec

All edits are in `spec/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.pi`, in the `usage` section.

**Per-run figures (the overcount)**
- Claude Code's `modelUsage` and `total_cost_usd` are now described as running totals for the whole conversation.
- A run's own figures are how much its conversation's totals rose since that conversation's previous run, each model counted separately.
- If any total went down, the conversation started over and the run counts in full. The first run of a conversation also counts in full.
- **One addition you didn't ask for:** a question asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation. Its rise is measured from the run it copied, so the copied history isn't counted twice.
- Runs are taken in the order they were sent, whether from the saved history or just reported, so each run counts exactly once.

**"This project" group**
- It covers every task in the history (each chain step as its own run) and every question saved in asks, not only runs since the project was opened.
- It is worked out from the harness lines each saved record already keeps.
- It keeps updating as new runs report. A run still going isn't counted yet.
- It is split into Tasks and Questions, each showing a run count and, muted, how many reported no usage, such as "42 runs · 3 without usage". The second part is left out when it's zero.
- Under them, each model the runs used gets its input, output, cache-read and cache-written tokens, tasks and questions together.

**Cost at API prices**
- Cost is worked out from the tokens at each model's published per-million prices, kept in the app. That covers input, output, cache reads, and cache writes at the 5-minute or 1-hour rate, using the split the harness reports.
- Harness-reported cost such as `total_cost_usd` is never used.
- A model whose prices aren't known gets no cost. It is marked "Price unknown", and the totals that leave it out say so.
- The total is shown with its breakdown into input, output, cache reads and cache writes, each in dollars and as a share of the total.
- A muted note says this is what the tokens would cost at API prices, not what a subscription charges.
- The summary's "Usage $…" and the Conversation group's cost now use the same calculation.

**Two choices I made that you didn't specify**
- **Cache writes without a split:** if the harness doesn't report a 5-minute/1-hour split, those writes are priced at the 5-minute rate.
- **Model matching:** models are matched to prices by id, ignoring any date or context-size suffix.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791114404-CalculateProjectLifetimeTokenCosts2.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ChatInputScope` → `#usage` in `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md`, for all of the above.
- `ProjectDataScope` → `#contents`: the task history and asks records the project totals are rebuilt from.
- `HarnessIntegrationScope` → `#context`: conversations per lane and for questions, and copies of conversations, which decide each run's "previous run".

content.content:
# Mode System Prompts Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The system prompt each mode sends, which tells the harness what kind of work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

### Shape

#### Description

What a prompt tells the harness besides itself comes in two parts. The system template is the conversation's system prompt: the same for every prompt of a conversation, whatever its mode, so the harness's prompt cache holds when the mode changes. Each lane's tasks, and the questions, carry on a conversation of their own, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, and each fills the system template in for what its runs can see, so it stays the same within each. Each of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) but Freeform has instructions of its own, which change from one prompt to the next, and so go in the prompt's own message, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head. A prompt's hidden anchor has a systemPrompt property, alongside its userPrompt, holding its mode's instructions.

#### Templates

The system template, each mode's instructions, and the injected prompts are Piton prose, like the prompt they are sent with, so they can reference the spec, with these placeholders, each written after a dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation:

- CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION, the code location and the spec location, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../../project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) says
- HARNESS_DIRECTORY, the directory of the harness in use
- SPEC_READING, the spec-reading prompt, injected where it is written
- PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, the path of the fluency file, from the project directory, as the pitonFluency below says
- UNDERSTANDING_FILE, the path of the task's understanding file

SPEC_READING is filled in first, so the placeholders it holds are filled in too; then the others, before the prompt is compiled, but UNDERSTANDING_FILE, which is filled in as the prompt is sent, once the task's history record is named, so a prompt sent from the queue is given its own. A question from the Ask tab has no understanding file, and UNDERSTANDING_FILE is filled in with nothing. Each can be moved or removed, like any other text of a template.
Every path a placeholder is filled in with points where the run that is sent it finds that file, whether it runs on the host or in a container, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says. So each is written relative to the project directory, the directory every run works in, the project directory itself on the host and `/workspace` in a container: CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION as `./` and the location's path, as `./spec`, HARNESS_DIRECTORY as the harness's directory, as `.claude`, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE and UNDERSTANDING_FILE as their paths, as `.suspense/fluency.md`. None is ever filled in with an absolute path: not the project's path on the host, which a run in a container can't reach, and not `/workspace`, which a run on the host has no such directory for.
A run fills CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION in only with what it can see, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says. A run of the spec lane, a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step, can't see the code location, and fills CODE_LOCATION in with nothing, its instructions and system template alike. A question can see the code location and the spec location, both read only, and fills both in. A run of the code lane, a Code task, a Chain prompt's code step, or a Freeform task, runs on the host and fills both in, as ever.
A paragraph that held nothing but a placeholder filled in with nothing goes with it. A paragraph holding CODE_LOCATION or SPEC_LOCATION filled in with nothing goes too, whatever else it says, so no prompt names, or tells the harness to keep off, a location its run can't see. A paragraph holding PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, filled in with nothing, goes too, whatever else it says, so a sentence pointing at a fluency file there is none of is never sent. A template left with nothing but blank space once filled in gives nothing at all.
HARNESS_DIRECTORY is the directory the harness that runs the prompt, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, reads its agentic Markdown and reference files from, written without a leading ./: .claude for Claude Code, .opencode for OpenCode, and .codex for Codex, the directories the [NewProjectScope](../../new-project/index.md#new-project-scope) names for them.

#### Reading The Spec

In every mode, the harness learns what the spec says from its compiled reference, the Markdown the spec build writes under HARNESS_DIRECTORY's reference folder, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with the adapter of the harness in use. It never reads the Piton source under the spec location to learn what the spec says. To a run that can see the spec location, the system template and the spec-reading prompt say so, and name the spec location only as where edits to the spec go. A question sees the spec location too, read only, so it can run `piton slice` there, and is told the same: that the spec is read from the compiled reference or from what `piton slice` prints, never from the Piton source. A question makes no edits, so the Ask instructions name the spec location for what it is, the spec's Piton source, that `piton slice` reads, which a question never changes, and nothing told to a question says or suggests that it may edit the spec. A run that can't see the spec location is told only that the spec is read from the compiled reference, with nothing about the spec source.

#### Writing The Spec

Only Spec, and a Chain prompt's first step, which writes the spec, work on the Piton source. Their instructions say to open a .pi file only to change it, since a harness may need a file read before it can edit it, and, once the edits are made, to run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference rather than by reading the source again.

#### Piton Fluency

The Piton fluency, what `piton agent --print-fluency` prints, run in the project directory, is how Piton is written. It is never part of the system prompt: only work that writes Piton is pointed at it.
It is written to the fluency file, `.suspense/fluency.md` in the project's data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, each time the application runs a spec build in the project, as the [SpecBuildScope](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, so it keeps in step with the project's piton and its FLUENCY_PROMPT.md. A Spec or Chain prompt sent before the file has ever been written has it written before the prompt is compiled. What it prints is written as text, never read as Piton, but for the project directory's absolute path on the host wherever it appears in it, which is written as `.` instead, a path within it as relative to it, as `./spec`, so the file holds no path a run in a container can't reach.

## Concept

### Pitch

The prompts the application gives the harness for its own work, rather than a prompt someone writes, written in Piton and built into the application.

### Shape

#### Description

- commit-message.pi, for writing a commit message
- file-search.pi, for the palette's search for a file by description
- prompt-title.pi, for titling a task or question so its hidden anchor can be named after it

content.content:
##### Spec

A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can run `piton build` itself; the project's `.piton` directory, which holds the build's manifest of the files it owns, read and write, for the same reason, bound in from the project itself, never an empty, temporary, or copied one, so the manifest a build in the container starts from is the host's, and what it writes there is the host's next build's, the application creating the directory in the project first where it isn't there; the fluency file, read only; piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file, read and write. Never the code location: in its place, an empty scratch directory, writable, that nothing else sees and that goes with the container, so `piton build` finds the code location it places the shape's guidance in.

##### Question

A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the spec location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read only, so it can run `piton slice` in its container. Nothing is writable but the harness's own volume and the questions' sessions folder. Where one of the code location and the spec location holds the other, both are still mounted, read only, and neither is hidden from the question by the other.

Each run is also given its own conversation's sessions folder, read and write, as Volumes says, and nothing of any other conversation's.
Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it, unless the run is given the one held as well, as a question is given both the code location and the spec location.
A task's understanding file is mounted on its own, never the history folder it is in, so a run sees no other task's record. Since a file has to be there to be mounted, the application writes it empty just before the run, and an empty understanding file is shown as one not written yet is.

39	    templates:
40	        The system template, each mode's instructions, and the injected
41	        prompts are Piton prose, like the prompt they are sent with, so they
42	        can reference the spec, with these placeholders, each written after a
43	        dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation:
44	
45	        - CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION, the code location and the spec location, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} says
46	        - HARNESS_DIRECTORY, the directory of the harness in use
47	        - SPEC_READING, the spec-reading prompt, injected where it is written
48	        - PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, the path of the fluency file, from the project directory, as the pitonFluency below says
49	        - UNDERSTANDING_FILE, the path of the task's understanding file
50	
51	        SPEC_READING is filled in first, so the placeholders it holds are
52	        filled in too; then the others, before the prompt is compiled, but
53	        UNDERSTANDING_FILE, which is filled in as the prompt is sent, once the
54	        task's history record is named, so a prompt sent from the queue is
55	        given its own. A question from the Ask tab has no understanding file,
56	        and UNDERSTANDING_FILE is filled in with nothing. Each can be moved or
57	        removed, like any other text of a template.
58	
59	        Every path a placeholder is filled in with points where the run that
60	        is sent it finds that file, whether it runs on the host or in a
61	        container, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. So each is
62	        written relative to the project directory, the directory every run
63	        works in, the project directory itself on the host and `/workspace`
64	        in a container: CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION as `./` and the
65	        location's path, as `./spec`, HARNESS_DIRECTORY as the harness's
66	        directory, as `.claude`, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE and
67	        UNDERSTANDING_FILE as their paths, as
68	        `.suspense/fluency.md`. None is ever filled in with an absolute path:
69	        not the project's path on the host, which a run in a container can't
70	        reach, and not `/workspace`, which a run on the host has no such
71	        directory for.
72	
73	        A run fills CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION in only with what it can
74	        see, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. A run of the spec
75	        lane, a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step, can't see the code
76	        location, and fills CODE_LOCATION in with nothing, its instructions and
77	        system template alike. A question can see the code location and the
78	        spec location, both read only, and fills both in. A run of the code
79	        lane, a Code task, a Chain prompt's code step, or a Freeform task,
80	        runs on the host and fills both in, as ever.
81	
82	        A paragraph that held nothing but a placeholder filled in with
83	        nothing goes with it. A paragraph holding CODE_LOCATION or
84	        SPEC_LOCATION filled in with nothing goes too, whatever else it says,
85	        so no prompt names, or tells the harness to keep off, a location its
86	        run can't see. A paragraph holding PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, filled
87	        in with nothing, goes too, whatever else it says, so a sentence
88	        pointing at a fluency file there is none of is never sent. A template
89	        left with nothing but blank space once filled in gives nothing at
90	        all.
91	
92	        HARNESS_DIRECTORY is the directory the harness that runs the prompt,
93	        as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, reads its agentic Markdown and
94	        reference files from, written without a leading ./: .claude for
95	        Claude Code, .opencode for OpenCode, and .codex for Codex, the
96	        directories the @{NewProjectScope} names for them.
97	
98	    readingTheSpec:
99	        In every mode, the harness learns what the spec says from its
100	        compiled reference, the Markdown the spec build writes under
101	        HARNESS_DIRECTORY's reference folder, where inheritance, expressions,
102	        and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what
103	        `piton slice` prints for it with the adapter of the harness in use.
104	        It never reads the Piton source under the spec location to learn what
105	        the spec says. To a run that can see the spec location, the system
106	        template and the spec-reading prompt say so, and name the spec
107	        location only as where edits to the spec go. A question sees the spec
108	        location too, read only, so it can run `piton slice` there, and is
109	        told the same: that the spec is read from the compiled reference or
110	        from what `piton slice` prints, never from the Piton source. A
111	        question makes no edits, so the Ask instructions name the spec
112	        location for what it is, the spec's Piton source, that `piton slice`
113	        reads, which a question never changes, and nothing told to a question
114	        says or suggests that it may edit the spec. A run that can't see the
115	        spec location is told only that the spec is read from the compiled
116	        reference, with nothing about the spec source.
117	
118	    writingTheSpec:
119	        Only Spec, and a Chain prompt's first step, which writes the spec,
120	        work on the Piton source. Their instructions say to open a .pi file
121	        only to change it, since a harness may need a file read before it can
122	        edit it, and, once the edits are made, to run `piton build` and check
123	        the result in the refreshed reference rather than by reading the
124	        source again.
125	
126	    pitonFluency:
127	        The Piton fluency, what `piton agent --print-fluency` prints, run in
128	        the project directory, is how Piton is written. It is never part of
129	        the system prompt: only work that writes Piton is pointed at it.
130	
131	        It is written to the fluency file, `.suspense/fluency.md` in the
132	        project's data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, each time the
133	        application runs a spec build in the project, as the @{SpecBuildScope}
134	        says, so it keeps in step with the project's piton and its
135	        FLUENCY_PROMPT.md. A Spec or Chain prompt sent before the file has
136	        ever been written has it written before the prompt is compiled. What
137	        it prints is written as text, never read as Piton, but for the
138	        project directory's absolute path on the host wherever it appears in
139	        it, which is written as `.` instead, a path within it as relative to
140	        it, as `./spec`, so the file holds no path a run in a container
141	        can't reach.
142	
143	        PITON_FLUENCY_FILE stands for the file's path. The Spec instructions
144	        and the Chain instructions, for a Chain prompt's first step, say, on a
145	        paragraph of their own, to read that file once in the conversation
146	        before creating or editing any .pi file. A Code task sent to Spec
147	        is pointed at it through the Spec instructions, as any Spec prompt is.
148	        The Code and Ask instructions, and the spec-to-code prompt given to a
149	        Chain prompt's code step, never mention it.
150	
151	        Where `piton` isn't installed, or printing the fluency fails, no file
152	        is written, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE is filled in with nothing, so the
153	        paragraph pointing at it is left out.
154	
155	    specReading:
156	        The spec-reading prompt explains how to read the spec before executing
157	        anything, as the readingTheSpec above says: from the compiled
158	        reference, reference links in the prompt being the spec for what they
159	        name, each read before anything it covers is changed. It is injected
160	        into the system template wherever SPEC_READING is written, and may
161	        itself use every placeholder but SPEC_READING, which in it is left as
162	        written. One left with nothing but blank space leaves SPEC_READING
163	        filled in with nothing. Like the templates, each project has its own,
164	        saved with its data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, in
165	        spec-reading.md beside them, and edited in the
166	        @{SettingsWindowScope}; with no file yet the project uses its default.
167	
168	    codeToSpec:
169	        The code-to-spec prompt is given to a Code task sent to Spec, as the
170	        @{PromptSendingScope} says, after the Spec instructions. It may use
171	        every placeholder the instructions may, filled in the same way, and
172	        two of its own: CODE_PROMPT, filled in with the code task's prompt as
173	        it was typed, and CODE_RESULT, with the code task's final output, or
174	        with a line saying the code task left none. What fills them in is
175	        taken as text, never read as Piton. Like the spec-reading prompt, each
176	        project has its own, saved with its data in code-to-spec.md beside the
177	        templates, and edited in the @{SettingsWindowScope}; with no file yet
178	        the project uses its default.
179	
180	        The spec-to-code prompt is given in the same way to the code step a
181	        Chain prompt hands on to, after the Code instructions, with
182	        SPEC_PROMPT and SPEC_RESULT, the Chain prompt as it was typed and its
183	        spec step's final output, saved in spec-to-code.md.
184	
185	    saving:
186	        Each project has its own system template, instructions, and injected
187	        prompts, saved with its data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, a
188	        Markdown file each, system.md for the system template, code.md,
189	        combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md for the modes, and edited
190	        in the @{SettingsWindowScope}. One with no file yet gives its default.
191	
192	    understandingFile:
193	        Each Code, Chain, or Spec task has an understanding file: the short
194	        list of constraints the harness has taken from the spec for it, which
195	        the @{RightSidebarScope} shows as it changes. It is saved
196	        beside the task's history record, with the same name and the
197	        extension `.understanding.md`, written by the harness itself. Nothing
198	        else writes it, and nothing is there until the harness writes it. Each
199	        constraint links to the compiled reference file it comes from, never
200	        to the spec's source.
201	
202	    defaults:
203	        The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own
204	        repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a
205	        project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are
206	        baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships
207	        with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults
208	        the next build has. A build can't be made without them.

        The system template, each mode's instructions, and the injected
        prompts are Piton prose, like the prompt they are sent with, so they
        can reference the spec, with these placeholders, each written after a
        dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation:

        - CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION, the code location and the spec location, as the @{ProjectLocationsScope} says
        - HARNESS_DIRECTORY, the directory of the harness in use
        - SPEC_READING, the spec-reading prompt, injected where it is written
        - PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, the path of the fluency file, from the project directory, as the pitonFluency below says
        - UNDERSTANDING_FILE, the path of the task's understanding file

        SPEC_READING is filled in first, so the placeholders it holds are
        filled in too; then the others, before the prompt is compiled, but
        UNDERSTANDING_FILE, which is filled in as the prompt is sent, once the
        task's history record is named, so a prompt sent from the queue is
        given its own. A question from the Ask tab has no understanding file,
        and UNDERSTANDING_FILE is filled in with nothing. Each can be moved or
        removed, like any other text of a template.

        Every path a placeholder is filled in with points where the run that
        is sent it finds that file, whether it runs on the host or in a
        container, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. So each is
        written relative to the project directory, the directory every run
        works in, the project directory itself on the host and `/workspace`
        in a container: CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION as `./` and the
        location's path, as `./spec`, HARNESS_DIRECTORY as the harness's
        directory, as `.claude`, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE and
        UNDERSTANDING_FILE as their paths, as
        `.suspense/fluency.md`. None is ever filled in with an absolute path:
        not the project's path on the host, which a run in a container can't
        reach, and not `/workspace`, which a run on the host has no such
        directory for.

        A run fills CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION in only with what it can
        see, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says. A run of the spec
        lane, a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step, can't see the code
        location, and fills CODE_LOCATION in with nothing, its instructions and
        system template alike. A question can see the code location and the
        spec location, both read only, and fills both in. A run of the code
        lane, a Code task, a Chain prompt's code step, or a Freeform task,
        runs on the host and fills both in, as ever.

        A paragraph that held nothing but a placeholder filled in with
        nothing goes with it. A paragraph holding CODE_LOCATION or

        run can't see. A paragraph holding PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, filled
        in with nothing, goes too, whatever else it says, so a sentence
        pointing at a fluency file there is none of is never sent. A template
        left with nothing but blank space once filled in gives nothing at
        all.
