        as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, reads its agentic Markdown and
        reference files from, written without a leading ./: .claude for
        Claude Code, .opencode for OpenCode, and .codex for Codex, the
        directories the @{NewProjectScope} names for them.

    readingTheSpec:
        In every mode, the harness learns what the spec says from its
        compiled reference, the Markdown the spec build writes under
        HARNESS_DIRECTORY's reference folder, where inheritance, expressions,
        and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what
        `piton slice` prints for it with the adapter of the harness in use.
        It never reads the Piton source under the spec location to learn what
        the spec says. To a run that can see the spec location, the system
        template and the spec-reading prompt say so, and name the spec
        location only as where edits to the spec go. A question sees the spec
        location too, read only, so it can run `piton slice` there, and is
        told the same: that the spec is read from the compiled reference or
        from what `piton slice` prints, never from the Piton source. A
        question makes no edits, so the Ask instructions name the spec
        location for what it is, the spec's Piton source, that `piton slice`
        reads, which a question never changes, and nothing told to a question
        says or suggests that it may edit the spec. A run that can't see the
        spec location is told only that the spec is read from the compiled
        reference, with nothing about the spec source.

    writingTheSpec:
        Only Spec, and a Chain prompt's first step, which writes the spec,
        work on the Piton source. Their instructions say to open a .pi file
        only to change it, since a harness may need a file read before it can
        edit it, and, once the edits are made, to run `piton build` and check
        the result in the refreshed reference rather than by reading the
        source again.

    pitonFluency:
        The Piton fluency, what `piton agent --print-fluency` prints, run in
        the project directory, is how Piton is written. It is never part of
        the system prompt: only work that writes Piton is pointed at it.

        It is written to the fluency file, `.suspense/fluency.md` in the
        project's data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, each time the
        application runs a spec build in the project, as the @{SpecBuildScope}
        says, so it keeps in step with the project's piton and its
        FLUENCY_PROMPT.md. A Spec or Chain prompt sent before the file has
        ever been written has it written before the prompt is compiled. What
        it prints is written as text, never read as Piton, but for the
        project directory's absolute path on the host wherever it appears in
        it, which is written as `.` instead, a path within it as relative to
        it, as `./spec`, so the file holds no path a run in a container
        can't reach.

        PITON_FLUENCY_FILE stands for the file's path. The Spec instructions
        and the Chain instructions, for a Chain prompt's first step, say, on a
        paragraph of their own, to read that file once in the conversation
        before creating or editing any .pi file. A Code task sent to Spec
        is pointed at it through the Spec instructions, as any Spec prompt is.
        The Code and Ask instructions, and the spec-to-code prompt given to a
        Chain prompt's code step, never mention it.

        is written, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE is filled in with nothing, so the
        paragraph pointing at it is left out.

        anything, as the readingTheSpec above says: from the compiled
        reference, reference links in the prompt being the spec for what they
        name, each read before anything it covers is changed. It is injected
        into the system template wherever SPEC_READING is written, and may
        itself use every placeholder but SPEC_READING, which in it is left as
        written. One left with nothing but blank space leaves SPEC_READING
        filled in with nothing. Like the templates, each project has its own,
        saved with its data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, in
        spec-reading.md beside them, and edited in the
        @{SettingsWindowScope}; with no file yet the project uses its default.

    codeToSpec:

        @{PromptSendingScope} says, after the Spec instructions. It may use
        every placeholder the instructions may, filled in the same way, and
        two of its own: CODE_PROMPT, filled in with the code task's prompt as
        it was typed, and CODE_RESULT, with the code task's final output, or
        with a line saying the code task left none. What fills them in is
        taken as text, never read as Piton. Like the spec-reading prompt, each
        project has its own, saved with its data in code-to-spec.md beside the
        templates, and edited in the @{SettingsWindowScope}; with no file yet
        the project uses its default.

        The spec-to-code prompt is given in the same way to the code step a
        Chain prompt hands on to, after the Code instructions, with
        SPEC_PROMPT and SPEC_RESULT, the Chain prompt as it was typed and its
        spec step's final output, saved in spec-to-code.md.

        Each project has its own system template, instructions, and injected
        prompts, saved with its data, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, a
        Markdown file each, system.md for the system template, code.md,
        combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md for the modes, and edited
        in the @{SettingsWindowScope}. One with no file yet gives its default.

    understandingFile:
        Each Code, Chain, or Spec task has an understanding file: the short
        list of constraints the harness has taken from the spec for it, which
        the @{RightSidebarScope} shows as it changes. It is saved
        beside the task's history record, with the same name and the
        extension `.understanding.md`, written by the harness itself. Nothing
        else writes it, and nothing is there until the harness writes it. Each
        constraint links to the compiled reference file it comes from, never
        to the spec's source.

    defaults:
        The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own
        repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a
        project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are
        baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships
        with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults
        the next build has. A build can't be made without them.

        The system template's default says what the project is, where its
        code is and where its spec is, each on a paragraph of its own, so the
        one a run can't see goes, that each prompt starts with a
        <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it
        may change, and then SPEC_READING on a paragraph of its own. It holds
        no fluency.

        The spec-reading prompt's default says:

        \\
        Read the spec from its compiled reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

        Never read the .pi source under ${SPEC_LOCATION} to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

        Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.
        \\

        The Spec and Chain defaults have, after what the mode is for, on a
        paragraph of its own:

        \\
        Before creating or editing any .pi file, read ${PITON_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.
        \\

        and then, on another:

        \\
        Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, not by reading the source again. Never finish with a spec that `piton check` or `piton build` reports errors in.
        \\

        The Code, Chain, and Spec defaults then end with, on a paragraph of
        its own:

        \\
        Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.
        \\

        The Ask default says what a question is for, and that it changes
        nothing, and, on a paragraph of its own, that SPEC_LOCATION is the

### Shape

#### Description

There are five modes, and wherever they are listed, they are in this order.

#### Modes

- Code: changes the code, leaving the spec as it is; a subtle red
- Chain: changes the code and the spec together; purple
- Spec: changes the spec, leaving the code as it is; a subtle blue
- Ask: asks a question about the code and the spec, changing neither; a subtle green
- Freeform: passes the prompt to the agent just as it is written; grey, the theme's tertiary text colour

#### Colours

Whatever shows a mode, or something sent in it, takes the mode's colour, a tint of the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope)'s hue of that name, readable in both light and dark mode. Chain is Code and Spec together, so wherever it shows Code and Spec as well, both are purple: the colour midway between Code's and Spec's. A colour chosen for Code, Chain, Spec, or Ask in the theme editor, as the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope) says, is used in place of that mode's, Chain staying midway between Code and Spec unless it is chosen too.

#### Tasks

A prompt sent in Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform is a task, sent as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. Tasks carry on one conversation, and run in two lanes, as it says: Code tasks in the code lane and Spec tasks in the spec lane, each queueing only behind tasks of its own lane, so a Spec task runs beside a Code task rather than waiting for it. A Chain task's steps each run in the lane of the work they do. Before one is sent, the spec is built ahead of it, as the [SpecBuildScope](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says. Once one finishes without error, having changed files, it adds a commit note to the [GitPanelScope](../../../ui/components/git-panel/index.md#git-panel-scope).

#### Questions

A prompt sent in Ask is a question. It runs straight away, alongside any task and any other question, and never queues, builds the spec, or adds a commit note. Questions carry on a conversation of their own, apart from the tasks', as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says.

#### Freeform

A prompt sent in Freeform is passed to the harness exactly as it was typed, with anything attached to it, and nothing else: no system prompt, no hidden anchor compiled from it, no spec built ahead of it, no slices, whatever the Slice toggle says, and no understanding file. Otherwise it is a task like any other, in the code lane, though it waits for both lanes to be free and keeps both busy while it runs, since it may change the code or the spec: it queues while either is busy, carries on the tasks' conversation, heads the message list, is saved in the prompt history, can be cancelled or resent, and adds a commit note once it finishes having changed files. It is saved in the history as a hidden anchor like any task's, recording its mode, so the queue and history hold it as they hold the others, but that anchor is never compiled, imports nothing, and has no system prompt. It is shown in the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list) as a regular chat, its prompt as it was sent, with no hidden anchor named, and the right sidebar doesn't slide out while it runs, since it references nothing. What is sent to a running Freeform task, from Send to task, goes just as it was typed 

#### System Prompts

Each mode but Freeform sends the project's system prompt, the same whatever the mode, and instructions of its own, from the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope). Only Spec, and a Chain prompt's first step, which write the spec, are pointed at the Piton fluency. A prompt keeps the mode it was sent in while it waits in the queue.

input.command:
cd /workspace; f=spec/scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.pi
cat > /tmp/sf <<'EOF'
    suspenseFluency:
        The Suspense fluency is how Suspense works, as a harness working in
        any project needs to know it to talk about it or write for it: what
        the modes are and what each may change, how a Chain prompt runs, how
        prompts and questions are handed back to the user, and what the
        application adds to a prompt of its own accord. Every mode but
        Freeform is pointed at it, so a question asked to write a Chain
        prompt, or a task asked about the queue, knows what that is, in a
        project that says nothing of Suspense itself. Like the Piton fluency,
        it is never part of the system prompt, so the prompt cache holds
        whatever the mode.

        It is the same for every project, and is the application's own, not
        a project's to edit: its source is a Markdown file in this
        application's own repository, `suspense-fluency.md` in its
        `.suspense/system-prompts` directory beside the defaults, baked into
        the application when it is built, as they are, so a build always
        ships with whatever it says, and a build can't be made without it.
        It is not among the prompts a project saves or the
        @{SettingsWindowScope} edits.

        It is written to the Suspense fluency file,
        `.suspense/suspense-fluency.md` in the project's data, as the
        @{ProjectDataScope} says, before any Code, Chain, Spec, or Ask prompt
        is compiled, whenever the file isn't there or doesn't hold what the
        application ships, so it keeps in step with the application rather
        than the project. It is written as text, never read as Piton, holds
        no placeholder and no path of the machine it was written on, and so
        reads the same on the host and in a container.

        It says, plainly and briefly, written for a harness rather than a
        user:

        \\
        - that Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code, and that a prompt is sent to the harness in one of five modes, in the order and with the meanings the PromptModesScope gives: Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is, Chain changes the spec and then the code to match, Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is, Ask asks a question and changes nothing, and Freeform passes a prompt to the harness exactly as typed
        - that Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks, run in a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each, queueing behind tasks of their own lane, and that questions run at once and never queue
        - that a Chain prompt runs as two steps: a spec step, which writes the prompt into the spec, then a code step, sent the prompt and what the spec step replied, which changes the code to match the spec as built, and that each step is its own run, in its own lane
        - that Suspense adds each mode's instructions to a prompt itself, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head, and the spec's references and the understanding file with them, so a prompt written for a mode is only what the user wants done, in the user's own terms, and never holds a <task-instructions> block, steps the mode already takes, or instructions about building, checking, or the understanding file
        - how to write a good prompt for each mode: a Chain or Spec prompt says what should be true of the application once it is met, not how to edit the spec; a Code prompt says what the code should do, and may link to the compiled reference for the spec it follows; an Ask prompt is a question; and a prompt that names part of the spec links to its compiled reference under the harness's directory, as the user would
        - that an answer hands a prompt back to the user, for them to read, edit, and send, as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, and asks the user something back as one whose info string is `suspense-question`, with any answers to pick from one per line, each starting with `- `, as the Ask instructions say, both shown as cards the user acts on, never sent by themselves
        - what a task's understanding file is, the short list of constraints it takes from the spec, shown beside the task as it runs
        - that the user can cancel, resend, or send a task to the other mode, send more to a running task, and start a new conversation, so a prompt never needs to say any of that is possible
        \\

        It names no project, location, harness, or file of any one project,
        and says nothing a mode's own instructions already tell a run that
        sees them, such as how the spec is read or written.

        SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE stands for the file's path. The Code, Chain,
        Spec, and Ask instructions each say, on a paragraph of its own, to
        read that file once in the conversation when the work is about
        Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or calls for
        writing a prompt or a question for the user, before doing so. A
        Chain prompt's code step is pointed at it through the Code
        instructions, and a Code task sent to Spec through the Spec
        instructions. Freeform sends no instructions, and is never pointed at
        it. Where the file can't be written, SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE is filled
        in with nothing, so the paragraph pointing at it is left out.

EOF
n=$(grep -n "^    specReading:" $f | cut -d: -f1); head -$((n-1)) $f > /tmp/x; cat /tmp/sf >> /tmp/x; tail -n +$n $f >> /tmp/x; cp /tmp/x $f
cat > /tmp/dp <<'EOF'
        The Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask defaults each have, after what the
        mode is for, on a paragraph of its own:

        \\
        When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read ${SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.
        \\

EOF
n=$(grep -n "^        The Ask default says what a question is for" $f | cut -d: -f1); head -$((n-1)) $f > /tmp/x; cat /tmp/dp >> /tmp/x; tail -n +$n $f >> /tmp/x; cp /tmp/x $f
piton check 2>&1 | tail -5

I added a "Suspense fluency" to the spec: a file explaining how Suspense works, which Code, Chain, Spec and Ask prompts are pointed at but Freeform never is. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 79 files, and the new sections appear in the refreshed reference.

**Existing projects won't get it on their own.** The spec already says a project keeps its saved mode prompts when a default changes. So the project you have in mind will only point its Ask at the fluency once you reset its Ask prompt in Settings, or add the paragraph by hand. New projects get it automatically. If you'd rather it reach existing projects without a reset, the spec could insert the pointer for every non-Freeform mode instead of relying on the saved prompt. Say if you want that.

## What changed in the spec

**1. New `#suspense-fluency` section** in `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md`
- **What it is:** a short, harness-facing description of Suspense, the same for every project.
- **Where it comes from:** the source is `suspense-fluency.md` in this repo's `.suspense/system-prompts/`, built into the app like the default prompts. A build can't be made without it, and projects can't edit it.
- **Where it's written:** to `.suspense/suspense-fluency.md` in each project, before any Code, Chain, Spec or Ask prompt is compiled, whenever the file is missing or out of date. It holds plain text with no placeholders or machine paths.
- **What it covers:**
  - the five modes and what each may change;
  - the two lanes and the queue, and that questions run straight away;
  - a Chain prompt's spec step, then its code step;
  - that Suspense adds the `<task-instructions>` block itself, so a prompt written for a mode is only the user's request;
  - how to write a good prompt for each mode;
  - the `suspense-prompt` and `suspense-question` blocks;
  - the understanding file;
  - that the user can cancel, resend, send to the other mode, and start a new conversation.
- **What it leaves out:** anything specific to one project, and anything a mode's own instructions already say.

**2. A new placeholder and default paragraph** in the same file
- **`SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE`** is added to the placeholders (`#templates`). It is filled in with a relative path, and its paragraph is dropped when the file can't be written.
- **Defaults (`#defaults`):** the Code, Chain, Spec and Ask defaults gain a paragraph of their own. It tells the run to read that file once per conversation when the work is about Suspense, or when it is to write a prompt or question for the user. Freeform never mentions it, and the Piton fluency rules are unchanged.

**3. Supporting changes**
- **Containers** (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md`, `#spec` and `#question`): Spec runs and questions mount the Suspense fluency file read only.
- **Project data** (`.claude/reference/scope/project-data/index.md`, `#contents` and `#machine-only`): `suspense-fluency.md` is listed, and counts as belonging to one machine.
- **Modes** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/modes/index.md#system-prompts`): every mode but Freeform is pointed at the Suspense fluency.
- **Settings window** (`.claude/reference/scope/settings-window/index.md`): the placeholder help now explains `SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE`.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791125882-RequireSuspenseFluencyForPromptModes.understanding.md`.

- `ModeSystemPromptsScope`: `#suspense-fluency`, `#templates`, `#defaults`. Also write the new default file and update `code.md`, `combined.md`, `spec.md` and `ask.md` in `.suspense/system-prompts`.
- `ContainerEnvironmentScope`: `#spec`, `#question`
- `ProjectDataScope`: `#contents`, `#machine-only`
- `PromptModesScope`: `#system-prompts`
- `SettingsWindowScope`: the placeholder description

content.content:
# How Suspense works

Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code. The user sends you prompts from it in one of five modes:

- Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is.
- Chain changes the spec, then the code to match it.
- Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is.
- Ask asks a question and changes nothing.
- Freeform passes a prompt to you exactly as typed.

Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks. Tasks run in two lanes, a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each; a task waits in the queue behind the tasks of its own lane. Questions from Ask run at once and never queue.

A Chain prompt runs as two steps, each its own run in its own lane. The spec step writes the prompt into the spec. Once the spec is built, the code step is sent the same prompt and what the spec step replied, and changes the code to match the spec as built.

Suspense adds each mode's instructions to a prompt itself, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head, together with the spec's references and the task's understanding file. So a prompt written for a mode is only what the user wants done, in the user's own terms. Never put a <task-instructions> block in a prompt you write, nor steps the mode already takes, nor instructions about building, checking, or the understanding file.

To write a good prompt for each mode:

- A Chain or Spec prompt says what should be true of the application once it is met, not how to edit the spec.
- A Code prompt says what the code should do, and may link to the compiled reference for the part of the spec it follows.
- An Ask prompt is a question.
- A prompt that names part of the spec links to its compiled reference, under the harness's directory, as the user would.

An answer hands a prompt back to the user as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text. It asks the user something back as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`: the question first, then any answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Suspense shows both as cards the user reads, edits, answers, and sends; neither is ever sent by itself.

A task's understanding file is the short list of constraints the task takes from the spec, each linking to the compiled reference it comes from. Suspense shows it beside the task as it runs.

The user can cancel a task, resend it, send it to the other mode, send more to a task while it runs, and start a new conversation. A prompt never needs to say that any of this is possible.
----
Questions asked while another is still running come in at the bottom in the order they were asked, each answered in its own place as its harness goes, so answers can be filling in at once.

#### Suggested Prompts

An answer can hand back a prompt for the user to send, as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt`, followed by a space and the mode it is meant for, `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) names them, and holding the prompt's text, as the Ask instructions tell the harness. Such a block is never shown as a code block. It is shown in the answer, where it stands among the reply's markdown, as a prompt card: a box on the theme's raised surface, faintly tinted the mode's colour, with corners rounded 6 pixels, across the answer's full width. Along its top runs a small header, the mode's icon and name in the mode's colour, as "Code prompt", and beneath it the prompt's text as it was written, wrapped, in the body's text colour, not rendered as markdown. Along its bottom, at its right, are two buttons, Copy, with a copy icon, which puts the prompt's text on the clipboard, and "Send to prompt", in the mode's colour, with an arrow icon.
Send to prompt puts the prompt's text in the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s text input and selects the mode's tab, Chain for Code and Spec selected together where the mode is `chain`, giving the input keyboard focus with the cursor at the end of the text. It never sends anything: the user reads, edits, and sends it as any prompt. Where the input already holds text, that text is set aside first as the chat input sets aside a prompt for editing a queued one, and comes back once the prompt from the card is sent or cleared, so nothing typed is lost. What is attached to the prompt being written stays attached. The button reads "Sent to prompt", with a check, for 2 seconds after.
A block whose mode is missing or isn't one of those five is still a prompt card, headed "Prompt", in Ask's colour, and Send to prompt selects Chain, the tab the chat input starts on. While a block is still streaming in, its card is shown with what has come so far and its buttons disabled until the block closes. A block never closed by the end of a finished answer is a card all the same, holding what came. An answer may hold any number of cards, each in its place.

#### Asking Back

An answer can ask the user something back, as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, holding the question on its first lines, and then, if the harness offers answers to pick from, one answer per line, each begun with a dash and a space, as a Markdown list item is. Such a block is never shown as a code block. It is shown in the answer, where it stands, as a question card: a box on the theme's raised surface, faintly tinted Ask's colour, with corners rounded 6 pixels, across the answer's full width, holding the question rendered as markdown, and beneath it a button per answer offered, in the order given, each reading that answer.

Questions asked while another is still running come in at the bottom in the order they were asked, each answered in its own place as its harness goes, so answers can be filling in at once.

#### Suggested Prompts

An answer can hand back a prompt for the user to send, as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt`, followed by a space and the mode it is meant for, `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) names them, and holding the prompt's text, as the Ask instructions tell the harness. Such a block is never shown as a code block. It is shown in the answer, where it stands among the reply's markdown, as a prompt card: a box on the theme's raised surface, faintly tinted the mode's colour, with corners rounded 6 pixels, across the answer's full width. Along its top runs a small header, the mode's icon and name in the mode's colour, as "Code prompt", and beneath it the prompt's text as it was written, wrapped, in the body's text colour, not rendered as markdown. Along its bottom, at its right, are two buttons, Copy, with a copy icon, which puts the prompt's text on the clipboard, and "Send to prompt", in the mode's colour, with an arrow icon.
Send to prompt puts the prompt's text in the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s text input and selects the mode's tab, Chain for Code and Spec selected together where the mode is `chain`, giving the input keyboard focus with the cursor at the end of the text. It never sends anything: the user reads, edits, and sends it as any prompt. Where the input already holds text, that text is set aside first as the chat input sets aside a prompt for editing a queued one, and comes back once the prompt from the card is sent or cleared, so nothing typed is lost. What is attached to the prompt being written stays attached. The button reads "Sent to prompt", with a check, for 2 seconds after.
A block whose mode is missing or isn't one of those five is still a prompt card, headed "Prompt", in Ask's colour, and Send to prompt selects Chain, the tab the chat input starts on. While a block is still streaming in, its card is shown with what has come so far and its buttons disabled until the block closes. A block never closed by the end of a finished answer is a card all the same, holding what came. An answer may hold any number of cards, each in its place.

#### Asking Back

An answer can ask the user something back, as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, holding the question on its first lines, and then, if the harness offers answers to pick from, one answer per line, each begun with a dash and a space, as a Markdown list item is. Such a block is never shown as a code block. It is shown in the answer, where it stands, as a question card: a box on the theme's raised surface, faintly tinted Ask's colour, with corners rounded 6 pixels, across the answer's full width, holding the question rendered as markdown, and beneath it a button per answer offered, in the order given, each reading that answer.

content.text:
I changed the spec so every Ask question is told to give prompts as cards, and each prompt card gets Send to Code, Send to Chain and Send to Spec buttons. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 79 files, and the new sections appear in the refreshed reference.

**The Send buttons send right away.** "Send to Code", "Send to Chain" and "Send to Spec" each send the prompt immediately in that mode, as if you'd typed it on that tab and pressed send. A task queues if its lane is busy. If you'd rather they only fill the chat input for you to send yourself, say so and I'll switch them. The new Edit button does that today.

## What changed in the spec

**1. New `#card-format` section** in `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md`
- **What it says:** whenever the user asks for a prompt, or the answer suggests one, give it as a `suspense-prompt` block with its mode, never as plain text, a quote or any other code block. Pick `chain` when the work changes both spec and code. It also keeps the existing `suspense-question` rule.
- **Not editable:** the app adds it to every question's `<task-instructions>` block, after the project's own Ask instructions. So it reaches projects whose `ask.md` was saved before this change, which a new default alone wouldn't.
- **Source:** the text is built into the app from `ask-cards.md` in this repo's `.suspense/system-prompts/`, and a build can't be made without it.
- **Ask default:** `#defaults` no longer holds this paragraph, so it isn't given twice.

**2. Prompt card buttons** in `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/ask-conversation/index.md#suggested-prompts`
- **Buttons, in order:** Copy, Edit, then Send to Code, Send to Chain, Send to Spec. Each is in its mode's colour, 4px apart, and the row wraps when the card is narrow.
- **Highlighting:** the button for the card's own mode is filled in its colour and the others are ghost buttons. An `ask` card has "Ask" first and a `freeform` card has "Send to Freeform" first, filled, with the three after it.
- **Sending:** sends with the Slice toggle as it is and nothing attached, and leaves whatever you're typing in the chat input alone. The button reads "Sent to Code" (and so on) with a check for 2 seconds, and clicking again sends again.
- **Edit:** does what "Send to prompt" used to do: puts the text in the chat input on the card's mode tab, setting aside anything already typed. It reads "Edited" for 2 seconds after.
- **Unknown mode:** a card whose mode is missing or unknown shows all three send buttons as ghosts, and its Edit selects Chain.

**3. Suspense fluency** (`#suspense-fluency`): it now says prompt cards have buttons that send to Code, Chain or Spec.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791129571-Prompt_12d373dbb0306780.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ModeSystemPromptsScope`: `#card-format` (append the fixed paragraph to every question and add `ask-cards.md`), `#defaults` (take the paragraph out of the default `ask.md`), `#suspense-fluency` (update `suspense-fluency.md`).
- `AskConversationScope`: `#suggested-prompts`.
- `PromptSendingScope`: how a send button's prompt is sent.

The Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Drive connectors still need authorizing in your claude.ai connector settings before they can be used. None of them were needed here.

content.content:
## Concept

### Pitch

The bottom panel of the [RightSidebarScope](../index.md#right-sidebar-scope), beneath the referenced files and the understanding: the subagents and background commands the harness started for the running task, each shown in the colour of the mode that started it, with how long it has been running, so one that seems stuck can be seen and stopped.

### Shape

#### Description

It lists the background tasks the harness started for the run, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../../../scope/harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) keeps them: its subagents, the agents it started, and its background commands, the shell commands it ran in the background, such as a long build. A background task of any other kind isn't shown.
It is shown only once the run has started one, and takes no room before. One row per background task, in the order they started, subagents and commands together, each 24 pixels tall, 8 pixels in from the panel's edges: a spinner while it is at work, then a tick, a cross, or a dash for how it ended, done, failed, or stopped, beside a small icon for its kind, a robot for a subagent and a terminal for a command, in the theme's muted grey, then what it was started to do, in small text, cut off with an ellipsis, muted once it has ended. For a subagent that is its description, and for a command the command itself, on one line, in monospace. Its tooltip gives what it was started to do, and beneath, muted, its kind, "Subagent" or "Command", and what it is doing or how it ended. The panel is only as tall as its rows need, up to 30% of the sidebar's height, scrolling beyond that.

#### Elapsed

At the right of each row, 8 pixels in from the panel's edge, is how long it has been running, from when the harness said it started, in extra small muted tabular figures, as a task's elapsed time is written beside its status: "0:42", "12:05", "1:02:33". While it is at work it counts up every second; once it has ended it stops at how long it ran. What it was started to do is cut off before the time rather than running beneath it.

#### Stopping

Each background task is shown according to the mode of the task that started it, as the [PromptModesScope](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours modes: its row has a bar 2 pixels wide down its left edge in that mode's colour, and its spinner and tick are drawn in it too, while a cross or dash keeps its own colour. A task whose mode isn't known, as one from the history saved before modes were, has no bar and keeps its spinner and tick in their own colours, its tooltip reading "Started by the task". content.text:
I changed the spec so the SubagentsPanel shows only work going on apart from the main thread, plus ordinary commands once they've run long. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 79 files, and the new text appears in the refreshed reference.

**"Long-running" means 15 seconds.** That was my choice; it's one number in the spec if you want it shorter or longer.

## What changed in the spec

All edits are in `spec/ui/components/right-sidebar/subagents/index.pi`, the `description` section (`.claude/reference/ui/components/right-sidebar/subagents/index.md#description`).

- **Purpose:** the panel is for what goes on apart from the main thread, so you still see it while the main thread waits, pauses or has finished its turn.
- **Subagents:** every subagent is shown, whether the main thread waits on it or it runs in the background.
- **Commands:**
  - Background commands are always shown.
  - An ordinary command (a Bash call the main thread waits on) appears only once it has run 15 seconds without its result coming back. Its time counts from when it started, and it sits among the other rows by start time.
  - A command that finishes within 15 seconds never appears, not even briefly.
- **Never shown:** commands a subagent runs, and every other tool call. All of them stay in the task's output table as before; the panel just leaves them out.
- **Long waited-on commands:**
  - They don't hold the run open.
  - They end when their result comes back, done or failed, or when the run ends.
  - Their tooltip kind reads "Command, waited on".
  - They have no Stop button, since only background tasks can be stopped on their own. The task's Cancel button still stops them.
- **Subagents the main thread waits on:**
  - They end when the harness reports their end, or when their tool call's result comes back, whichever is first.
  - They can be stopped only where the harness gave them a task id. Otherwise they have no Stop button.
- **Showing the panel:** it appears once the run has something to show in it, not before.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791131709-FilterSubagentsPanelForBackground.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `SubagentsPanel`: `#description` for the filtering and the 15-second rule. `#elapsed`, `#stopping` and `#by-mode` are unchanged but apply to the new rows.
- `HarnessIntegrationScope`: `#feeding`, for how background tasks are tracked and stopped by id.
- `TaskTableScope`: `#types`. All tool calls, short commands included, stay in the task's output table.

The Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Drive connectors still need authorizing in your claude.ai connector settings before they can be used. None of them were needed here.

25:##### Description
27:A task's header shows the compiled markdown that was actually sent to the harness, rendered as markdown, once it has compiled, along with the name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from.
29:#### Status
31:##### Description
33:A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green, "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and dark mode.
35:##### Elapsed
37:Beside its status label, a task shows how long it has been under way, from when it was sent, building and compiling included, in small muted tabular figures: minutes and seconds, "0:42" or "12:05", with hours ahead of them once it reaches an hour, "1:02:33". While the task is building, compiling, or running, it counts up every second, so a task that seems stuck can be told from one that has only just started. Once the task is over, however it ended, it stops and stays at how long the task took. It shows wherever the status label does, the latest task's header and the heading of each previous task, including a task running in the other lane. A task from the history whose record holds no start and end shows none.
39:#### Output Table
41:##### Description
43:A task's output is a [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope), whose rows are what the harness did for the task. While the task is under way, its table ends in the waiting row for whatever the harness does next. Tasks never collapse their steps, since their whole chain is of interest.
45:#### Links
47:##### Description
49:Links in the compiled prompt and in reply text are clickable. A link to a file opens it, as the [OpenFileScope](../../open-file/index.md#open-file-scope) says, and a web link opens in the browser. The file path on a Read, Edit, Write, or MultiEdit row is shown as a link and opens that file the same way.
51:#### Backgrounds
53:##### Description
55:The header for the latest task is coloured like the tab the task was sent from, the colour of its mode, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), as the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) body shows for that tab. A task from the history that doesn't say which tab it was sent from keeps the tab bar's colour. The queue along the bottom and the previous tasks row along the top both have the same background colour as the tab bar.
56:Each task in the previous tasks list hints at the mode it was sent in: its heading's background is a faint tint of that mode's colour, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), red for Code, purple for Chain, blue for Spec, green for Ask, and grey for Freeform, far fainter than the latest task's header, so the list reads as a column of the list's own background with each task only touched by its colour. A task whose mode isn't known, as one from the history that doesn't say, keeps the list's background untinted. Its status label, prompt, checkbox, and buttons stay readable over the tint, in light and dark mode, and its hover and open states still show over it. An open task's prompt and output beneath its heading are not tinted.
58:#### Referenced Spec
60:##### Description
62:While a task is running, a [RightSidebarScope](../../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope) slides out from the message list's right edge, listing the spec files the task references, and slides back once the run is over.
64:#### Scrolling
66:##### Description
68:The latest task's table scrolls with its lock to the bottom off to start with, until switched on. Each open project keeps how far its latest task's table was scrolled and whether it was locked, and the rest of its message list as it was left, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says, so switching back to it shows the list just as it was.
69:However long the list of previous tasks grows, drawing it costs no more than drawing the tasks in view, so scrolling, animations, and new output stay smooth.
71:##### Scrolling Past
73:Scrolling carries on past either end of the latest task and the previous tasks, from one to the other, through an elastic stretch at that end. A scroll that reaches an end doesn't stop dead there: the same scroll keeps going, with no pause needed, into the stretch, which resists it, and it crosses over only once it has pushed far enough into the stretch to get past a barrier at its far side. The only scroll that stops at an end is a fling's momentum still running when it gets there, and a scroll that has already crossed over is spent (below).
74:How the view came to be at its end makes no difference. A scroll begun with the view already resting there, scrolled there some time before, opened there by clicking the previous tasks row, or left there when a slide settled, pulls into the stretch from its very first step, exactly as one that scrolls the view there and carries on; it never has to move the view first, and nothing it does is swallowed by the view before the stretch takes it.
75:The barrier is a distance to scroll past. The distance a scroll goes past the end builds up, and it crosses over the moment that reaches 768 pixels, about twelve or thirteen notches of a mouse wheel or a firm swipe on a trackpad, however quickly or slowly it gets there, so the end is felt as a real resistance before the view gives way. The scroll that brings the view to its end counts too: whatever of it goes past the end starts the build-up, rather than being lost. Scrolling back the other way takes the build-up down again, and scrolls the view once it is gone.
76:The build-up never drains while the scroll goes on. A scroll goes on for as long as the wheel or trackpad keeps scrolling, with less than 200 milliseconds between one step and the next, as between the notches of a wheel spun steadily, however slowly; each step adds all of itself to the build-up, so a steady scroll of any speed reaches the barrier and crosses over without being stopped and started again. Only once the scroll has stopped, 200 milliseconds after its last step, does the build-up drain away on its own, back to nothing within half a second of that last step, so a nudge into the stretch that goes no further never crosses over later. Momentum, and any scroll during a slide, add nothing to it.
77:The stretch is felt as well as seen. While anything has built up, the view at that end is pulled past its end, following the scroll but by less than it scrolled, and by less the further it is pulled, as a rubber band gives: at the start it moves nearly as far as the scroll, and by the barrier it has been pulled about 64 pixels, never more. Scrolling up at the latest task's top, its header and output move down together, leaving an empty band above them, in the body's colour; scrolling down at the previous tasks' bottom, they move up, leaving the band below them. The previous tasks row and the queue stay where they are, and nothing is drawn outside the space between them. The pull follows the build-up as it grows and drains, smoothly rather than in steps, so as the build-up drains the view springs back to its end, settling without bouncing. The view's own scroll position doesn't change while it is pulled; it is still at its end once it springs back.
78:While anything has built up against an end, a glow shows where the crossing will happen: a soft radial glow, centred in the space between the previous tasks row and the queue, fading from its middle to nothing at its edge, in the colour of the mode selected in the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope), as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it. It starts small and faint and grows larger and slightly brighter as the build-up nears the barrier, at its largest a little under the height of that space and still only a subtle wash of colour, never hiding what is beneath it. It follows the build-up as it grows and drains, smoothly rather than in steps. It never takes a click or a scroll. As the view crosses over, the glow fades out quickly while the slide begins; with nothing built up, there is no glow at all.
79:With the latest task's output scrolled to its top, a scroll up past the barrier expands the previous tasks, as clicking their row does, opening scrolled to the bottom, on the tasks sent most recently, as the [HistoryListScope](../../../ui/components/history-list/index.md#history-list-scope) says. Before any task has been sent, or with no previous tasks, scrolling up does nothing more: the view stops at its top without stretching, and no glow shows.
80:With the previous tasks expanded and scrolled to their bottom, a scroll down past the barrier closes them, as clicking "Back to the latest task" does, bringing back the latest task and its output as they were left.
81:However the previous tasks are closed, by a scroll or by clicking "Back to the latest task", the latest task's output comes back scrolled just where it was when they were opened, with its lock to the bottom as it was. Locked, it comes back at its bottom and still locked, showing whatever output arrived while the previous tasks were open, and goes on following new output. Unlocked, it comes back at the same place in its output, however much arrived meanwhile; if that place no longer exists, as when the latest task has changed since, it comes back at its top, unlocked.
82:A fling's momentum still running when an end is reached stops there, never pulling into the stretch or crossing over. Momentum is only what comes after the platform says the fingers have lifted from the trackpad; where it never says, as on Linux, no scroll is taken for momentum, and every one pulls into the stretch. Output or a list too short to scroll is always at both its ends, so any scroll over it that leads somewhere pulls into the stretch. Only the wheel or trackpad crosses over. Scrolling sideways, dragging a scrollbar to an end, and scrolling anything inside that scrolls on its own, such as an open task's table in the list, never do.
83:Crossing over by scrolling is animated, starting from wherever the stretch has pulled the view. Scrolling up, the previous tasks slide down into view from above, already scrolled to their bottom, pushing the latest task's header and output out below them, the two moving together as one column. Scrolling down, the latest task's header and output slide up into view from below, already scrolled where they will settle, pushing the previous tasks out above them. The slide is quick and settles without bouncing, as the right sidebar's does. Only the space between the previous tasks row and the queue moves, and nothing is drawn outside it; the row and the queue stay where they are, the row reading what it will once the slide settles, from the moment it starts.
84:The scroll that crosses over stops at the moment of the switch. The step that takes it past the barrier is used up by the crossing, all of it, however far past the barrier it reached, and none of it scrolls the view beneath. Whatever more of that same scroll follows, as the wheel keeps turning, the fingers keep moving, or a fling's momentum runs on, is swallowed: during the slide and after it has settled, it scrolls neither view, pulls into no stretch, and never crosses back, so the view it switched to is left exactly as it arrived, scrolled where the slide brought it. Only a new scroll moves anything again: one begun once the wheel or trackpad has been still for 80 milliseconds, counted from the last scroll step whether that came during the slide or after, or once fingers are lifted from the trackpad and put back. That new scroll behaves as any other, scrolling the view, or, with the view at its end, pulling into the stretch from its first step. Expanding or closing the previous tasks by clicking their row is not animated.
86:#### Changed Files
88:##### Description
90:In a project that is a git repository, every task, the latest and each of the previous tasks, lists the files that changed while it ran, between the two snapshots of the working tree taken as it started and ended, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope)'s task snapshots say. In a project that isn't one, no task shows any of this.
92:##### List
94:The files are those `git diff --name-status` gives between the two snapshots, each one added, modified, deleted, or renamed. Each is a row with its path in the project, a small letter for how it changed, A, M, D, or R, in the colour the git panel gives that change, and, for a renamed file, the path it was renamed from, muted, before an arrow. They are listed in path order, below the task's output, beneath the latest task's output table, and beneath an open previous task's table, headed "Files changed" with how many there are. The list is collapsed to its heading to start with, and expands when the heading is clicked.
95:Only the project's own files are listed, its spec, its code, and anything else of its own, never what the application keeps for
97:###### Itself
99:nothing in the project's .suspense directory, its history,
101:questions, reports, and the rest, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, and not the draft, .suspense-draft.pi, wherever it is. They are left out of the list and of its count alike, for every task, those recorded before as well, and a file renamed into or out of .suspense is listed only by its path outside it, as added or deleted.
102:While a task is still running, it has only its first snapshot, so it shows no list yet. A task whose run changed nothing else, nothing at all or only what the application keeps, reads "No files changed", muted. A task with no snapshots, as one from before they were taken or one whose snapshot couldn't be taken, shows no list.
104:##### Who Changed
106:The snapshots catch everything that changed while the task ran, including the user's own edits made meanwhile, as in the side editor. Each file is compared with the files the harness's tool calls reported writing or editing, as the referenced spec works them out, from its file tools and its shell commands, a subagent's included. A file the agent reported is shown as changed by the agent, its row plain; any other is shown as changed during the task, its row muted, with a small clock icon and a tooltip saying it changed while the task ran but not through the agent.
108:##### Opening
110:Clicking a file opens its diff between the two snapshots, the file as it was when the task started against the file as it was when it ended, in the [DiffViewScope](../../../ui/components/diff-view/index.md#diff-view-scope), as the git panel opens a file's uncommitted changes.
112:#### Freeform
114:##### Description
116:A Freeform task is shown as a regular chat, not as a task: its prompt as a message on the right, and the harness's reply as a message on the left, read as prose, as the [AskConversationScope](../ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation-scope) shows a question and its answer.
118:##### Conversation
120:While the latest task was sent in Freeform, the space between the previous tasks row and the queue shows its conversation as a chat, in place of the latest task's header and output table. The chat holds the latest task and the Freeform tasks sent straight before it, back to the last task of another mode, or to the first that started a new conversation, oldest at the top and newest at the bottom. Sending another Freeform prompt adds it at the bottom; sending a task in any other mode shows that task as ever, and the chat goes with it.
122:##### Messages
124:Each prompt is shown as it was typed, in a box on the theme's raised surface, faintly tinted Freeform's grey, as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it, with corners rounded 6 pixels, set against the chat's right edge and at most 80% of its width, with the text and images attached to it listed beneath its text. Beneath the box, at its right, a small muted line gives the time it was sent and, once its task is over, its Resend button, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says; while it runs, its Cancel button is there instead. A message sent to the task while it ran is a box of its own, laid out the same way, placed among the reply where the harness took it in.
125:Each reply follows beneath its prompt, against the chat's left edge, at the chat's full width, with no box, laid out as the [AskConversationScope](../ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation-scope)'s answers are: the reply text after the harness's last tool call rendered as markdown in the body's text colour, everything before it summed up in one small muted line that expands into the steps, a status line with a spinner and the latest thing the harness did in that line's place while the task runs, and the error it failed with, "Cancelled", or "No answer." at its end. Beneath the reply, in a git repository, come the files changed while it ran, as every task lists them. Prompts are 16 pixels apart, and a reply starts 8 pixels beneath its prompt.
127:##### No Task Trappings
129:Nothing in the chat is shown as a task: there is no header, no status label, no hidden anchor's name, no compiled prompt, and no output table.

25:##### Description
27:A task's header shows the compiled markdown that was actually sent to the harness, rendered as markdown, once it has compiled, along with the name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from.
29:#### Status
31:##### Description
33:A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green, "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and dark mode.
35:##### Elapsed
37:Beside its status label, a task shows how long it has been under way, from when it was sent, building and compiling included, in small muted tabular figures: minutes and seconds, "0:42" or "12:05", with hours ahead of them once it reaches an hour, "1:02:33". While the task is building, compiling, or running, it counts up every second, so a task that seems stuck can be told from one that has only just started. Once the task is over, however it ended, it stops and stays at how long the task took. It shows wherever the status label does, the latest task's header and the heading of each previous task, including a task running in the other lane. A task from the history whose record holds no start and end shows none.
39:#### Output Table
41:##### Description
43:A task's output is a [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope), whose rows are what the harness did for the task. While the task is under way, its table ends in the waiting row for whatever the harness does next. Tasks never collapse their steps, since their whole chain is of interest.
45:#### Links
47:##### Description
49:Links in the compiled prompt and in reply text are clickable. A link to a file opens it, as the [OpenFileScope](../../open-file/index.md#open-file-scope) says, and a web link opens in the browser. The file path on a Read, Edit, Write, or MultiEdit row is shown as a link and opens that file the same way.
51:#### Backgrounds
53:##### Description
55:The header for the latest task is coloured like the tab the task was sent from, the colour of its mode, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), as the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) body shows for that tab. A task from the history that doesn't say which tab it was sent from keeps the tab bar's colour. The queue along the bottom and the previous tasks row along the top both have the same background colour as the tab bar.
56:Each task in the previous tasks list hints at the mode it was sent in: its heading's background is a faint tint of that mode's colour, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), red for Code, purple for Chain, blue for Spec, green for Ask, and grey for Freeform, far fainter than the latest task's header, so the list reads as a column of the list's own background with each task only touched by its colour. A task whose mode isn't known, as one from the history that doesn't say, keeps the list's background untinted. Its status label, prompt, checkbox, and buttons stay readable over the tint, in light and dark mode, and its hover and open states still show over it. An open task's prompt and output beneath its heading are not tinted.
58:#### Referenced Spec
60:##### Description
62:While a task is running, a [RightSidebarScope](../../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope) slides out from the message list's right edge, listing the spec files the task references, and slides back once the run is over.
64:#### Scrolling
66:##### Description
68:The latest task's table scrolls with its lock to the bottom off to start with, until switched on. Each open project keeps how far its latest task's table was scrolled and whether it was locked, and the rest of its message list as it was left, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says, so switching back to it shows the list just as it was.
69:However long the list of previous tasks grows, drawing it costs no more than drawing the tasks in view, so scrolling, animations, and new output stay smooth.
71:##### Scrolling Past
73:Scrolling carries on past either end of the latest task and the previous tasks, from one to the other, through an elastic stretch at that end. A scroll that reaches an end doesn't stop dead there: the same scroll keeps going, with no pause needed, into the stretch, which resists it, and it crosses over only once it has pushed far enough into the stretch to get past a barrier at its far side. The only scroll that stops at an end is a fling's momentum still running when it gets there, and a scroll that has already crossed over is spent (below).
74:How the view came to be at its end makes no difference. A scroll begun with the view already resting there, scrolled there some time before, opened there by clicking the previous tasks row, or left there when a slide settled, pulls into the stretch from its very first step, exactly as one that scrolls the view there and carries on; it never has to move the view first, and nothing it does is swallowed by the view before the stretch takes it.
75:The barrier is a distance to scroll past. The distance a scroll goes past the end builds up, and it crosses over the moment that reaches 768 pixels, about twelve or thirteen notches of a mouse wheel or a firm swipe on a trackpad, however quickly or slowly it gets there, so the end is felt as a real resistance before the view gives way. The scroll that brings the view to its end counts too: whatever of it goes past the end starts the build-up, rather than being lost. Scrolling back the other way takes the build-up down again, and scrolls the view once it is gone.
76:The build-up never drains while the scroll goes on. A scroll goes on for as long as the wheel or trackpad keeps scrolling, with less than 200 milliseconds between one step and the next, as between the notches of a wheel spun steadily, however slowly; each step adds all of itself to the build-up, so a steady scroll of any speed reaches the barrier and crosses over without being stopped and started again. Only once the scroll has stopped, 200 milliseconds after its last step, does the build-up drain away on its own, back to nothing within half a second of that last step, so a nudge into the stretch that goes no further never crosses over later. Momentum, and any scroll during a slide, add nothing to it.
77:The stretch is felt as well as seen. While anything has built up, the view at that end is pulled past its end, following the scroll but by less than it scrolled, and by less the further it is pulled, as a rubber band gives: at the start it moves nearly as far as the scroll, and by the barrier it has been pulled about 64 pixels, never more. Scrolling up at the latest task's top, its header and output move down together, leaving an empty band above them, in the body's colour; scrolling down at the previous tasks' bottom, they move up, leaving the band below them. The previous tasks row and the queue stay where they are, and nothing is drawn outside the space between them. The pull follows the build-up as it grows and drains, smoothly rather than in steps, so as the build-up drains the view springs back to its end, settling without bouncing. The view's own scroll position doesn't change while it is pulled; it is still at its end once it springs back.
78:While anything has built up against an end, a glow shows where the crossing will happen: a soft radial glow, centred in the space between the previous tasks row and the queue, fading from its middle to nothing at its edge, in the colour of the mode selected in the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope), as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it. It starts small and faint and grows larger and slightly brighter as the build-up nears the barrier, at its largest a little under the height of that space and still only a subtle wash of colour, never hiding what is beneath it. It follows the build-up as it grows and drains, smoothly rather than in steps. It never takes a click or a scroll. As the view crosses over, the glow fades out quickly while the slide begins; with nothing built up, there is no glow at all.
79:With the latest task's output scrolled to its top, a scroll up past the barrier expands the previous tasks, as clicking their row does, opening scrolled to the bottom, on the tasks sent most recently, as the [HistoryListScope](../../../ui/components/history-list/index.md#history-list-scope) says. Before any task has been sent, or with no previous tasks, scrolling up does nothing more: the view stops at its top without stretching, and no glow shows.
80:With the previous tasks expanded and scrolled to their bottom, a scroll down past the barrier closes them, as clicking "Back to the latest task" does, bringing back the latest task and its output as they were left.
81:However the previous tasks are closed, by a scroll or by clicking "Back to the latest task", the latest task's output comes back scrolled just where it was when they were opened, with its lock to the bottom as it was. Locked, it comes back at its bottom and still locked, showing whatever output arrived while the previous tasks were open, and goes on following new output. Unlocked, it comes back at the same place in its output, however much arrived meanwhile; if that place no longer exists, as when the latest task has changed since, it comes back at its top, unlocked.
82:A fling's momentum still running when an end is reached stops there, never pulling into the stretch or crossing over. Momentum is only what comes after the platform says the fingers have lifted from the trackpad; where it never says, as on Linux, no scroll is taken for momentum, and every one pulls into the stretch. Output or a list too short to scroll is always at both its ends, so any scroll over it that leads somewhere pulls into the stretch. Only the wheel or trackpad crosses over. Scrolling sideways, dragging a scrollbar to an end, and scrolling anything inside that scrolls on its own, such as an open task's table in the list, never do.
83:Crossing over by scrolling is animated, starting from wherever the stretch has pulled the view. Scrolling up, the previous tasks slide down into view from above, already scrolled to their bottom, pushing the latest task's header and output out below them, the two moving together as one column. Scrolling down, the latest task's header and output slide up into view from below, already scrolled where they will settle, pushing the previous tasks out above them. The slide is quick and settles without bouncing, as the right sidebar's does. Only the space between the previous tasks row and the queue moves, and nothing is drawn outside it; the row and the queue stay where they are, the row reading what it will once the slide settles, from the moment it starts.
84:The scroll that crosses over stops at the moment of the switch. The step that takes it past the barrier is used up by the crossing, all of it, however far past the barrier it reached, and none of it scrolls the view beneath. Whatever more of that same scroll follows, as the wheel keeps turning, the fingers keep moving, or a fling's momentum runs on, is swallowed: during the slide and after it has settled, it scrolls neither view, pulls into no stretch, and never crosses back, so the view it switched to is left exactly as it arrived, scrolled where the slide brought it. Only a new scroll moves anything again: one begun once the wheel or trackpad has been still for 80 milliseconds, counted from the last scroll step whether that came during the slide or after, or once fingers are lifted from the trackpad and put back. That new scroll behaves as any other, scrolling the view, or, with the view at its end, pulling into the stretch from its first step. Expanding or closing the previous tasks by clicking their row is not animated.

# Prompt Editor

## How To Build

A PromptEditor should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A PromptEditor should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

An interface for sending tasks to a local coding harness like Claude Code, written directly with compiled-on-depand Piton.

### Shape

#### Description

Not a chat. Each prompt sent is a task for the harness, tasks can queue, and each task shows its output until it finishes. There are no message bubbles.

#### Basic Design And Layout

The [MessageList](./message-list/index.md#message-list) fills the body's Chat tab: all the space between the body's tab bar and the [ChatInputScope](./chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) along the bottom. From top to bottom it holds the previous tasks row, the header for the latest task, the latest task's output, and the queue.
Before any task has been sent, the space shows a hint instead, which wraps when the view is narrow. It reads "Write a prompt below. Enter adds a line; Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it." or, while no project is open, as the [NoProjectStateScope](../no-project/index.md#no-project-state-scope) says, "Open a project to start prompting."

#### Chat History

[MessageList](./message-list/index.md#message-list)

#### Previous Tasks

Previous tasks are a [HistoryListScope](../../ui/components/history-list/index.md#history-list-scope) along the top of the view, listing every task sent. Its row counts every task but the latest, which heads the view: "No previous tasks", "1 previous task", or "N previous tasks", and each offers Resend. Expanded, the list takes the place of the latest task and its output, and the row reads "Back to the latest task".
Every task in the list has a checkbox at the left of its heading, before its status, and clicking it selects or deselects the task without opening or closing it. Shift-clicking one selects every task between it and the one last clicked, never deselecting any; with none clicked before, it selects or deselects that one as a plain click does. The selection is kept while the list is closed and opened again, until it is cleared or sent. Each open project keeps its own, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says.
While any task is selected, the row shows the batch actions at its right, in place of nothing: "N selected", muted, counting every task selected, then "Send N to Spec" and "Send N to Code", small ghost buttons with a swap icon, each tinted the colour of the mode it sends to, then "Clear", which deselects them all. Send N to Spec counts, and sends, the selected tasks that offer Send to Spec, and Send N to Code those that offer Send to Code, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says; each is shown only while its count isn't zero. Tasks that don't offer it, sent in Chain or Freeform, whose mode isn't known, already sent to the other mode or being sent there, marked done, or complete, can be selected, and are counted in "N selected", but neither action sends them. Clicking an action never opens or closes the list.
A batch action sends each of its tasks to the other mode, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says for one, oldest first: the first starts straight away while its lane is free and the rest queue behind it in that lane, so they run in the order they were first sent, each saved in the history as a new task. Once sent, the tasks it sent are deselected, the rest of the selection is kept, and the list stays as it was, still expanded, with nothing opened. With no project open, it sends nothing, a notification says a project must be opened first, and the selection is kept.

#### Previous Task Filters

While the previous tasks are expanded, a filter bar sits along the top of the list, beneath their row and above the first item, on the tab bar's background with the theme's line beneath it, and scrolls with

cd /workspace; cat > spec/scope/prompt-mode/message-list/RunningTasks.pi <<'EOF'
use /lib

export shape MessageListRunningTasksShape:
    description:
        The header heads the view with every task under way, not only the
        latest: the latest task, and every other task building, compiling,
        or running, as when a Spec task and a Code task run in their two
        lanes at once, or a chain's step runs beside a task of the other
        lane. Only one of them is selected at a time, and only it is shown in
        full: its header as a task's header always is, its compiled prompt,
        hidden anchor's name, status label and elapsed time, and buttons, and
        beneath it its output table and the files it changed. The others are
        compact rows, one each, stacked above the selected task's header, in
        the order they were sent, oldest at the top. With only one task to
        show, there are no compact rows, and the header is just as it was.

    compactRow:
        A compact row is one line, 28 pixels tall, across the view's full
        width, on a faint tint of its task's mode's colour, as a previous
        task's heading is tinted, with a thin line in the theme's line colour
        between one row and the next and beneath the last. From left to
        right, 8 pixels in: its status label and elapsed time, as every
        task's are, then the first line of its prompt, as it was typed, in
        small text, cut off with an ellipsis, then, at its right, its Cancel
        button while it is under way, as the PromptSendingScope gives every
        task one, and nothing else: no compiled prompt, no hidden anchor's
        name, no Resend or Send to the other mode, no output, and no changed
        files. Its tooltip gives the prompt's first lines and the mode it was
        sent in. Hovering it shows the theme's hover over the tint.

    selecting:
        Clicking a compact row, anywhere but its Cancel button, selects its
        task: it takes the full form, in its place beneath the compact rows,
        and the task selected before becomes a compact row, in its own place
        in the order sent, the switch made at once, without a slide. Each
        task's output keeps how far it was scrolled, and whether its lock to
        the bottom was on, while another is selected, so selecting it again
        shows it just as it was left, locked tables showing all that arrived
        meanwhile. The selected task's header keeps its mode's colour, as the
        latest task's always has, and the right sidebar shows the selected
        task's referenced spec, understanding, and subagents while it runs,
        and the other running task's once it has finished while another
        still runs.

        A newly sent task, once it starts building, is selected, as the
        latest task always has been, the one selected before becoming a
        compact row. Otherwise the selection stays where it was put: a task
        finishing doesn't move it. A task other than the latest that
        finishes leaves the header for the previous tasks as soon as it isn't
        selected, there showing as any finished task does; one finishing
        while selected stays, in full, until another is selected, and then
        leaves. The latest task always stays, compact or in full, finished
        or not, as it always heads the view. Each open project keeps its own
        selection, as it keeps the rest of its message list.

    previousTasks:
        A task in the header, compact or in full, is not among the previous
        tasks, and isn't counted in their row, which counts every task but
        those the header shows. Once it leaves the header, it is among them
        as any task is.
EOF
f=spec/scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.pi
sed -i 's#^from ./ReferencedSpec import MessageListReferencedSpecShape$#from ./ReferencedSpec import MessageListReferencedSpecShape\nfrom ./RunningTasks import MessageListRunningTasksShape#' $f
sed -i 's#^    status: {MessageListStatusShape}$#    status: {MessageListStatusShape}\n    runningTasks: {MessageListRunningTasksShape}#' $f
piton check 2>&1 | tail -3
