content.text:
I changed the spec so the header shows every task under way, with one selected in full and the rest as compact rows. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 79 files, and the new "Running Tasks" section is in the refreshed reference.

## What changed in the spec

**1. New "Running Tasks" section** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#running-tasks`, from the new `spec/scope/prompt-mode/message-list/RunningTasks.pi`)
- **What the header holds:** the latest task plus every other task that is building, compiling or running, such as a Spec task and a Code task running at once.
- **Selected task:** only one is selected. It shows in full: compiled prompt, hidden anchor's name, status and elapsed time, buttons, and beneath it its output table and changed files.
- **Compact rows (`#compact-row`):** the others are one-line rows stacked above the selected task, oldest at the top.
  - Each is 28px tall, faintly tinted in its mode's colour, with a thin line between rows.
  - Each shows its status label and elapsed time, the first line of its prompt (cut off with an ellipsis), and its Cancel button while it's under way. Nothing else.
  - The tooltip gives the prompt's first lines and its mode.
- **Only one task:** with nothing else under way there are no compact rows, and the header looks as it does today.
- **Selecting (`#selecting`):**
  - Clicking a compact row selects it straight away, with no animation, and the previously selected task becomes a compact row.
  - Each task keeps its scroll position and bottom lock while another is selected.
  - The right sidebar follows the selected task while it runs.
  - A newly sent task is selected once it starts building. Otherwise the selection only moves when you click.
  - A task that isn't the latest leaves the header once it has finished and isn't selected. If it finishes while selected, it stays until you pick another.
  - The latest task always stays.
  - Each open project keeps its own selection.
- **Previous tasks (`#previous-tasks`):** tasks shown in the header aren't in the previous tasks list and aren't counted in its row.

**2. Supporting changes**
- **Layout** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md`, `#basic-design-and-layout` and `#previous-tasks`): the view's layout and the previous tasks row count are updated to match.
- **Cancelling** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/sending/index.md#cancelling`): Cancel sits on the selected task's header. Each compact row has its own Cancel, and clicking it never selects the row. A task running in the other lane no longer shows among the previous tasks as "Running".
- **Activity list** (`.claude/reference/scope/running-activity/index.md#list`): clicking a running task there selects it in the header and shows its output in full, rather than opening it among the previous tasks.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791132300-Prompt_ea29fc7e259b1dbd.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `MessageList`: `#running-tasks` (`#description`, `#compact-row`, `#selecting`, `#previous-tasks`), with `#status`/`#elapsed` and `#backgrounds` as they stand.
- `PromptEditor`: `#basic-design-and-layout`, `#previous-tasks`.
- `PromptSendingScope`: `#cancelling`.
- `RunningActivityScope`: `#list`.
- `RightSidebarScope`: it follows the selected task, as `#running-tasks` says.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

I changed the spec so the harness is never given your claude.ai account's connectors, so connector notices can't reach your replies. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 79 files, and the new paragraph is in the refreshed reference.

The message came from the harness, not from Suspense: Claude Code was loading those connectors and telling the model to report the ones still waiting for sign-in. I'll stop passing it on in my own replies from now on as well.

## What changed in the spec

I added one paragraph to the Harnesses section in `spec/scope/harness-integration/index.pi` (`.claude/reference/scope/harness-integration/index.md#harnesses`):

- **No connectors:** no run Suspense starts, on the host or in a container, gets your claude.ai account's connectors such as Gmail, Calendar or Drive. That applies whatever is connected or left unauthorized.
- **How:** Claude Code is run with `ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS=false` in its environment.
- **Effect:** the harness is never told a connector needs authorizing or is still connecting. It never searches for or calls one, and never passes such a notice on, so nothing like it shows in task output, answers or anywhere else.
- **Project servers kept:** MCP servers your project configures for host runs are left alone. Container runs still have none, as before.

**One thing I haven't confirmed:** I believe `ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS` is the setting that turns these connectors off in Claude Code, but I haven't checked it against the installed version. The code step should verify the exact name.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791132568-HideConnectorAuthorizationMessage.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `HarnessIntegrationScope`: `#harnesses`. Set the variable in the environment of every Claude Code run: tasks, questions, one-off runs, file search, and the notes, commit messages and titles, both on the host and in containers.
- `ContainerEnvironmentScope`: unchanged; container runs still get no MCP servers.

### Shape

#### Description

A form titled "New Project", with a close button, holding the project's name, where it goes, the template it starts from, and its Belay options, and along the bottom a "Cancel" button and a primary "New" button that creates it. The name field has focus when the form opens.

#### Layout

The form's body is two columns of equal width side by side, top aligned, scrolling together when the panel is too short for them. The first holds the project itself: its name, its location, the Git checkbox, and the spec, code, and shape roots. The second holds what it starts from and what it's written for: the template, then the agents.

#### Name

A "Name" field for the project's name, which is also the name of its folder. It can't be empty, contain a slash or backslash, or be "." or "..".

#### Location

A "Location" row showing the folder the project's folder goes in, with a "Browse…" button beside it. It starts in the folder holding the open project, or the user's home folder when no project is open. Beneath it, muted, the full path of the folder that will be created.
Browse opens a [FolderBrowserScope](../../ui/components/folder-browser/index.md#folder-browser-scope) in place of the form, titled "Choose where the project goes" and starting in the current location. A new folder for the project to go in can be created from there. Choosing a folder makes it the location, and choosing or cancelling goes back to the form, just as it was left.

#### Git

Beneath the location, an "Initialize a Git repository" checkbox, checked to start with. Its label is shown in full, like the agents' labels.

#### Templates

At the top of the second column, a "Template" group lists the templates a project can start from, one row each, in order, as radio buttons, only one chosen at a time: each shows the template's name, and beneath it, muted, what it holds. The first is chosen to start with. There are two:

- "Base", with nothing more than the project needs: an empty index.pi in the spec root
- "Scope, concept, and shape", which seeds the spec root with a lib of the abstract scope, concept, and shape anchors a spec is written with, each in a file of its own, an index.pi in the lib exporting them all, an index.pi in the spec root using the lib, and an example scope, with its concept and shape, to start from

The templates are folders in the project-templates folder at the root of the Suspense repository, one per template, and are built into the application when it is built, so changing or adding one changes what the next build offers. Each holds a template.json giving its name, its description, and its place in the order, and, in a spec folder, the files it seeds the spec root with, laid out as they are to be written there. A template with no spec folder seeds nothing more than the base does.

#### Agents

Beneath the template, in the second column, an "Agents" group of checkboxes, one per agent Belay has an adapter for, each with the directory it writes into: "Claude Code" (.claude), "OpenCode" (.opencode), and "Codex" (.codex). Only Claude Code starts checked. At least one must be checked.
Each checkbox's label is shown in full beside it, vertically centred on it, with room below its baseline so the bottoms of letters like p and y, and of the brackets, are never cut off.

#### Folders

Three fields, each a path relative to the project folder: "Spec root", starting as ./spec; "Code root", starting as ./src; and "Shape root", starting as ./spec/shape, which can be left empty to go without one. Spec root and code root can't be empty. A path is written with a leading ./ whether or not it was typed with one, and none can be absolute or climb out of the project with "..".

#### Config

The piton.config.pi written for the project uses @piton/config and @piton/belay. It exports a piton-config anchor named after the project, its name in PascalCase from its letters and digits, or "Project" when that leaves nothing or starts with a digit, whose root is the spec root, whose entry is index.pi in the spec root, and whose only framework is a belay-config anchor named BelayConfiguration. That anchor has the code root as its codeRoot, the shape root as its shapeRoot unless there is none, and an adapter for each checked agent, in the order they are

##### Listed

ClaudeCodeAdapter, OpenCodeAdapter, and CodexAdapter, each

imported from @piton/belay. The file is written in Piton's canonical formatting.
With OpenCode checked, an opencode.json is also written in the project's folder, unless there is one: it lists the AGENTS.md files under the code root, as `<code root>/**/AGENTS.md`, as instructions, since OpenCode doesn't load the guidance Belay places throughout the code on its own, and denies the skills whose names start with x-, the ones Belay writes for commands, so OpenCode doesn't also offer them as ordinary skills.

#### Creating

"New" is disabled, with a tooltip saying why, until the name is valid, the paths are, and an agent is checked, and while a project is being created. A field that isn't valid says why beneath it once something has been typed in it.
Pressing it creates the project's folder, and any folders leading to it, then writes piton.config.pi there, creates the spec root, writes the chosen template's files into it, or an empty index.pi when the template gives none, and creates the code root and any shape root. It never overwrites anything: a folder that already holds a piton.config.pi is refused, a file already in the spec root is left as it is, and folders that already exist are kept. A project created from either template builds with `piton build` straight away.
With "Initialize a Git repository" checked, once the rest is created the project's folder is made a Git repository with `git init`, unless it already is the top of one, and a .gitignore is written there ignoring what Suspense keeps for this machine alone rather than for the project, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. An existing .gitignore is left as it is. Nothing is committed. If Git fails, the project still opens, and a warning notification says the repository couldn't be initialized, and why.
Once created, the project opens as if opened with the [OpenProjectScope](../project/open-project/index.md#open-project-scope), becoming the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope), and the form closes. If anything fails, the form stays open and says what went wrong above its buttons.

A "Location" row showing the folder the project's folder goes in, with a "Browse…" button beside it. It starts in the folder holding the open project, or the user's home folder when no project is open. Beneath it, muted, the full path of the folder that will be created.
Browse opens a [FolderBrowserScope](../../ui/components/folder-browser/index.md#folder-browser-scope) in place of the form, titled "Choose where the project goes" and starting in the current location. A new folder for the project to go in can be created from there. Choosing a folder makes it the location, and choosing or cancelling goes back to the form, just as it was left.

#### Git

Beneath the location, an "Initialize a Git repository" checkbox, checked to start with. Its label is shown in full, like the agents' labels.

#### Templates

At the top of the second column, a "Template" group lists the templates a project can start from, one row each, in order, as radio buttons, only one chosen at a time: each shows the template's name, and beneath it, muted, what it holds. The first is chosen to start with. There are two:

- "Base", with nothing more than the project needs: an empty index.pi in the spec root
- "Scope, concept, and shape", which seeds the spec root with a lib of the abstract scope, concept, and shape anchors a spec is written with, each in a file of its own, an index.pi in the lib exporting them all, an index.pi in the spec root using the lib, and an example scope, with its concept and shape, to start from

The templates are folders in the project-templates folder at the root of the Suspense repository, one per template, and are built into the application when it is built, so changing or adding one changes what the next build offers. Each holds a template.json giving its name, its description, and its place in the order, and, in a spec folder, the files it seeds the spec root with, laid out as they are to be written there. A template with no spec folder seeds nothing more than the base does.

#### Agents

Beneath the template, in the second column, an "Agents" group of checkboxes, one per agent Belay has an adapter for, each with the directory it writes into: "Claude Code" (.claude), "OpenCode" (.opencode), and "Codex" (.codex). Only Claude Code starts checked. At least one must be checked.
Each checkbox's label is shown in full beside it, vertically centred on it, with room below its baseline so the bottoms of letters like p and y, and of the brackets, are never cut off.

#### Folders

Three fields, each a path relative to the project folder: "Spec root", starting as ./spec; "Code root", starting as ./src; and "Shape root", starting as ./spec/shape, which can be left empty to go without one. Spec root and code root can't be empty. A path is written with a leading ./ whether or not it was typed with one, and none can be absolute or climb out of the project with "..".

#### Config

The piton.config.pi written for the project uses @piton/config and @piton/belay. It exports a piton-config anchor named after the project, its name in PascalCase from its letters and digits, or "Project" when that leaves nothing or starts with a digit, whose root is the spec root, whose entry is index.pi in the spec root, and whose only framework is a belay-config anchor named BelayConfiguration. That anchor has the code root as its codeRoot, the shape root as its shapeRoot unless there is none, and an adapter for each checked agent, in the order they are

##### Listed

ClaudeCodeAdapter, OpenCodeAdapter, and CodexAdapter, each

imported from @piton/belay. The file is written in Piton's canonical formatting.
With OpenCode checked, an opencode.json is also written in the project's folder, unless there is one: it lists the AGENTS.md files under the code root, as `<code root>/**/AGENTS.md`, as instructions, since OpenCode doesn't load the guidance Belay places throughout the code on its own, and denies the skills whose names start with x-, the ones Belay writes for commands, so OpenCode doesn't also offer them as ordinary skills.

#### Creating

"New" is disabled, with a tooltip saying why, until the name is valid, the paths are, and an agent is checked, and while a project is being created. A field that isn't valid says why beneath it once something has been typed in it.
Pressing it creates the project's folder, and any folders leading to it, then writes piton.config.pi there, creates the spec root, writes the chosen template's files into it, or an empty index.pi when the template gives none, and creates the code root and any shape root. It never overwrites anything: a folder that already holds a piton.config.pi is refused, a file already in the spec root is left as it is, and folders that already exist are kept. A project created from either template builds with `piton build` straight away.
With "Initialize a Git repository" checked, once the rest is created the project's folder is made a Git repository with `git init`, unless it already is the top of one, and a .gitignore is written there ignoring what Suspense keeps for this machine alone rather than for the project, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. An existing .gitignore is left as it is. Nothing is committed. If Git fails, the project still opens, and a warning notification says the repository couldn't be initialized, and why.
Once created, the project opens as if opened with the [OpenProjectScope](../project/open-project/index.md#open-project-scope), becoming the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope), and the form closes. If anything fails, the form stays open and says what went wrong above its buttons.

The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command, and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.
On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user, with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages.

#### Missing Podman

components: [gpui-kit](https://gpui-kit.com/)
```

#### Platforms

- windows
- mac
- linux

#### Child Processes

On Windows, no program the application runs opens a window of its own. A release build on Windows is a GUI application with no console, so Windows gives every console program it starts a window of its own unless told not to. So every child process the application starts on the host, git, piton, for its builds, slicing, its language server, and the fluency, podman, the harness and its one-off runs, a run target's shell, and the commands that stop a process, is started without a console window, so nothing flashes on screen while the application works, in a release build as in a development one.
What these programs print is still read as ever, and the login view's command, run under a pseudo-terminal, still works as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says. On macOS and Linux, nothing changes in how a program is started.

content.text:
I couldn't find the cause in the spec. It said nothing about who owns the files Suspense creates, so I added a rule that everything it creates belongs to the signed-in user. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 79 files, and the new text is in the refreshed reference.

**The two likely causes:**
- **Suspense running as administrator.** Files an elevated process creates on Windows end up owned by the Administrators group.
- **Files written from the Podman machine.** A container run writes into the Windows project folder from inside a virtual machine, which can leave odd ownership.

The spec now rules out both, but the code step should confirm which one actually happened to you.

## What changed in the spec

**1. New "File Ownership" section** (`.claude/reference/scope/application/index.md#file-ownership`)
- **Who owns what:** every file and folder Suspense creates belongs to the user, as if you'd made it yourself, on every platform. That covers new project folders and their contents, `.suspense` data, files written by tasks or the editor, and Suspense's own files such as preferences.
- **No elevation on Windows:** Suspense declares that it runs with the rights of whoever starts it and never requires elevation. Its installer and self-update must not start it elevated either.
- **If it runs elevated anyway:** each file and folder it creates is still owned by the signed-in user, not Administrators, and takes its permissions from the folder it's in. The same applies to the programs it starts, including git's repository, so git never refuses a project as owned by someone else.
- **Never left behind:** nothing is ever left owned by Administrators, SYSTEM or another account.

**2. New Project** (`.claude/reference/scope/new-project/index.md#creating`): everything the form creates, Git repository included, belongs to you, so the project can be edited, built and committed right away with no ownership to take.

**3. Containers** (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md#description`): on macOS and Windows, container runs act as you rather than root inside the Podman machine. Files they write into a folder mounted from Windows are yours and inherit that folder's permissions.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791132843-ProjectsCreatedWithWindowsAdmin.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ApplicationScope`: `#file-ownership`. This covers the Windows build's setting that it runs without elevation, the installer, self-update, and setting ownership when Suspense finds itself elevated.
- `NewProjectScope`: `#creating`.
- `ContainerEnvironmentScope`: `#description`, for the user Podman runs containers as on Windows and macOS.

# Open Project Scope

## How To Build

A OpenProjectScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A OpenProjectScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Pitch

Opens an existing Piton project by choosing its piton.config.pi, making the folder holding it the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../../project-directory/index.md#project-directory-scope).
37:system: The application's own commands, each doing what its toolbar control or shortcut does: "Open Project…", which opens the [OpenProjectScope](../project/open-project/index.md#open-project-scope), "Build", "Dark mode" or "Light mode" (whichever is not the current one), "Settings…", which opens the [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope), and "Quit". Build

cd /workspace; mkdir -p spec/scope/import-project; cat > spec/scope/import-project/index.pi <<'EOF'
use /lib
use /ui
from /scope/application import ApplicationScope
from /scope/new-project import NewProjectScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/project-directory import ProjectDirectoryScope
from /scope/project/open-project import OpenProjectScope
from /ui/components/folder-browser import FolderBrowserScope

export ui-component ImportProjectScope:
    concept: {ImportProjectConcept}

concept ImportProjectConcept:
    pitch:
        Makes an existing folder, such as a codebase that has never had a
        spec, into a Piton project, writing its piton.config.pi set up for
        Belay and the agents it should write for, as a new project's is, and
        opens it, leaving everything already in the folder as it was.

    shape: {ImportProjectShape}

shape ImportProjectShape:
    description:
        A form titled "Import Project", with a close button, laid out as the
        @{NewProjectScope}'s form is, two columns of equal width, and along
        the bottom a "Cancel" button and a primary "Import" button. It holds
        the same fields as a new project's, each looking and checked just as
        it does there, but for where the project is: in place of the Name
        field and the Location row, a "Folder" row, at the top of the first
        column, beneath which come the Git checkbox, the spec, code, and
        shape roots, and, in the second column, the template and the agents.
        The folder's Browse button has focus when the form opens.

    folder:
        A "Folder" row showing the existing folder to import, with a
        "Browse…" button beside it, empty to start with, reading "Choose a
        folder", muted. Browse opens a @{FolderBrowserScope} in place of the
        form, titled "Choose the folder to import", starting in the folder
        holding the open project, or the user's home folder when no project
        is open. Choosing a folder makes it the folder, and choosing or
        cancelling goes back to the form, just as it was left. Beneath the
        row, muted, the folder's full path. The project's name, which names
        its config's anchor as a new project's name does, is the folder's
        name.

        A folder that already holds a piton.config.pi is already a project,
        and can't be imported: the row says so beneath it, with an "Open it
        instead" link that opens it as the @{OpenProjectScope} would and
        closes the form. A folder the user can't write to says that instead.

    defaults:
        Once a folder is chosen, the fields start from what is in it, and
        what has been typed in a field since is kept when another folder is
        chosen. The spec root starts as ./spec. The code root starts as ./src
        where the folder has a src folder, and as ./, the folder itself,
        where it doesn't, since an imported codebase's code is most often all
        of it. The shape root starts as ./spec/shape. "Initialize a Git
        repository" starts checked where the folder isn't in a Git
        repository; where it is, the checkbox is checked, disabled, and reads
        "Already a Git repository". The template and the agents start as a
        new project's do.

        The roots are written and checked as a new project's are, but the
        code root may be ./, the folder itself, holding the spec root, as the
        project's locations allow. A root that already exists in the folder
        is used as it is, and says so beneath its field, muted, "Uses the
        existing folder".

    importing:
        "Import" is disabled, with a tooltip saying why, until a folder that
        can be imported is chosen, the paths are valid, and an agent is
        checked, and while it is importing.

        Pressing it writes the folder's piton.config.pi, just as a new
        project's config is written, named after the folder, with its roots
        and an adapter for each checked agent, and opencode.json as a new
        project writes it, unless there is one. It creates the spec root, the
        code root, and any shape root where they aren't there, and writes the
        chosen template's files into the spec root, each only where no file
        of that name is there already, or an empty index.pi where the
        template gives none and the spec root has no index.pi. It never
        overwrites, moves, renames, or deletes anything already in the
        folder: the folder's own files, its code, and anything already in a
        root are left exactly as they were, and nothing outside the folder
        is touched.

        With "Initialize a Git repository" checked, once the rest is written
        the folder is made a Git repository with `git init`, as a new
        project's is, and nothing is committed. Whether or not Git was just
        initialized, where the folder is in a Git repository, a .gitignore in
        the folder is given the lines ignoring what Suspense keeps for this
        machine alone, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says: written as a new
        project's is where there is none, and where there is one, only the
        lines it lacks are added at its end, beneath a "# Suspense" comment,
        the rest of the file left as it was. If Git fails, the project still
        opens, and a warning notification says the repository couldn't be
        initialized, and why.

        Everything it creates belongs to the user, as the @{ApplicationScope}
        says. Once imported, the project opens as if opened with the
        @{OpenProjectScope}, becoming the @{ProjectDirectoryScope}, and the
        form closes. If anything fails, the form stays open and says what
        went wrong above its buttons, and nothing it wrote before the failure
        is left half done: the piton.config.pi is written last, so a folder
        whose import failed is never taken for a project.
EOF

content.text:
I added an Import Project feature to the spec: it makes an existing folder into a project, with the same agent, template and root choices as New Project. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 80 files, and the new page is at `.claude/reference/scope/import-project/index.md`.

## What changed in the spec

**1. New Import Project form** (`spec/scope/import-project/index.pi`)
- **`#description`:** an "Import Project" form laid out like New Project. The Name and Location fields are replaced by a single "Folder" row. Everything else is the same: the Git checkbox, spec/code/shape roots, template and agents. The buttons are Cancel and Import.
- **`#folder`:**
  - Browse opens the folder browser, titled "Choose the folder to import".
  - The project is named after the folder.
  - A folder that already has a `piton.config.pi` is refused, with an "Open it instead" link.
  - A folder you can't write to says so.
- **`#defaults`:**
  - The spec root starts as `./spec`.
  - The code root starts as `./src` if that folder exists, otherwise `./`, meaning the whole folder.
  - The shape root starts as `./spec/shape`.
  - If the folder is already a Git repository, the Git checkbox is checked, disabled and reads "Already a Git repository".
  - A root that already exists is marked "Uses the existing folder".
- **`#importing`:**
  - It writes `piton.config.pi`, and `opencode.json` if OpenCode is checked and there isn't one, the same way New Project does.
  - It creates any missing roots, and adds template files only where no file of that name exists.
  - It never overwrites, moves, renames or deletes anything already in the folder.
  - It optionally runs `git init`. Where the folder is in a Git repository, Suspense's machine-only ignore lines are added to `.gitignore`. An existing `.gitignore` keeps its contents and only the missing lines are added at the end, under a `# Suspense` comment.
  - `piton.config.pi` is written last, so a failed import is never mistaken for a project.
  - On success the project opens as with Open Project; on failure the form stays open and says what went wrong.

**2. Where you open it**
- **Ribbon** (`.claude/reference/ui/components/ribbon/project-tab/index.md`): a slim primary "Import Project…" button sits between New Project and Open Project (`#groups`, `#commands`).
- **Main window** (`.claude/reference/scope/application/MainWindow.md`): `#import-project` opens it in the inset panel, fresh each time, replacing any diff or New Project form there.
- **Palette** (`.claude/reference/scope/palette/index.md`): the system commands now include "New Project…" and "Import Project…".

**Three choices of mine you may want to change:**
- The code root defaults to `./` when there is no `src` folder.
- An existing `.gitignore` gets Suspense's lines added at the end, rather than being left alone as New Project does.
- The import can be used on a folder that's already a Git repository.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791132918-AddImportProjectFeature.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ImportProjectScope`: `#description`, `#folder`, `#defaults`, `#importing`.
- `NewProjectScope`: `#config`, `#agents`, `#folders`, `#templates`, which the import reuses.
- `RibbonProjectTabScope`: `#groups`, `#commands`.
- `MainWindowScope`: `#import-project`.
- `PaletteScope`: its system commands.
- `ApplicationScope`: `#file-ownership`.

Importing a folder that's already inside a Git repository can no longer run `git init` on it. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 80 files, and the new text is in `.claude/reference/scope/import-project/index.md`.

## What changed in the spec

Both changes are in `spec/scope/import-project/index.pi`.

**1. The Git checkbox (`#defaults`)**
- The form checks for a repository with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`. That catches a folder at the top of a repository and a folder inside one, such as a subfolder of a larger repo.
- If the folder is in a repository, "Initialize a Git repository" is unchecked and disabled and reads "Already a Git repository". Its tooltip names the repository's top folder.
- Before this, the checkbox was shown checked but disabled in that case, which could still lead to `git init`.

**2. When Import is pressed (`#importing`)**
- Just before `git init`, the folder is checked again. If it's in a repository by then, `git init` is skipped whatever the checkbox says.
- A nested repository is never created inside an existing one.
- The existing repository's history, branches, index, hooks and configuration are left untouched.
- Adding Suspense's lines to `.gitignore` still happens for a folder that's in a repository, as before.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791133003-Prompt_7ad0d2aa453a3464.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ImportProjectScope`: `#defaults` (detecting a repository and the checkbox state) and `#importing` (checking again and never running `git init` inside a repository).
- `NewProjectScope`: `#creating` is unchanged.

# Ribbon Application Tab Scope

## How To Build

A RibbonApplicationTabScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A RibbonApplicationTabScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The ribbon's Application tab: the commands for the application itself, rather than the project.

### Shape

#### Description

The Application tab of the ribbon, last of the tabs.

#### Groups

```
appearance: An "Appearance" group holds the Brightness command, its one control; there is no Dark mode switch, since the slider reaches both modes.
colours: A "Colours" group, between Appearance and Preferences, holds the Theme command.
preferences: A "Preferences" group holds the Settings command.
help: A "Help" group, the last, after Preferences, holds the Welcome command, then the Walkthrough command, then the Check for Updates command.
```

#### Commands

```
brightness: A "Brightness" slider, which runs the whole interface from its darkest to its lightest: a moon icon, then a horizontal slider 120 pixels wide, then a sun icon, with nothing showing the setting as a number. As a ribbon setting, it has no background of its own, and sits straight on the commands' area, as tall as a slim button. Its tooltip says it makes the whole interface darker or lighter, from its darkest to its lightest, keeping its contrast, and that double-clicking it resets it.
  Its one track runs through every appearance the [ThemeScope](../../../theme/index.md#theme-scope) allows, darkest first: dark mode from its darkest brightness to its lightest, then light mode from its darkest to its lightest, one position for each step, with no switch between them. So all the way left is dark mode at its darkest, and all the way right light mode at its lightest; dragging past dark mode's lightest step changes the window to light mode, and back.
  Dragging it changes the mode and the brightness straight away as it moves, and once it is let go saves the mode showing and each mode's brightness among the [UserPreferencesScope](../../../../scope/user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope). A mode that can't be saved shows a notification titled "Could not save brightness", with why; a brightness that can't be saved fails quietly. Its thumb follows the appearance showing, however that was changed, such as from the palette, but not while it is being dragged.
  Double-clicking anywhere on it, its icons or its track, puts the mode showing back to its brightness at 0, keeping the mode, and saves it; the second click doesn't also move the thumb.
  It is primary, so the collapsed ribbon keeps it: its icons and track as they are, only as wide as they are, as tall as a small button.
theme: A "Theme" button with a palette icon. Clicking it opens the [ThemeEditorScope](../../theme-editor/index.md#theme-editor-scope). Its tooltip says it chooses the base colour, and the colours of Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask.
  It is a full button, and not primary, so the collapsed ribbon leaves it out.
settings: A "Settings" button with a gear icon. Clicking it opens the [SettingsWindowScope](../../../../scope/settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope), where the system prompt each chat tab sends is edited. Its tooltip says so, and gives its keyboard shortcut, Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS).
  It is primary, and a full button.
welcome: A "Welcome" button with a checklist icon. Clicking it opens the [WelcomeScope](../../../../scope/welcome/index.md#welcome-scope), running its checks anew. Its tooltip says it checks that Suspense is ready to run.
  It is a full button, and not primary, so the collapsed ribbon leaves it out.
walkthrough: A "Walkthrough" button with a signpost icon. Clicking it starts the [WalkthroughScope](../../../../scope/walkthrough/index.md#walkthrough-scope) from its first step. Its tooltip says it walks through creating a project and the prompt modes.
  It is a full button, and not primary, so the collapsed ribbon leaves it out.
checkForUpdates: A "Check for Updates" button with a refresh icon. Clicking it checks for an update straight away, as the Updates section's Check for updates does, as the [SelfUpdateScope](../../../../scope/self-update/index.md#self-update-scope) says, whether automatic checks are on or not, and says how it went in a notification, which reads "Suspense is up to date", with the version running; "Downloading Suspense 0.1.N…" when a newer release is found, followed by the "Suspense 0.1.N is ready" notification, with its Restart and Later buttons, once it is staged; or, titled "Could not check for updates", why the check or download failed.
  While a check or download is under way, it shows a spinner in place of its icon and is disabled, its tooltip saying what is under way. While an update is already staged, clicking it shows the "Suspense 0.1.N is ready" notification again, without checking. In a build that can't update itself, as one made on a developer's machine, it is disabled, its tooltip saying why, as the Updates section does. Otherwise its tooltip says it checks for a newer version of Suspense.
  It is a full button, and not primary, so the collapsed ribbon leaves it out.
```

# Ribbon Application Tab Scope

## How To Build

A RibbonApplicationTabScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A RibbonApplicationTabScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The ribbon's Application tab: the commands for the application itself, rather than the project.

### Shape

#### Description

The Application tab of the ribbon, last of the tabs.

#### Groups

```
appearance: An "Appearance" group holds the Brightness command, its one control; there is no Dark mode switch, since the slider reaches both modes.
colours: A "Colours" group, between Appearance and Preferences, holds the Theme command.
preferences: A "Preferences" group holds the Settings command.
help: A "Help" group, the last, after Preferences, holds the Welcome command, then the Walkthrough command, then the Check for Updates command.
```

#### Commands

```
brightness: A "Brightness" slider, which runs the whole interface from its darkest to its lightest: a moon icon, then a horizontal slider 120 pixels wide, then a sun icon, with nothing showing the setting as a number. As a ribbon setting, it has no background of its own, and sits straight on the commands' area, as tall as a slim button. Its tooltip says it makes the whole interface darker or lighter, from its darkest to its lightest, keeping its contrast, and that double-clicking it resets it.
  Its one track runs through every appearance the [ThemeScope](../../../theme/index.md#theme-scope) allows, darkest first: dark mode from its darkest brightness to its lightest, then light mode from its darkest to its lightest, one position for each step, with no switch between them. So all the way left is dark mode at its darkest, and all the way right light mode at its lightest; dragging past dark mode's lightest step changes the window to light mode, and back.
  Dragging it changes the mode and the brightness straight away as it moves, and once it is let go saves the mode showing and each mode's brightness among the [UserPreferencesScope](../../../../scope/user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope). A mode that can't be saved shows a notification titled "Could not save brightness", with why; a brightness that can't be saved fails quietly. Its thumb follows the appearance showing, however that was changed, such as from the palette, but not while it is being dragged.
  Double-clicking anywhere on it, its icons or its track, puts the mode showing back to its brightness at 0, keeping the mode, and saves it; the second click doesn't also move the thumb.
  It is primary, so the collapsed ribbon keeps it: its icons and track as they are, only as wide as they are, as tall as a small button.
theme: A "Theme" button with a palette icon. Clicking it opens the [ThemeEditorScope](../../theme-editor/index.md#theme-editor-scope). Its tooltip says it chooses the base colour, and the colours of Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask.
  It is a full button, and not primary, so the collapsed ribbon leaves it out.
settings: A "Settings" button with a gear icon. Clicking it opens the [SettingsWindowScope](../../../../scope/settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope), where the system prompt each chat tab sends is edited. Its tooltip says so, and gives its keyboard shortcut, Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS).
  It is primary, and a full button.
welcome: A "Welcome" button with a checklist icon. Clicking it opens the [WelcomeScope](../../../../scope/welcome/index.md#welcome-scope), running its checks anew. Its tooltip says it checks that Suspense is ready to run.
  It is a full button, and not primary, so the collapsed ribbon leaves it out.
walkthrough: A "Walkthrough" button with a signpost icon. Clicking it starts the [WalkthroughScope](../../../../scope/walkthrough/index.md#walkthrough-scope) from its first step. Its tooltip says it walks through creating a project and the prompt modes.
  It is a full button, and not primary, so the collapsed ribbon leaves it out.
checkForUpdates: A "Check for Updates" button with a refresh icon. Clicking it checks for an update straight away, as the Updates section's Check for updates does, as the [SelfUpdateScope](../../../../scope/self-update/index.md#self-update-scope) says, whether automatic checks are on or not, and says how it went in a notification, which reads "Suspense is up to date", with the version running; "Downloading Suspense 0.1.N…" when a newer release is found, followed by the "Suspense 0.1.N is ready" notification, with its Restart and Later buttons, once it is staged; or, titled "Could not check for updates", why the check or download failed.
  While a check or download is under way, it shows a spinner in place of its icon and is disabled, its tooltip saying what is under way. While an update is already staged, clicking it shows the "Suspense 0.1.N is ready" notification again, without checking. In a build that can't update itself, as one made on a developer's machine, it is disabled, its tooltip saying why, as the Updates section does. Otherwise its tooltip says it checks for a newer version of Suspense.
  It is a full button, and not primary, so the collapsed ribbon leaves it out.

use /lib

export ui-component AboutScope:
    concept: {AboutConcept}

concept AboutConcept:
    pitch:
        What this copy of Suspense is: its name, its version, and the build it
        came from, so it can be told which one is running, as when reporting
        a bug.

    shape: {AboutShape}

shape AboutShape:
    description:
        A small panel titled "About Suspense", with a close button, its
        contents centred: the application's icon, 64 pixels square, then
        "Suspense" in large semibold text, then a line saying what it is, "A
        desktop application for writing a Piton spec and the code it
        describes with a coding agent", muted, wrapping.

    details:
        Beneath, a short list of labelled figures, a label at the left,
        muted, and its value at the right, in tabular figures where it is a
        number:

        \\
        - Version: the version running, as the @{EdgeReleasesScope} bakes it into the binary, "0.1.42", followed, muted, by "edge" for an edge build or "development build" for one made elsewhere, as on a developer's machine
        - Commit: the commit it was built from, its short hash, where the build records one, left out otherwise
        - Built: the date it was built, where the build records it, left out otherwise
        - Platform: the operating system and architecture it was built for, as "Windows x86-64", "macOS arm64", or "Linux x86-64"
        - Piton: the version of piton found on the machine, as `piton --version` prints it, or "Not installed"
        \\

        Each figure is found without anything being run but `piton --version`,
        which is run once the panel opens, its row reading "Checking…" until
        it answers, never holding the panel back from opening.

    links:
        Beneath the figures, for an edge build, a link to the repository it
        is published from, on GitHub, reading its `owner/name`, and one to
        this version's release, "Release notes", each opening in the browser.
        A build with no repository shows neither.

    actions:
        Along the bottom, a "Copy details" button, with a copy icon, which
        puts the figures on the clipboard as plain text, one "Label: value"
        per line, "Suspense" first, for pasting into a bug report, and reads
        "Copied", with a check, for 2 seconds after; and, where the build can
        update itself, a "Check for Updates" button, doing what the ribbon's
        does, as the @{SelfUpdateScope} says. A primary "Close" button, or
        <Escape>, closes the panel.

content.content:
## Concept

### Pitch

Suspense keeps itself up to date: it looks for a newer edge release, downloads it in the background, and puts it in place of its own binary when it restarts, so the newest build is only a restart away.

### Shape

#### Description

Updates come from the edge releases, as the [EdgeReleasesScope](../edge-releases/index.md#edge-releases-scope) says, published in the GitHub repository the running build was published from, which it knows because that is baked into it. Only such a build updates itself. A build made anywhere else, as on a developer's machine, never looks for an update, never downloads one, and never replaces its binary, and the Updates section says why.

#### Checking

A check asks GitHub's releases API for the repository's releases, pre-releases included, and takes the one with the highest version `0.1.N`, comparing N as a number, never as text. It is newer only when its N is greater than the running build's; an older or equal one is never taken, so an update never goes back. A release without the asset for the running platform is passed over for the newest one that has it.
Suspense checks a few seconds after it starts, and then every 6 hours while it runs, in the background, never holding up anything else, and only while "Check for updates automatically" is on, as it is until turned off. That choice is remembered for the user, as the [UserPreferencesScope](../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope) says. Check for updates, in the Updates section, checks straight away, whether it is on or not. A check that can't be made, as with no network or GitHub refusing it, is quiet when automatic, trying again at the next, and says why when asked for.

#### Downloading

A newer release found is downloaded straight away, in the background, taking the asset for the platform and architecture running, `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`, `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip`, or `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`. It is checked against the size GitHub gives for it, and against its SHA-256 digest where GitHub gives one, and one that doesn't match is thrown away and never used. The binary is taken out of the archive and staged beside the running binary, in the same directory, so it can be put in place by a rename, marked executable where the platform has such a mark. One download runs at a time; a newer release found while one is staged replaces it. A download that fails says so in the Updates section, and is tried again at the next check.
Where the running binary's directory can't be written, nothing is downloaded, and the Updates section says that Suspense can't update itself there, with the directory, and a link to the release's page, opened in the browser, so it can be updated by hand.

#### Restarting

Once an update is staged, a notification says "Suspense 0.1.N is ready", with a Restart button and a Later button. The Updates section says the same, with a Restart button, for as long as it stays staged. Later only closes the notification; the update stays staged, and is put in place whenever Suspense next quits.
Restart quits as quitting does, as the [MainWindowScope](../application/MainWindow.md#main-window-scope) says, asking first while work is running, and doing nothing more if the quit is cancelled, then starts Suspense again from the same path once the update is in place. However Suspense quits, a staged update is put in place as it does: the staged binary is renamed over the running one, the running one renamed aside first where the platform won't replace a running binary, as on Windows. The binary set aside is deleted at the next launch. An update left staged by a quit that never finished, as a crash, is put in place at the next launch, before anything else, and takes effect at the launch after, the Updates section saying a restart finishes it.
Putting an update in place never leaves Suspense without a binary: a step that fails puts back the binary that was there, and the Updates section says why it couldn't update.

#### Updates Section

The [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) has an "Updates" section. It says the running version, as "Suspense 0.1.42", and where it can't update itself, as for a build made elsewhere, why, and offers nothing else. Otherwise it shows a checkbox reading "Check for updates automatically", a "Check for updates" button, disabled while a check or download is under way, and a line saying where things stand: "Checking for updates…", "Suspense is up to date", checked when, as "Checked 5 minutes ago", "Downloading 0.1.N…" with how much has come, "Suspense 0.1.N is ready" with a Restart button, or, in the theme's error colour, why the last check, download, or update failed.
## Concept

### Pitch

Every commit that lands on main is built for Linux, Windows, and macOS, and published on GitHub as an edge release anyone can download, so the newest Suspense is always one download away.

### Shape

#### Description

A GitHub Actions workflow in this application's own repository, `.github/workflows/edge.yml`, builds and publishes an edge release for each push to its `main` branch, and for nothing else: not pull requests, not other branches, and not tags. It runs once per push, for the commit at its head. Edge releases are nightly-like builds of whatever main holds, not stable releases, and are marked as such.

#### Version

An edge release's version is `0.1.N`, where N is the commit's sequence number on main: how many commits its history holds, counted by `git rev-list --count` on that commit, so each commit on main has its own number, one more than its parent's, and the same commit always gets the same version. The workflow checks out the whole history to count it, never a shallow clone.
The version is baked into the binary when it is built, so the application knows its own version, and so is the repository it is published from, as `owner/name`, which marks it as an edge build that can update itself. A build made anywhere else, as on a developer's machine, has the version Cargo.toml gives it, and no repository.

#### Builds

The application is built in release mode, one job per platform, run side by side, each on a GitHub-hosted runner of that platform:

- Linux, x86_64, on Ubuntu
- Windows, x86_64
- macOS, Apple silicon, aarch64

Each job runs the project's tests before building, and installs whatever the platform needs to build the application's GUI, as Linux's windowing and font libraries. Each builds from the repository as it is at that commit, the default prompts in `.suspense/system-prompts` included, as the application's build needs them. The Windows binary is a GUI application, opening no console of its own, as the [ApplicationScope](../application/index.md#application-scope) says.
The code compiles, its tests included, on each of the three platforms, with no compiler warnings on any of them. What differs between platforms, as a system call whose signature differs between Linux and macOS, or an import only one platform uses, is written for each platform it builds on, and gated to the platforms that use it, so nothing is unused or mistyped on another. No deprecated function is called where its replacement is available. Each job denies warnings in its build and its tests, so a warning fails the job, and no edge release is published, as for an error. A build script's own notes, as one saying where the default prompts were taken from, are not compiler warnings, and don't fail it.
Every test passes on each of the three platforms, on a fresh GitHub-hosted runner, every time, run in parallel as `cargo test` runs them, in any order. A test asks for what the platform it runs on does, never what one platform does:

- A shortcut is pressed as the platform binds it, as the application binds it there, <Cmd> on macOS where <Ctrl> elsewhere, as <Cmd+Shift+Enter> opening the chat input's send menu on macOS, so a test that opens a menu, sends, or saves with a keystroke does so on every platform.
- A path is built with the platform's own separators and compared as the platform compares paths, never written as a literal with `/` and compared as text, and line endings are compared without regard to `\r\n` or `\n`.
- Nothing a test needs is taken from the machine: not piton, Podman, a harness, a network, the user's home or config directories, or a display's scale. What it needs, it makes or fakes in a temporary directory of its own, removed when it ends, so the runners, which have no piton or Podman, run it as a developer's machine does. Git, which every runner has, is the one exception, configured with a name and email for the test alone.
- A test that waits on something running in the background waits for it to happen, with a timeout generous enough for the slowest runner, never for a fixed time.
- A test finds what it clicks or reads by the element ids the interface gives it, kept in step with the interface: an id a test uses is one the interface has, under the scope it is looked for in, in the frame it is looked for, as a menu's options once the menu is open.

#### Publishing

Once every platform's job has succeeded, one GitHub release is published for the commit, tagged `v0.1.N` on that commit, titled "Suspense 0.1.N (edge)", and marked as a pre-release, never as the latest stable release. Its notes give the commit's short hash, linked to the commit, and its message's first line.
Its assets are one archive per platform, each holding the binary alone, named for the version and the platform:

- `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`
- `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip`
- `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`

The binaries are not signed or notarized.
If any platform's job fails, nothing is published for that commit, so no edge release ever lacks a platform; the workflow run shows which job failed. A release already published for a version, as when a run is re-run, is never published twice: the run publishes nothing more for it and succeeds.
Pushes are handled in the order they came: a run waits for the one before it to finish rather than cancelling it, so every commit on main gets its edge release. The workflow is given only the permission it needs to publish, writing the repository's contents, and uses the token GitHub gives each run, needing no secrets of its own.

An update left staged by a quit that never finished, as a crash, is put in place at the next launch, before anything else, and takes effect at the launch after, the Updates section saying a restart finishes it.
Putting an update in place never leaves Suspense without a binary: a step that fails puts back the binary that was there, and the Updates section says why it couldn't update.

#### Updates Section

The [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) has an "Updates" section. It says the running version, as "Suspense 0.1.42", and where it can't update itself, as for a build made elsewhere, why, and offers nothing else. Otherwise it shows a checkbox reading "Check for updates automatically", a "Check for updates" button, disabled while a check or download is under way, and a line saying where things stand: "Checking for updates…", "Suspense is up to date", checked when, as "Checked 5 minutes ago", "Downloading 0.1.N…" with how much has come, "Suspense 0.1.N is ready" with a Restart button, or, in the theme's error colour, why the last check, download, or update failed.
## Concept

### Pitch

Every commit that lands on main is built for Linux, Windows, and macOS, and published on GitHub as an edge release anyone can download, so the newest Suspense is always one download away.

### Shape

#### Description

A GitHub Actions workflow in this application's own repository, `.github/workflows/edge.yml`, builds and publishes an edge release for each push to its `main` branch, and for nothing else: not pull requests, not other branches, and not tags. It runs once per push, for the commit at its head. Edge releases are nightly-like builds of whatever main holds, not stable releases, and are marked as such.

#### Version

An edge release's version is `0.1.N`, where N is the commit's sequence number on main: how many commits its history holds, counted by `git rev-list --count` on that commit, so each commit on main has its own number, one more than its parent's, and the same commit always gets the same version. The workflow checks out the whole history to count it, never a shallow clone.
The version is baked into the binary when it is built, so the application knows its own version, and so is the repository it is published from, as `owner/name`, which marks it as an edge build that can update itself. A build made anywhere else, as on a developer's machine, has the version Cargo.toml gives it, and no repository.

#### Builds

The application is built in release mode, one job per platform, run side by side, each on a GitHub-hosted runner of that platform:

- Linux, x86_64, on Ubuntu
- Windows, x86_64
- macOS, Apple silicon, aarch64

Each job runs the project's tests before building, and installs whatever the platform needs to build the application's GUI, as Linux's windowing and font libraries. Each builds from the repository as it is at that commit, the default prompts in `.suspense/system-prompts` included, as the application's build needs them. The Windows binary is a GUI application, opening no console of its own, as the [ApplicationScope](../application/index.md#application-scope) says.
The code compiles, its tests included, on each of the three platforms, with no compiler warnings on any of them. What differs between platforms, as a system call whose signature differs between Linux and macOS, or an import only one platform uses, is written for each platform it builds on, and gated to the platforms that use it, so nothing is unused or mistyped on another. No deprecated function is called where its replacement is available. Each job denies warnings in its build and its tests, so a warning fails the job, and no edge release is published, as for an error. A build script's own notes, as one saying where the default prompts were taken from, are not compiler warnings, and don't fail it.
Every test passes on each of the three platforms, on a fresh GitHub-hosted runner, every time, run in parallel as `cargo test` runs them, in any order. A test asks for what the platform it runs on does, never what one platform does:

- A shortcut is pressed as the platform binds it, as the application binds it there, <Cmd> on macOS where <Ctrl> elsewhere, as <Cmd+Shift+Enter> opening the chat input's send menu on macOS, so a test that opens a menu, sends, or saves with a keystroke does so on every platform.
- A path is built with the platform's own separators and compared as the platform compares paths, never written as a literal with `/` and compared as text, and line endings are compared without regard to `\r\n` or `\n`.
- Nothing a test needs is taken from the machine: not piton, Podman, a harness, a network, the user's home or config directories, or a display's scale. What it needs, it makes or fakes in a temporary directory of its own, removed when it ends, so the runners, which have no piton or Podman, run it as a developer's machine does. Git, which every runner has, is the one exception, configured with a name and email for the test alone.
- A test that waits on something running in the background waits for it to happen, with a timeout generous enough for the slowest runner, never for a fixed time.
- A test finds what it clicks or reads by the element ids the interface gives it, kept in step with the interface: an id a test uses is one the interface has, under the scope it is looked for in, in the frame it is looked for, as a menu's options once the menu is open.

#### Publishing

Once every platform's job has succeeded, one GitHub release is published for the commit, tagged `v0.1.N` on that commit, titled "Suspense 0.1.N (edge)", and marked as a pre-release, never as the latest stable release. Its notes give the commit's short hash, linked to the commit, and its message's first line.
Its assets are one archive per platform, each holding the binary alone, named for the version and the platform:

- `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`
- `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip`
- `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`

The binaries are not signed or notarized.
If any platform's job fails, nothing is published for that commit, so no edge release ever lacks a platform; the workflow run shows which job failed. A release already published for a version, as when a run is re-run, is never published twice: the run publishes nothing more for it and succeeds.
Pushes are handled in the order they came: a run waits for the one before it to finish rather than cancelling it, so every commit on main gets its edge release. The workflow is given only the permission it needs to publish, writing the repository's contents, and uses the token GitHub gives each run, needing no secrets of its own.

cd /workspace; f=spec/scope/self-update/index.pi; cat >> $f <<'EOF'

    requests:
        Every request to GitHub sends a User-Agent naming Suspense and its
        version, as "Suspense/0.1.42", since GitHub refuses requests without
        one, and asks for its JSON with `Accept: application/vnd.github+json`.
        A check asks for the repository's releases at
        `https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<name>/releases`, 100 to a page,
        so the newest edge release is never missed for being past the first
        page, and takes the highest N among the releases whose tag is
        `v0.1.N`, ignoring drafts and any release whose tag isn't of that
        form. An asset is downloaded from its `browser_download_url`,
        following GitHub's redirects to where it is stored, and its digest,
        given as `sha256:<hex>`, is compared without regard to case.

        GitHub's limit on requests made without signing in is respected: a
        check refused for it, with a 403 or 429 and its rate-limit headers,
        says so, "GitHub's rate limit was reached; try again after" and the
        time it resets, and an automatic check isn't tried again before then.
        Any other refusal says the status GitHub gave and its message, never
        only that the check failed.

    afterUpdate:
        An update that has been put in place is confirmed at the next
        launch: the version now running is compared with the one staged, and
        where they match, a notification says "Updated to Suspense 0.1.N",
        and the Updates section says so until the next check. Where they
        don't, as when the binary put in place still reports the old
        version, the Updates section says, in the theme's error colour, that
        the update to 0.1.N didn't take effect, and the same release is never
        downloaded and put in place again by itself, so an update can never
        loop, one restart after another; a Check for updates asked for by
        hand still tries it.

        The binary set aside is deleted at the next launch, and where it
        can't be yet, as on Windows while the process that ran it is still
        exiting, it is tried again at each launch after, never stopping the
        launch. A staged binary left beside the running one that is no newer
        than it is deleted rather than put in place.

    diagnostics:
        Suspense keeps a log of what updating does, `updates.log` in its own
        data directory, beside its preferences, as the
        @{UserPreferencesScope} keeps them: one line per step, with the time,
        each check with the repository and running version it checked for,
        the releases it found and the one it took or why it took none, each
        download with its asset, size, and digest check, each staging, each
        putting in place with its paths and how it went, and each launch's
        confirmation, every failure with its whole error. It keeps the last
        1,000 lines.

        The Updates section has a "Details" disclosure, collapsed to start
        with, that shows what updating rests on: the running version, the
        repository it updates from, or that it has none and so is not an edge
        build, the running binary's path and whether its directory can be
        written, the last check's time and the newest release it found, and
        what is staged, if anything, with a "Show log" button that opens
        `updates.log` as the @{OpenFileScope} opens a file, and a "Copy"
        button that puts all of it, with the log's last 50 lines, on the
        clipboard, for a bug report.
EOF
head -6 $f; f2=spec/scope/edge-releases/index.pi
perl -0pi -e 's/(        machine, has the version Cargo\.toml gives it, and no repository\.\n)/$1\n        The workflow gives both to the build of every platform, the version\n        from the count and the repository from the run\x27s own, and a build\n        never falls back to Cargo.toml\x27s version or to no repository on the\n        runner. The binary prints its version and repository, and nothing\n        else, when run with `--version`, as "Suspense 0.1.42 (owner\/name)",\n        or "Suspense 0.1.0 (development build)" for a build with none,\n        exiting at once without opening a window. I couldn't find the actual bug from here. This step runs in a container that can't see the code, and Suspense has no update log yet. So I tightened the spec where self-update most often breaks silently, and added a log and diagnostics so the next failure is visible. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 81 files, and the new sections are in the refreshed reference.

**Likeliest causes, worth checking first in the code step:**
1. **Version or repository not baked into the edge build.** If the workflow doesn't pass them in, the build never updates, or thinks it's version 0.1.0 and updates again on every launch.
2. **No User-Agent on GitHub requests.** GitHub refuses requests without one.
3. **Downloading the asset without following GitHub's redirect.**
4. **Leaving the renamed-aside binary on Windows** while the old process is still exiting.

## What changed in the spec

**Edge releases** (`.claude/reference/scope/edge-releases/index.md#version`)
- The workflow must pass the version and `owner/name` to every platform's build. A build never falls back to Cargo.toml's version or to no repository on the runner.
- `suspense --version` prints, for example, "Suspense 0.1.42 (owner/name)" or "Suspense 0.1.0 (development build)", and exits without opening a window. On Windows it writes to standard output even though the app has no console.
- Each job runs the binary it built with `--version` before archiving it, and fails if the output doesn't match what it was given. So no edge release can ship a binary that can't update itself or that keeps updating.

**Self-update** (`.claude/reference/scope/self-update/index.md`)
- **`#requests`:**
  - Every request sends a `Suspense/0.1.N` User-Agent and `Accept: application/vnd.github+json`.
  - The releases list is fetched 100 to a page, ignoring drafts and tags not of the form `v0.1.N`.
  - Assets are downloaded from `browser_download_url`, following redirects, and the `sha256:` digest is compared ignoring case.
  - When GitHub's rate limit is hit, the message names the reset time and automatic checks wait until then. Any other refusal shows GitHub's status and message.
- **`#after-update`:**
  - The launch after an update confirms the running version matches what was staged, and shows "Updated to Suspense 0.1.N".
  - If it doesn't match, the Updates section reports an error and that release is never put in place again automatically, so an update can't loop. Check for updates by hand still tries it.
  - On Windows, the set-aside binary is deleted at a later launch if it can't be deleted yet.
  - A staged binary that is no newer than the running one is deleted.
- **`#diagnostics`:**
  - An `updates.log` (last 1,000 lines) in Suspense's data directory records every check, download, staging, swap and launch confirmation, with full errors.
  - A "Details" disclosure in the Updates section shows the running version, the repository or that this isn't an edge build, the binary's path and whether it can be written, the last check and newest release found, and what's staged.
  - Details has "Show log" and "Copy" buttons for bug reports.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791134228-DebugSelfUpdate.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `EdgeReleasesScope`: `#version`, for `edge.yml` and the `--version` flag and its check.
- `SelfUpdateScope`: `#requests`, `#after-update`, `#diagnostics`, plus the existing `#checking`, `#downloading` and `#restarting`, read against the code to find what differs.
- `UserPreferencesScope`: where the log goes.
- `OpenFileScope`: how Show log opens it.

It is extra small and dimmer than muted text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.

The send button's colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes, straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap around, so pressing <Ctrl+Tab> on Freeform fades grey straight to Code's red, and <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Freeform's grey; neither lights up Chain, Spec, or Ask on the way. 163:#### Grow To Fit
165:The text input is a [GrowingTextInputScope](../../../ui/components/growing-text-input/index.md#growing-text-input-scope) growing to 12 rows at most. Its first row lines up with the send button, both at the top of the input row, and it grows downward from there.
---
## Concept

### Pitch

A multi-line text input that is only as tall as its text, so it takes a single row until there is more to show.

### Shape

#### Description

A multi-line text input whose long lines soft wrap, starting at a single row.

#### Grow To Fit

It grows to fit its text, one row per visual line: both lines broken with <Enter> and long lines that soft wrap, wrapped where it wraps them. It shrinks again as text is removed, and fits again when its width changes, as when the window is resized. Its height is what its rows and their padding and border take, and nothing more: there is no empty row beneath the last line.
Its rows are counted as the input itself lays its text out, in the very font it draws the text in, weight and all, so the count never differs from what shows: while the text is within its most rows, no row is ever cut off or scrolled out of view, and no empty row is left. Should a count made ahead of drawing still differ from how the text was laid out, the input takes the laid out count by the next frame.

#### Most Rows

Whatever uses it says how many rows it grows to at most. Once its text takes more, it stays that tall and scrolls.

#### Steadiness

It grows or shrinks in the very frame its text changes, and at any display scale its height is rounded up to a whole device pixel, so the text never flickers a row up and back as a line is added.

        It never takes its height from a frame before. Its rows are counted
        at the width it is drawn at in this frame, the width its text wraps
        at, so the first line to wrap adds its row in the frame it wraps, at
        its final height, with no frame drawn at the old height with the
        text already wrapped, nor at a height between, nor at a width it
        then wraps again at. Its height is set once a frame, from that count,
        never adjusted after the frame is drawn, so it never settles over
        two or more frames.

        The width its text wraps at never depends on whether it scrolls. Its
        scrollbar, once its text takes more than its most rows, overlays the
        text's right padding rather than taking width from the text, so
        reaching its most rows never rewraps the text, never changes its
        count of rows, and never moves a line from one row to another.

    scrolling:
        Once its text takes more than its most rows, it scrolls only to keep
        the cursor in view, and then by no more than it takes: typing,
        pasting, or moving the cursor to a row beneath the last shown
        scrolls just far enough to show it as the last row, and to a row
        above the first shown, just far enough to show it as the first. A
