The spec already required growing without jumps, so these are code bugs. I can't see the code from this step, so I tightened the spec around the three likely causes, so the coding step has exact rules to fix them against. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files; the new sections are in the refreshed reference.

**Likely causes:**
- **Jump at the first wrap:** the height is probably worked out at the previous frame's width, then corrected a frame later.
- **Jumping when it gets long:** probably two things together. The scrollbar appears and narrows the text, so it rewraps and the row count changes. The scroll position is also probably reset or chased each frame.
- **Not growing at all:** something around the input, such as the input row, the button column or the tab body, is probably fixing its height.

## What changed in the spec

**1. Growing text input** (`.claude/reference/ui/components/growing-text-input/index.md`)
- **`#steadiness`, two new rules:**
  - Rows are counted at the width the text wraps at in this frame. The height is set once per frame from that count and never adjusted afterwards, so the first wrap lands at its final height with no in-between frame.
  - The scrollbar sits over the right padding instead of taking width from the text. Reaching 12 rows never rewraps the text or changes the row count.
- **`#scrolling` (new):** past its row limit it only scrolls to keep the cursor in view, by the least needed.
  - Typing at the end keeps the last line steadily at the bottom.
  - A change that leaves the cursor visible never scrolls it.
  - It never jumps to the top and back.
  - A wheel or trackpad scroll stays where you put it until the cursor leaves view.
  - The scroll position is kept in whole pixels.
- **`#nothing-else-caps-it` (new):** whatever holds the input never fixes, caps or stretches its height. Only its row limit stops it growing.

**2. Chat input** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#grow-to-fit`)
- The chat input grows from the first wrapped line up to 12 rows, and shrinks back, in the same frame as the text changes.
- The tab body, the input row and the button column never fix its height. The input row is as tall as the text or the buttons, whichever is taller.
- The message list above gives up the room in that same frame.
- The tabs, buttons and session bar never jump while it grows or scrolls.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791137158-Prompt_7b61e528bf74c99f.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `GrowingTextInputScope`: `#grow-to-fit`, `#most-rows`, `#steadiness`, `#scrolling`, `#nothing-else-caps-it`.
- `ChatInputScope`: `#grow-to-fit` and `#description`, for the text box's height against the button column.

use /lib
from /scope/application/MainWindow import MainWindowScope
from /scope/edge-releases import EdgeReleasesScope
from /scope/open-file import OpenFileScope
from /scope/settings-window import SettingsWindowScope
from /scope/user-preferences import UserPreferencesScope

export scope SelfUpdateScope:
    concept: {SelfUpdateConcept}

concept SelfUpdateConcept:
    pitch:
        Suspense keeps itself up to date: it looks for a newer edge release,
        downloads it in the background, and puts it in place of its own
        binary when it restarts, so the newest build is only a restart away.

    shape: {SelfUpdateShape}

shape SelfUpdateShape:
    description:
        Updates come from the edge releases, as the @{EdgeReleasesScope}
        says, published in the GitHub repository the running build was
        published from, which it knows because that is baked into it. Only
        such a build updates itself. A build made anywhere else, as on a
        developer's machine, never looks for an update, never downloads one,
        and never replaces its binary, and the Updates section says why.

    checking:
        A check asks GitHub's releases API for the repository's releases,
        pre-releases included, and takes the one with the highest version
        `0.1.N`, comparing N as a number, never as text. It is newer only
        when its N is greater than the running build's; an older or equal one
        is never taken, so an update never goes back. A release without the
        asset for the running platform is passed over for the newest one
        that has it.

        Suspense checks a few seconds after it starts, and then every 6
        hours while it runs, in the background, never holding up anything
        else, and only while "Check for updates automatically" is on, as it
        is until turned off. That choice is remembered for the user, as the
        @{UserPreferencesScope} says. Check for updates, in the Updates
        section, checks straight away, whether it is on or not. A check that
        can't be made, as with no network or GitHub refusing it, is quiet
        when automatic, trying again at the next, and says why when asked
        for.

    downloading:
        A newer release found is downloaded straight away, in the background,
        taking the asset for the platform and architecture running,
        `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`, `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip`, or
        `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`. It is checked against the size
        GitHub gives for it, and against its SHA-256 digest where GitHub
        gives one, and one that doesn't match is thrown away and never used.
        The binary is taken out of the archive and staged beside the running
        binary, in the same directory, so it can be put in place by a rename,
        marked executable where the platform has such a mark. One download
        runs at a time; a newer release found while one is staged replaces
        it. A download that fails says so in the Updates section, and is
        tried again at the next check.

        Where the running binary's directory can't be written, nothing is
        downloaded, and the Updates section says that Suspense can't update
        itself there, with the directory, and a link to the release's page,
        opened in the browser, so it can be updated by hand.

    restarting:
        Once an update is staged, a notification says "Suspense 0.1.N is
        ready", with a Restart button and a Later button. The Updates section
        says the same, with a Restart button, for as long as it stays staged.
        Later only closes the notification; the update stays staged, and is
        put in place whenever Suspense next quits.

        Restart quits as quitting does, as the @{MainWindowScope} says,
        asking first while work is running, and doing nothing more if the
        quit is cancelled, then starts Suspense again from the same path once
        the update is in place. However Suspense quits, a staged update is
        put in place as it does: the staged binary is renamed over the
        running one, the running one renamed aside first where the platform
        won't replace a running binary, as on Windows. The binary set aside
        is deleted at the next launch. An update left staged by a quit that
        never finished, as a crash, is put in place at the next launch, before
        anything else, and takes effect at the launch after, the Updates
        section saying a restart finishes it.

        Putting an update in place never leaves Suspense without a binary:
        a step that fails puts back the binary that was there, and the
        Updates section says why it couldn't update.

    updatesSection:
        The @{SettingsWindowScope} has an "Updates" section. It says the
        running version, as "Suspense 0.1.42", and where it can't update
        itself, as for a build made elsewhere, why, and offers nothing else.
        Otherwise it shows a checkbox reading "Check for updates
        automatically", a "Check for updates" button, disabled while a check
        or download is under way, and a line saying where things stand:
        "Checking for updates…", "Suspense is up to date", checked when, as
        "Checked 5 minutes ago", "Downloading 0.1.N…" with how much has
        come, "Suspense 0.1.N is ready" with a Restart button, or, in the
        theme's error colour, why the last check, download, or update failed.

    requests:
        Every request to GitHub sends a User-Agent naming Suspense and its
        version, as "Suspense/0.1.42", since GitHub refuses requests without
        one, and asks for its JSON with `Accept: application/vnd.github+json`.
        A check asks for the repository's releases at
        `https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<name>/releases`, 100 to a page,
        so the newest edge release is never missed for being past the first
        page, and takes the highest N among the releases whose tag is
        `v0.1.N`, ignoring drafts and any release whose tag isn't of that
        form. An asset is downloaded from its `browser_download_url`,
        following GitHub's redirects to where it is stored, and its digest,
        given as `sha256:<hex>`, is compared without regard to case.

        GitHub's limit on requests made without signing in is respected: a
        check refused for it, with a 403 or 429 and its rate-limit headers,
        says so, "GitHub's rate limit was reached; try again after" and the
        time it resets, and an automatic check isn't tried again before then.
        Any other refusal says the status GitHub gave and its message, never
        only that the check failed.

    afterUpdate:
        An update that has been put in place is confirmed at the next
        launch: the version now running is compared with the one staged, and
        where they match, a notification says "Updated to Suspense 0.1.N",
        and the Updates section says so until the next check. Where they
        don't, as when the binary put in place still reports the old
        version, the Updates section says, in the theme's error colour, that
        the update to 0.1.N didn't take effect, and the same release is never
        downloaded and put in place again by itself, so an update can never
        loop, one restart after another; a Check for updates asked for by
        hand still tries it.

        The binary set aside is deleted at the next launch, and where it
        can't be yet, as on Windows while the process that ran it is still
        exiting, it is tried again at each launch after, never stopping the
        launch. A staged binary left beside the running one that is no newer
        than it is deleted rather than put in place.

    diagnostics:
        Suspense keeps a log of what updating does, `updates.log` in its own
        data directory, beside its preferences, as the
        @{UserPreferencesScope} keeps them: one line per step, with the time,
        each check with the repository and running version it checked for,
        the releases it found and the one it took or why it took none, each
        download with its asset, size, and digest check, each staging, each
        putting in place with its paths and how it went, and each launch's
        confirmation, every failure with its whole error. It keeps the last
        1,000 lines.

        The Updates section has a "Details" disclosure, collapsed to start
        with, that shows what updating rests on: the running version, the
        repository it updates from, or that it has none and so is not an edge
        build, the running binary's path and whether its directory can be
        written, the last check's time and the newest release it found, and
        what is staged, if anything, with a "Show log" button that opens
        `updates.log` as the @{OpenFileScope} opens a file, and a "Copy"
        button that puts all of it, with the log's last 50 lines, on the
        clipboard, for a bug report.

The panic most likely comes from Restart quitting inside its own click handler. The quit then tries to read or close the window that's still handling the click, which GPUI refuses with "attempted to read a window that is already on the stack". I can't see the code from this step, so that's a diagnosis from the error, but it's the usual cause. I changed the spec so Restart, and every other way of quitting, waits until the click has been fully handled. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files.

## What changed in the spec

New text in `spec/scope/self-update/index.pi`, under `#restarting` (`.claude/reference/scope/self-update/index.md#restarting`):

- **Restart is deferred:** clicking Restart, on the notification or in the Updates section, only asks for a restart. The restart starts later, once that click is finished and no window is being updated.
- **No window re-entry:** asking whether to quit, closing the window, swapping in the new binary, and starting it again must never touch a window that's still being updated. The spec names this exact panic.
- **Every quit, not just Restart:** Ctrl+Q, the palette's Quit, the window's close button, the quit dialog's Quit button, and restarts reached through the About panel all ask for the quit and let it run once their window is free.
- **Order of a restart:** the update is put in place, then the new Suspense starts, then the old one exits. The old one is never left running beside the new one.
- **If the new binary won't start:** Suspense doesn't quit. It keeps running, leaves the update in place for next launch, and shows a notification saying why, which is also logged.
- **No panics:** any failing step is reported and logged. Suspense ends up either still running as before, or quit with the update in place and the new version running.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791140053-FixSelfUpdateWindowPanic2.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `SelfUpdateScope`: `#restarting`, especially the two new paragraphs. Also `#diagnostics` for logging restart failures.
- `MainWindowScope`: `#quitting`, so every quit path uses the same deferred quit.
- `RunningActivityScope`: the quit confirmation dialog, whose Quit button must also defer.

18:The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command, and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.
19:On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user, with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages. There too, what a run writes to the project belongs to the user, as the [ApplicationScope](../application/index.md#application-scope) says of every file the application creates: the container runs as the user rather than as root inside the machine, and a file it writes into a folder mounted from Windows is the user's, owned by them and inheriting the folder's permissions, never owned by Administrators or another account.
21:#### Missing Podman
23:Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task, a Chain prompt's spec steps, or a question. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed does, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, or as one whose spec build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's installation instructions for the platform it is running on:
25:- on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
26:- on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
27:- on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux
29:A Code task, and a Chain prompt's code step, never needs Podman, and runs whether it is installed or not.
31:#### Podman Machine
33:On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`. Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.
35:#### Podman Access
37:Where `podman` is installed, and on macOS and Windows its machine is running, but the application can't get Podman to run a container for it, as where the user may not use it, its rootless setup is missing, as the user's subordinate IDs, or it can't reach its service or machine, the run fails because of Podman, never because of the harness: it never reads "the harness reported an error", or any message that blames the harness or leaves the cause unnamed. The application tells this apart from a harness that ran and failed by what Podman itself reports, its exit status and what it prints before the harness starts in the container. The task's or question's output says plainly that the harness couldn't be run because Podman couldn't be accessed, and then gives, as written, what Podman printed about why. It is never run on the host instead. The same holds for a `podman build` of its image that fails for that reason: it says Podman couldn't be accessed, not only that the build failed.
39:#### Image
41:Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`, and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions changes.
42:Each command the image holds has to run in it, not only be there. The build ends by running each one's version command in the image, as `piton --version`, and a build where one fails, as a piton built against a newer C library than the image has, fails, saying which command couldn't run and what it printed. An image whose piton can't run is never used, so a Spec run is never sent where it can't run `piton build` to check its work.
43:A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own, `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add what its runs in a container need, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. The project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the project's runs use the default image.
44:While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.
46:#### Mounts
48:What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing else from the host. The project is mounted at the same fixed path in the container, `/workspace`, on every platform, each location given at its place relative to the project directory under `/workspace`, and the run works in `/workspace`. So a harness that keys its sessions on its working directory, as Claude Code does, finds them again after the project moves, whatever its path on the host. What each kind of run is given, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) names the locations, follows.
50:##### Spec
52:A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can run `piton build` itself; the project's `.piton` directory, which holds the build's manifest of the files it owns, read and write, for the same reason, bound in from the project itself, never an empty, temporary, or copied one, so the manifest a build in the container starts from is the host's, and what it writes there is the host's next build's, the application creating the directory in the project first where it isn't there; the Suspense fluency file, read only; the fluency file, read only; piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file, read and write. Never the code location: in its place, an empty scratch directory, writable, that nothing else sees and that goes with the container, so `piton build` finds the code location it places the shape's guidance in.
54:##### Question
56:A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the spec location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read only, so it can run `piton slice` in its container, and the Suspense fluency file, read only. Nothing is writable but the harness's own volume and the questions' sessions folder. Where one of the code location and the spec location holds the other, both are still mounted, read only, and neither is hidden from the question by the other.
58:Each run is also given its own conversation's sessions folder, read and write, as Volumes says, and nothing of any other conversation's.
59:Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it, unless the run is given the one held as well, as a question is given both the code location and the spec location.
60:A task's understanding file is mounted on its own, never the history folder it is in, so a run sees no other task's record. Since a file has to be there to be mounted, the application writes it empty just before the run, and an empty understanding file is shown as one not written yet is.
62:#### Paths
64:On every platform, every path a run reports from its container is mapped back to its host path, `/workspace` standing for the project directory, before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec in the right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its understanding file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls touched. Only a path that is `/workspace`, or begins with `/workspace/`, is mapped, never text that merely holds it, as `/workspace-old`. A path that maps to nothing on the host is shown as the run gave it, and opens nothing.
66:#### Volumes
68:The only volumes are one per harness, for its login and settings, ~/.claude, ~/.codex, or OpenCode's data directory as the harness keeps it, owned and named by the application and shared by every project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them. Losing one costs only a login.
69:The harness's sessions are never kept in a volume. They are kept in the project, in `.suspense/sessions/`, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, one folder per conversation: `spec` for the spec lane's, and `questions` for the Ask tab's questions. Each run mounts only its own conversation's folder, read and write, where the harness keeps its sessions under its home, as Claude Code's ~/.claude/projects, never `.suspense/sessions/` as a whole, so no run sees another conversation's sessions. The application creates the folder before the run if it isn't there. So a conversation carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of the project, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says.
70:Losing the project's sessions folder costs only the conversations'
72:##### Context
74:the next run starts a new conversation, as when a session
76:can't be resumed. Sessions kept in volumes before this aren't carried over; each conversation starts fresh.
78:#### Logging In
80:When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the command prints. Any login URL the command prints opens in the host's browser. Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is cancelled or fails.
81:The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every run. The [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) shows whether each harness is logged in in its container, and can log it in again.
83:#### Guards
85:A run in a container has no protected locations, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) names them: it isn't guarded, and its harness is given no rule against reading or editing any location, since nothing it mustn't touch is there. Its prompts, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, name only what it can see. Runs on the host keep their protected locations as ever.
87:#### Spec Build
89:A Spec run can run `piton build` in its container, to check its work in the refreshed reference, and that build succeeds whenever the spec is sound: it owns the reference files it finds, through the manifest in the mounted `.piton` directory, and places the shape's guidance in the scratch directory standing in for the code location, where it goes nowhere. A build there that fails fails only because of the spec, never because of what the container leaves out, so its errors are the run's own to fix. Once a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step is over, however it ended, the application runs `piton build` on the host, as the [SpecBuildScope](../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, so the host's reference and shape guidance are those of the spec as the run left it.

18:The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command, and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.
19:On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user, with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages. There too, what a run writes to the project belongs to the user, as the [ApplicationScope](../application/index.md#application-scope) says of every file the application creates: the container runs as the user rather than as root inside the machine, and a file it writes into a folder mounted from Windows is the user's, owned by them and inheriting the folder's permissions, never owned by Administrators or another account.
21:#### Missing Podman
23:Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task, a Chain prompt's spec steps, or a question. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed does, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, or as one whose spec build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's installation instructions for the platform it is running on:
25:- on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
26:- on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
27:- on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux
29:A Code task, and a Chain prompt's code step, never needs Podman, and runs whether it is installed or not.
31:#### Podman Machine
33:On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`. Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.
35:#### Podman Access
37:Where `podman` is installed, and on macOS and Windows its machine is running, but the application can't get Podman to run a container for it, as where the user may not use it, its rootless setup is missing, as the user's subordinate IDs, or it can't reach its service or machine, the run fails because of Podman, never because of the harness: it never reads "the harness reported an error", or any message that blames the harness or leaves the cause unnamed. The application tells this apart from a harness that ran and failed by what Podman itself reports, its exit status and what it prints before the harness starts in the container. The task's or question's output says plainly that the harness couldn't be run because Podman couldn't be accessed, and then gives, as written, what Podman printed about why. It is never run on the host instead. The same holds for a `podman build` of its image that fails for that reason: it says Podman couldn't be accessed, not only that the build failed.
39:#### Image
41:Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`, and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions changes.
42:Each command the image holds has to run in it, not only be there. The build ends by running each one's version command in the image, as `piton --version`, and a build where one fails, as a piton built against a newer C library than the image has, fails, saying which command couldn't run and what it printed. An image whose piton can't run is never used, so a Spec run is never sent where it can't run `piton build` to check its work.
43:A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own, `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add what its runs in a container need, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. The project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the project's runs use the default image.
44:While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.
46:#### Mounts
48:What each run sees is what is mounted into its container, and nothing else from the host. The project is mounted at the same fixed path in the container, `/workspace`, on every platform, each location given at its place relative to the project directory under `/workspace`, and the run works in `/workspace`. So a harness that keys its sessions on its working directory, as Claude Code does, finds them again after the project moves, whatever its path on the host. What each kind of run is given, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) names the locations, follows.
50:##### Spec
52:A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can run `piton build` itself; the project's `.piton` directory, which holds the build's manifest of the files it owns, read and write, for the same reason, bound in from the project itself, never an empty, temporary, or copied one, so the manifest a build in the container starts from is the host's, and what it writes there is the host's next build's, the application creating the directory in the project first where it isn't there; the Suspense fluency file, read only; the fluency file, read only; piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file, read and write. Never the code location: in its place, an empty scratch directory, writable, that nothing else sees and that goes with the container, so `piton build` finds the code location it places the shape's guidance in.
54:##### Question
56:A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the spec location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read only, so it can run `piton slice` in its container, and the Suspense fluency file, read only. Nothing is writable but the harness's own volume and the questions' sessions folder. Where one of the code location and the spec location holds the other, both are still mounted, read only, and neither is hidden from the question by the other.
58:Each run is also given its own conversation's sessions folder, read and write, as Volumes says, and nothing of any other conversation's.
59:Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the project's git directory. 60:A task's understanding file is mounted on its own, never the history folder it is in, so a run sees no other task's record. Since a file has to be there to be mounted, the application writes it empty just before the run, and an empty understanding file is shown as one not written yet is.

64:On every platform, every path a run reports from its container is mapped back to its host path, `/workspace` standing for the project directory, before it is shown or opened anywhere: the referenced spec in the right sidebar, file links in the task's output, its understanding file, the files it changed, and what its tool calls touched. content.text:
I couldn't see the actual error, so I made the spec cover the likeliest causes of a first-login image failure. If you paste the error text, I can narrow it down to one. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files.

**Likeliest causes:**
- **Host binaries copied into the image.** If the build copies the host's harness or piton binary in, it can't run on macOS or Windows, because the image is Linux.
- **A brand-new harness volume owned by root.** The container runs as you, so the login command can't write its credentials.
- **Two image builds at once.** The login and the Welcome or Settings check can each start a build of the same image, and they collide.

## What changed in the spec

**Image** (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md#image`)
- **Linux tools only:** the image is always Linux. Each harness and piton is installed from its own Linux release at the version found on the host, never copied from the host. Anything not found or not published for Linux is installed at its latest.
- **Isolated build:** the build gets a fresh temporary directory containing only the Containerfile the app writes. It never sees the project or your home folder, and needs only the network.
- **One build at a time:** a run, login or check that needs an image already being built waits for that build instead of starting another.
- **No half-built images:** the image is tagged only after the build succeeds, so a failed or interrupted build is never mistaken for a good one.
- **Full errors:** a failed build shows the step it failed at and everything Podman printed, and the same goes to a build log kept beside the preferences.

**Logging in** (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md#logging-in`)
- **Image first:** the login view builds the image if it's missing or out of date, showing "Preparing environment" and the build output. The login command starts only after the build succeeds.
- **Retry:** if the build fails, the login view shows why, with a "Try again" button.
- **Volume ready before first use:** the harness's volume is created with `podman volume create` before the first login. It is mounted so the container's user owns it and can write to it, for example with Podman's `:U` option.
- **HOME:** the container's home folder, where the volume is mounted beneath it as `~/.claude`, is owned by that same user, so the first login can write its credentials.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791140688-PodmanImageCreationError.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ContainerEnvironmentScope`:
  - `#image`: the Containerfile, build context, build lock, tagging only on success, and error output.
  - `#logging-in`: build before login, Try again, volume creation and ownership, HOME.
  - `#volumes`: where each volume is mounted.
  - `#podman-access`: for failures where Podman can't be reached.
- `WelcomeScope` and `SettingsWindowScope`: their login checks and buttons, which share the one build.

content.text:
The websites most likely opened because of the old rule that "any login URL the command prints opens in the browser". The login view also shows the image build's output, and package installs print plenty of URLs, so each one was being opened. I changed the spec so only the harness's own sign-in link ever opens, and only once. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files.

## What changed in the spec

New text in `spec/scope/container-environment/index.pi`, under `#logging-in` (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md#logging-in`):

- **Login output only:** URLs are watched for only once the login command has started. Anything the image build or Podman prints while pulling, building or starting the container is shown as text and never opened; at most its URLs are clickable.
- **Sign-in URLs only:** a URL opens only if it leads to the harness's sign-in, for example:
  - Claude Code's link to claude.ai or console.anthropic.com
  - Codex's link to auth.openai.com
  - OpenCode's link to whichever provider it's logging in with
  - a localhost callback the login asks to be visited

  Links to documentation, release notes or package homepages are only shown.
- **One URL at most:** a login opens at most one URL by itself, the first sign-in one. Any later sign-in URL is shown as a link for you to click.
- **Nothing recognized, nothing opened:** if no sign-in URL is recognized, nothing opens and every URL the command printed is shown as a link.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791218318-PreventPodmanFromOpeningWebsites.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ContainerEnvironmentScope`: `#logging-in`, for which output is watched for URLs, which URLs count as sign-in, and the open-once rule. Also `#image`, since build output goes to the login view and must not be scanned for URLs to open.
- `WelcomeScope` and `SettingsWindowScope`: both start the same login view, so the fix covers them too.

23:Tasks run in two lanes, the code lane and the spec lane, each with a queue of its own, so work on the spec never waits on work on the code, or the other way round. .claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md:60:A prompt sent in Chain runs as steps, each saved in the history as a task of its own: first the Chain task itself, which writes the spec; then the same prompt sent to Code, told what the spec step did; and, when the chain asks for a post-build spec update, the same prompt sent to Spec once more, told what the code step did. Each step knows the one it was sent from, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. Only the steps the chain sends itself belong to it; a task sent to the other mode by hand, or resent, from one of its steps is a task of its own.
.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md:61:Each step runs in the lane of the work it does, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says: the Chain task and its spec follow-up in the spec lane, the code step in the code lane. A step is sent once the step before it finishes, never before, and goes to the head of its lane's queue, ahead of the prompts already waiting there, so it runs as soon as that lane is free, and straight away if it already is. The lane it leaves is free for its own queue meanwhile, so a Spec task sent while a chain's code step runs runs beside it. A step waiting for its lane shows in the queue like any prompt, and can be cancelled there, ending the chain. A step whose chain step before it failed or was cancelled is never sent.
.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md:62:Each step also runs where the work of its lane runs, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says: the spec steps in a container holding the spec and no code, the code step always on the host, with its protected locations. Each carries on its own lane's conversation, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, so a step is told what the step before it did only through its prompt: the Chain prompt as typed and that step's final output, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](./mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says.
.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md:69:The latest task heads the view whether or not the harness is working. It is always the most recent task still active: of the tasks under way, building, compiling, or running, in either lane, the one sent most recently. Only while no task is under way is it the task that finished most recently, or, before any has finished, the one sent most recently. A finished task never heads the view while another is under way: when it finishes while a task in the other lane still runs, that task heads the view in its place at once, and the task that finished goes among the previous tasks. So with two Chain tasks sent one after the other, once both their spec steps have finished, the first chain's code step heads the view while it runs, not the second chain's finished spec step, and the second chain's code step heads it in turn once it is sent. A task still running in the other lane that is not the latest is among the previous tasks, shown running there, as any previous task is. Whichever task heads the view, its header and output show as they do for a task just sent, and the previous tasks, their row's count, and the chain grouping follow it. The header shows its status, with a spinner while it is under way, the name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from, and the compiled markdown the harness actually received, which scrolls once it gets tall. Until it has compiled, the prompt as typed is shown instead. At its right, a Resend button sends it again, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. The header shows the prompt the task was sent with, however much is sent to it while it runs; what is sent is shown in its output.

content.text:
Yes, there was a reason: the spec told the code to do it. It said a chain's next step "goes to the head of its lane's queue, ahead of the prompts already waiting there". So whenever a chain's spec step finished, its code step jumped ahead of every Code prompt already waiting. That included other chains' code steps queued earlier, which is the out-of-order sending you saw. I changed the rule; `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files.

## What changed in the spec

**Chained tasks** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/index.md#chained-tasks`)
- A chain step now takes its place in its lane's queue by when its chain was sent, not when the step itself was ready.
  - It waits behind every prompt sent before its chain, including earlier chains' steps.
  - It goes ahead of every prompt sent after its chain.
- A chain's code step never jumps ahead of a Code prompt or another chain's code step sent before it.
- A Code prompt sent while a chain's spec step is running waits for that chain's code step, so nothing lands between a chain's steps.
- Two chains' code steps run in the order the chains were sent, whichever spec step finished first.
- If nothing sent earlier is waiting, the step runs as soon as its lane is free, as before.

**Saved queue** (`.claude/reference/scope/project-data/index.md#contents`)
- A queued chain step is saved marked with when its chain was sent, so it keeps its place in the queue after a restart.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791224395-ChainModePromptOrderInvestigation.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `PromptEditor`: `#chained-tasks`, for where a step is inserted into its lane's queue.
- `PromptSendingScope`: `#lanes`, for each queue running first to last.
- `ProjectDataScope`: `#contents`, for how `queue/` files are named and marked so their order survives a restart.

"Run again" button runs it afresh in its place.

        stopping:
            Stopping a target stops everything it started, however deep: the
            shell its command runs in, what the shell runs, and every process
            those start in turn, as a `npm run dev` runs npm, which runs node,
            which runs Vite and its esbuild, or a `cargo run` runs the binary
            it built. A server a target starts, a dev server, a watcher, or
            anything listening on a port, is stopped with it, so its port is
            free once the target reads "Stopped", and running it again never
            fails for the port being taken by the run before. Nothing it
            started is left running, nor left behind as an orphan of the
            shell, whatever the platform.

            So a target's command is started as the head of a process group
            of its own on macOS and Linux, a new session, and on Windows in a
            job object that every process it starts belongs to, its children's
            children included. Stopping it first asks the whole group or job
            to end, as Ctrl+C in a terminal would, SIGINT and then SIGTERM to
            the process group on macOS and Linux, and on Windows a Ctrl+Break
            to its console group, so a server can shut down cleanly; whatever
            is still running 3 seconds later is killed outright, SIGKILL to
            the group on macOS and Linux, and the job terminated on Windows.
            A process that left the group on its own, as one that starts a
            session of its own, is found among the target's descendants and
            stopped the same way.

            The target reads "Stopped" only once every process it started has
            exited, and its Stop button shows a spinner and is disabled until
            then, so "Stopped" always means nothing of it is still running.
            Stopping it the other ways, by running another target in its
            place, finding the targets, closing its panel, or quitting, stops
            it just the same, and quitting doesn't leave a process of it
            running after Suspense has gone. A target that ends by itself,
            as when its command exits, leaves nothing it started running
            either: what is left of its group is stopped as above.

content.text:
The spec already said Stop ends the target "and every process it started with it", but it never said how. The likely bug is that only the shell gets killed, so the npm → node → Vite chain under it keeps the server running. I added a section spelling out how the whole process tree is stopped. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 81 files, and it's under `.claude/reference/scope/run-targets/index.md#stopping`.

## What changed in the spec

New "stopping" section in `spec/scope/run-targets/index.pi`, under the panel's description:

- **Everything goes, however deep:** stopping a target ends its shell, what that runs, and every process those start. For example, `npm run dev` → npm → node → Vite and esbuild.
  - Dev servers, watchers and anything listening on a port stop with it.
  - The port is free once it reads "Stopped", so Run again never fails because the old server still holds it.
  - No process is left orphaned, on any platform.
- **How it's grouped:** on macOS and Linux the command starts in its own process group and session. On Windows it starts in a job object that every descendant belongs to.
- **How it's stopped:**
  - First it asks nicely, so servers can shut down cleanly: SIGINT then SIGTERM to the group on macOS and Linux, Ctrl+Break on Windows.
  - Anything still running 3 seconds later is killed: SIGKILL to the group, or the job is terminated.
  - Processes that left the group are found among the target's descendants and stopped the same way.
- **Honest status:** while it's stopping, the Stop button shows a spinner and is disabled. "Stopped" appears only once every process has exited.
- **Every way of stopping is the same:** running another target, finding targets, closing the panel and quitting all stop it this way. Nothing outlives Suspense.
- **Ending on its own:** if the target's command exits by itself, anything it left running in its group is cleaned up too.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791382870-StopServerOnButtonClick.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `RunTargetsScope`: `#stopping` for spawning in a group or job, the graceful-then-kill sequence and when "Stopped" shows, plus `#while-running`, `#one-at-atime` and `#minimizing` for the other ways a target is stopped.
- `ApplicationScope`: `#child-processes`, which still applies on Windows. A target's shell starts without a console window, even inside its job.

        A background command that never ends on its own, as a dev server

        going, a background command still running holds the run open only

        the task finishes in the state of that last result, never left
        running. Whatever the run started is ended with it: no server a task
        started is left running once the task is shown as finished, so its

content.text:
The likeliest cause is that the agent started the dev server as a background command. The spec says every background command keeps a task running until it ends, and a server never ends, so the task stays "Running" forever. I added rules so a server can't hold a task open once the work is done. I also covered a run-target case with the same symptom, in case that's where you saw it. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files.

## What changed in the spec

**Tasks** (`.claude/reference/scope/harness-integration/index.md#feeding`)
- **Idle commands:** after the agent has given its result, all messages are taken in and no subagent is running, a background command that has printed nothing for 60 seconds counts as idle. That's what a server does once it has started.
- **Stopping them:** when only idle commands are left, Suspense asks the harness to stop each one by id. The result that already came becomes the last, and the task finishes as Done.
- **Busy commands still count:** a background build or test run that keeps printing still holds the task open until it ends or goes quiet.
- **While waiting:** the status still reads "Running", and its tooltip says how many background commands it's waiting on. They're listed with Stop buttons in the subagents panel.
- **Process timeout:** if the harness's process hasn't exited 10 seconds after the last result, for example because a server still holds its output open, it is ended with its whole process group. The task then finishes. No server a task started survives the task finishing, so its port is free.

**Run targets** (`.claude/reference/scope/run-targets/index.md#stopping`)
- A target is over when its command exits, not when its output closes. A leftover child holding the output open can't keep it at "Running". Whatever is left is stopped.
- A target whose command *is* the server keeps running until you stop it.

**My choices:** 60 seconds of silence and the 10-second exit timeout are my own numbers, so adjust them if they feel wrong.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791386842-NodeServerStuckRunning.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `HarnessIntegrationScope`: `#feeding`, for spotting idle commands, stopping them by id, the 10-second exit timeout and ending the process group.
- `SubagentsPanel`: `#description` and `#stopping`, where the waited-on commands are listed.
- `RunTargetsScope`: `#stopping`, for detecting the end by process exit.

## Concept

### Pitch

The tasks waiting their turn while their lane is busy, listed above the chat input, where they can be reordered, edited, or cancelled before they are sent.

### Shape

#### Description

The queue holds the tasks sent while their lane is busy, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says, in the order they were sent unless they have been moved since. It is one list holding both lanes' queues: the code lane's and the spec lane's prompts together, in one order. Each lane sends its own prompts one at a time, first to last in that order, whenever it is free, whatever the other lane's prompts are doing, so a Spec prompt behind a Code prompt in the list is sent as soon as the spec lane is free, without waiting for the Code prompt. A Freeform prompt, which needs both lanes free, holds back the spec lane's prompts queued after it until it has been sent, so it isn't passed over for ever.

#### Lanes

Each queued prompt's row shows which lane it waits for: a small label just before its text reading its mode, "Code", "Spec", or "Freeform", tinted that mode's colour, as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it. A prompt sent from the Chain tab waits in the spec lane, as its first step writes the spec, and reads "Chain" in the Chain colour; a chain's later step waiting for its lane reads what it is, "Code" or "Spec follow-up", in that step's mode colour.

#### Placement

The queue sits along the bottom of the view, below the output and directly above the chat input, with a border along its top. It is not part of the header. A row saying how many prompts are queued, with a chevron, expands to list each queued prompt in order, a line or two of each, with a button to cancel it. Each prompt in the list is numbered, with its number, text, and cancel button vertically centred in its row, and the list scrolls once it gets tall, with a [ScrollbarScope](../../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope). Each time it is expanded, it opens scrolled to the bottom, on the prompts queued most recently, however it was scrolled when last closed. The same area holds the auto-send switch and the "Send next" button.
Editing a queued prompt from the chat input's <Up>, as the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says, expands the list while the queue holds more than one prompt, scrolled so the prompt being edited is in view, following it as <Up> and <Down> move the edit along the queue. Once the edit is saved or cancelled, a list it expanded collapses again; one already expanded stays as it was. The queue is shown only while it has anything in it.

#### Cancel

A queued prompt that has not been sent yet can be cancelled, which removes it from the queue for good. A prompt already sent is no longer in the queue.

#### New Conversation

Each queued prompt in the list has a small toggle switch, a slider, first of its controls, switched on while the prompt will start a new conversation rather than carry on the tasks', as its hidden anchor records, as the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says. Clicking it switches between the two, saving the prompt again with the project. Its tooltip says which the prompt does, and that clicking does the other instead. The choice stays with the prompt wherever it is moved in the queue.
Prompts that will share a context are joined by a subtle connector line drawn between their switches: a vertical line 1 pixel wide in the theme's line colour, centred on the switches, running from the bottom of one prompt's switch to the top of the next one's, across the gap between their rows. A prompt that carries on is joined to the one above it; one that starts a new conversation is not, so each run of joined switches is one context. The first prompt in the queue is never joined to anything above it. Nothing else marks the grouping: there is no gutter, dot, or line at the row's left edge. The line follows the prompts as they are moved or switched, and is never under a switch, only between them. Each switch sits centred up and down in its row, however tall the row's text or attached images make it, and the line runs unbroken from one switch to the next across both rows' padding, with no gap where one row ends and the next begins.
The toggle can only make a prompt start a new conversation; it can't bring back one that was left. Once New conversation has been pressed for the tasks, the next task to run starts a new conversation whichever prompt it is, even when the prompt it marked has been moved further down or switched back to carrying on.

#### Reorder

Queued prompts are reordered by dragging them, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says: each row starts with a grip, and the prompt dragged follows the pointer as a line of its text. Dropped in a gap, it moves there, and the order is saved with the project, so the queue comes back in its new order when the project is opened again. A prompt still being saved, as its spinner shows, can't be dragged, and no gap past a prompt still being saved shows the indicator. A prompt being edited can still be moved, and the chat input's "Editing queued prompt N" follows it to its new place. A move that can't be saved leaves the queue as it was, and a notification titled "Could not move the prompt" says why.

#### Editing

Each queued prompt in the list also has a button with a pencil icon, after its move buttons and before its cancel button, whose tooltip says it edits the prompt. Clicking it edits the prompt in the [ChatInputScope](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope), as it says, and its row is highlighted while it is being edited. While it is, it is held where it is: it is never sent, and its lane, waiting on it, waits, even with auto-send on; the other lane carries on. Saving the edit puts the new text, in the mode and with the attachments it was saved with, in its place in the queue, saved with the project in place of what it held, then lets the queue go on as before. An edit that can't be saved leaves the prompt as it was, and a notification titled "Could not save the queued prompt" says why. Cancelling the edit, or cancelling the prompt from the list meanwhile, leaves the queue as it was, less that prompt when it was cancelled.

#### Queueing On Purpose

A prompt queued on purpose from the chat input's send menu, while its lane is free, waits at the end of the queue rather than being sent at once: it goes when "Send next" is clicked, or when the next task is in its lane is over and auto-send is on.

#### Auto Send

A "Send next automatically" switch picks between sending each lane's next queued prompt as soon as that lane is free, and waiting. It starts switched on, and holds for both lanes. Switching it on sends the next queued prompt of each free lane straight away. Whenever a queued prompt's lane is free, a "Send next" button sends the first such prompt in the list; with both lanes free and prompts of each queued, clicking it again sends the other lane's.

#### Persistence

Queued prompts are saved with the project's data as they are queued, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. The queue is restored the first time the project is opened in a launch; a restored queue waits for "Send next" rather than sending on its own. A queued prompt's file is removed when it is cancelled, or when it is sent, at which point it is saved to the prompt history like any other prompt.

content.content:
## Concept

### Pitch

How anything that can be reordered by dragging shows where it will end up, as macOS lists and tab bars do: with a line in the gap between two items, never a highlighted item that leaves the drop ambiguous. Every list, tab bar, or row of items that is reordered by drag and drop behaves this way.

### Shape

#### Description

While an item is dragged over the items it can be reordered among, what it would be dropped into is always a gap between two items, or before the first or after the last, never an item itself. That gap is shown by an insertion indicator, and nothing else marks the drop: no item is highlighted, tinted, or outlined as a target.

#### Indicator

The indicator is a line 2 pixels thick in the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope)'s accent, with rounded ends and a small open circle, 6 pixels across and in the same colour, at its leading end. It lies across the gap, centred on the gap, horizontal between the rows of a list, running the list's width less its padding, and vertical between the tabs of a tab bar or the items of a row, running their height. It is drawn over the items, taking no room of its own, so nothing moves to make space while the drag is under way, and it never takes the mouse.

#### Choosing The Gap

Which gap is shown follows the pointer: over the first half of an item, the gap before it; over the second half, the gap after it, halves taken along the direction the items run. Past the last item, the gap after it; before the first, the gap before it. The two gaps either side of the dragged item itself are where it already is, so neither shows an indicator, and dropping there changes nothing. A gap an item may not be dropped into, as its user says, shows no indicator either, and nothing is marked while the pointer is over it.
The indicator moves from gap to gap at once as the pointer crosses the middle of an item, with no animation, so it is always exactly where a drop would land.

#### Dragging

The item dragged follows the pointer as a small floating copy, the item's own label on a raised surface with a soft shadow, as its user says. The item stays where it was in the list, dimmed to half its opacity, until it is dropped.

#### Dropping

Released over a gap that shows the indicator, the item moves into that gap, the items between shifting over by one. Released anywhere else, outside the items, over a gap it may not go into, or back where it started, nothing changes. Either way the indicator and the dimming go at once.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
use /lib
use /ui
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /ui/behaviours/drag-reorder import DragReorderBehaviour
from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope

export ui-component QueueListScope:
    concept: {QueueListConcept}

concept QueueListConcept:
    pitch:
        The tasks waiting their turn while their lane is busy, listed above the
        chat input, where they can be reordered, edited, or cancelled before
        they are sent.

    shape: {QueueListShape}

shape QueueListShape:
    description:
        The queue holds the tasks sent while their lane is busy, as the
        @{PromptSendingScope} says, in the order they were sent unless they
        have been moved since. It is one list holding both lanes' queues: the
        code lane's and the spec lane's prompts together, in one order. Each
        lane sends its own prompts one at a time, first to last in that order,
        whenever it is free, whatever the other lane's prompts are doing, so a
        Spec prompt behind a Code prompt in the list is sent as soon as the
        spec lane is free, without waiting for the Code prompt. A Freeform
        prompt, which needs both lanes free, holds back the spec lane's
        prompts queued after it until it has been sent, so it isn't passed
        over for ever.

    lanes:
        Each queued prompt's row shows which lane it waits for: a small label
        just before its text reading its mode, "Code", "Spec", or "Freeform",
        tinted that mode's colour, as the @{PromptModesScope} colours it. A
        prompt sent from the Chain tab waits in the spec lane, as its first
        step writes the spec, and reads "Chain" in the Chain colour; a chain's
        later step waiting for its lane reads what it is, "Code" or "Spec
        follow-up", in that step's mode colour.

    placement:
        The queue sits along the bottom of the view, below the output and
        directly above the chat input, with a border along its top. It is not
        part of the header. A row saying how many prompts are queued, with a
        chevron, expands to list each queued prompt in order, a line or two of
        each, with a button to cancel it. Each prompt in the list is numbered,
        with its number, text, and cancel button vertically centred in its
        row, and the list scrolls once it gets tall, with a @{ScrollbarScope}.
        Each time it is expanded, it opens scrolled to the bottom, on the
        prompts queued most recently, however it was scrolled when last
        closed. The same area holds the auto-send switch and the "Send next"
        button.

        Editing a queued prompt from the chat input's <Up>, as the
        @{ChatInputScope} says, expands the list while the queue holds more
        than one prompt, scrolled so the prompt being edited is in view,
        following it as <Up> and <Down> move the edit along the queue. Once
        the edit is saved or cancelled, a list it expanded collapses again;
        one already expanded stays as it was.
        The queue is shown only while it has anything in it.

    cancel:
        A queued prompt that has not been sent yet can be cancelled, which
        removes it from the queue for good. A prompt already sent is no longer
        in the queue.

    newConversation:
        Each queued prompt in the list has a small toggle switch, a slider,
        first of its controls, switched on while the prompt will start a new
        conversation rather than carry on the tasks', as its hidden anchor
        records, as the @{ChatInputScope} says. Clicking it switches between
        the two, saving the prompt again with the project. Its tooltip says
        which the prompt does, and that clicking does the other instead. The
        choice stays with the prompt wherever it is moved in the queue.

        Prompts that will share a context are joined by a subtle connector
        line drawn between their switches: a vertical line 1 pixel wide in
        the theme's line colour, centred on the switches, running from the
        bottom of one prompt's switch to the top of the next one's, across
        the gap between their rows. A prompt that carries on is joined to the
        one above it; one that starts a new conversation is not, so each run
        of joined switches is one context. The first prompt in the queue is
        never joined to anything above it. Nothing else marks the grouping:
        there is no gutter, dot, or line at the row's left edge. The line
        follows the prompts as they are moved or switched, and is never under
        a switch, only between them. Each switch sits centred up and down in its
        row, however tall the row's text or attached images make it, and the
        line runs unbroken from one switch to the next across both rows'
        padding, with no gap where one row ends and the next begins.

        The toggle can only make a prompt start a new conversation; it can't
        bring back one that was left. Once New conversation has been pressed
        for the tasks, the next task to run starts a new conversation
        whichever prompt it is, even when the prompt it marked has been moved
        further down or switched back to carrying on.

    reorder:
        Queued prompts are reordered by dragging them, as the
        @{DragReorderBehaviour} says: each row starts with a grip, and the
        prompt dragged follows the pointer as a line of its text. Dropped in a
        gap, it moves there, and the order is saved with the project, so the
        queue comes back in its new order when the project is opened again. A
        prompt still being saved, as its spinner shows, can't be dragged, and
        no gap past a prompt still being saved shows the indicator. A prompt being edited can still be moved,
        and the chat input's "Editing queued prompt N" follows it to its new
        place. A move that can't be saved leaves the queue as it was, and a
        notification titled "Could not move the prompt" says why.

    editing:
        Each queued prompt in the list also has a button with a pencil icon,
        after its move buttons and before its cancel button, whose tooltip
        says it edits the prompt. Clicking it edits the prompt in the
        @{ChatInputScope}, as it says, and its row is highlighted while it is
        being edited. While it is, it is held where it is: it is never sent,
        and its lane, waiting on it, waits, even with auto-send on; the other
        lane carries on. Saving the
        edit puts the new text, in the mode and with the attachments it was
        saved with, in its place in the queue, saved with the project in
        place of what it held, then lets the queue go on as before. An edit
        that can't be saved leaves the prompt as it was, and a notification
        titled "Could not save the queued prompt" says why. Cancelling the
        edit, or cancelling the prompt from the list meanwhile, leaves the
        queue as it was, less that prompt when it was cancelled.

    queueingOnPurpose:
        A prompt queued on purpose from the chat input's send menu, while its
        lane is free, waits at the end of the queue rather than being sent
        at once: it goes when "Send next" is clicked, or when the next task is
        in its lane is over and auto-send is on.

    autoSend:
        A "Send next automatically" switch picks between sending each lane's
        next queued prompt as soon as that lane is free, and waiting. It starts
        switched on, and holds for both lanes. Switching it on sends the next
        queued prompt of each free lane straight away. Whenever a queued
        prompt's lane is free, a "Send next" button sends the first such
        prompt in the list; with both lanes free and prompts of each queued,
        clicking it again sends the other lane's.

    persistence:
        Queued prompts are saved with the project's data as they are queued,
        as the @{ProjectDataScope} says. The queue is restored the first time
        the project is opened in a launch; a restored queue waits for "Send
        next" rather than sending on its own. A queued prompt's file is
        removed when it is cancelled, or when it is sent, at which point it is
        saved to the prompt history like any other prompt.

        within 32 pixels of its top or bottom for a list, or of its left or
        right for a row, the area scrolls that way on its own, slowly at
        first and faster the nearer the pointer is to the edge, or the
        further past it, up to about a row every 50 milliseconds, smoothly
        frame by frame rather than in jumps, and stops at its end. Moving
        the pointer away from the edge stops it at once. The wheel and
        trackpad scroll the area too while the item is dragged, as they do
        at any time, without dropping it.

        However the area scrolls, the dragged copy stays under the pointer,
        and the gap shown is chosen anew each frame from where the pointer is
        over the items now there, so the indicator is always exactly where a
        drop would land. An area that doesn't scroll, or holds every item in
        view, doesn't scroll on its own.

        shown by an insertion indicator, and nothing else marks the drop: no
        item is highlighted, tinted, or outlined as a target.

content.text:
Queued prompts now show as one line each, clicking one opens it in the editor, and dragging scrolls the list. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files.

## What changed in the spec

**Queue rows** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/queue-list/index.md#placement`)
- **One line per row:** every row is 28px tall and shows only the prompt's first non-blank line. It's cut off with an ellipsis and never wraps.
- **Images:** attached images show as a small muted icon with a count, such as "2", never the images themselves.
- **Tooltip:** shows the prompt's first few lines.
- **Click to edit:** clicking the text, or anywhere in the row except its grip, switch and buttons, opens the whole prompt in the chat input with its tab selected. This does what the pencil button already does.
- **Drag from the grip:** a press on the grip that turns into a drag reorders the row instead of opening it.

**Drag reordering** (`.claude/reference/ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#scrolling-while-dragging`)

This is a new section, and it applies to every drag-to-reorder list, not just the queue.
- **Auto-scroll near the edges:** while you drag, holding the pointer within 32px of a scrolling list's edge, or past it, scrolls the list that way.
  - It starts slow and speeds up the closer or further past you go, up to about a row every 50ms.
  - It scrolls smoothly and stops at the list's end, or as soon as you move away from the edge.
- **Wheel and trackpad:** they scroll the list during a drag without dropping the item.
- **Accurate drop line:** the dragged copy stays under the pointer, and the drop line is recalculated every frame as the list scrolls, so it always shows where the item would land.
- **Lists that fit:** a list with everything in view doesn't auto-scroll.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791402289-CollapsePromptsToSingleLine.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `QueueListScope`: `#placement` for single-line rows and click-to-edit, `#editing` for what the click does, `#reorder` for drag from the grip, and `#new-conversation` for the connector line, which keeps working with the shorter rows.
- `DragReorderBehaviour`: `#scrolling-while-dragging`, plus `#choosing-the-gap` and `#dragging`, recalculated as the list scrolls.

#### Language Support

```
overview: A Piton file (`.pi`) is edited with the project's [LSP](../lsp/index.md#lsp) server, shared with the chat input, which sees the editor's unsaved text: the file is opened with `textDocument/didOpen`, kept current with full-text `textDocument/didChange`, reported with `textDocument/didSave` when saved, and closed with `textDocument/didClose` when the editor closes or shows another file. Other files are edited without language support, as is a Piton file while the server is not running.
completions: `textDocument/completion` is requested after typing a letter, a digit, an opening curly brace, a period, a dollar sign, an at sign, a colon, or an underscore, and narrowed and ordered as in the chat input. Accepting a completion also applies the import the server attaches to it.
hover: Hovering a name shows the server's `textDocument/hover`. Typing in the editor clears whatever the pointer's hover shows, the name's hover and a diagnostic's message alike, as soon as a key changes the text, and nothing hovered shows again until the pointer next moves over the text.
definitions: Ctrl-clicking (Cmd-clicking on macOS) a name goes to its `textDocument/definition`. A definition in another file opens that file at the definition, as the [OpenFileScope](../open-file/index.md#open-file-scope) says.
diagnostics: What the server publishes for the file is underlined, with the message shown on hover, and kept while the text is edited until the server publishes again.
quickFixes: Ctrl+. (Cmd+. on macOS) lists the server's `textDocument/codeAction` fixes at the cursor, and picking one applies its edits to the file.
```

The popover appears because the editor shows whatever the Piton language server returns for any word, and the server answers for plain text too, with "compiled to …". I changed the spec so the editor decides what's worth showing, rather than trusting every answer the server gives. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files.

## What changed in the spec

The `hover` rule in `spec/scope/editor/index.pi` (`.claude/reference/scope/editor/index.md#language-support`) now says:

- **Names only:** a hover popover only appears over names:
  - a key or property name
  - an anchor's name where it's declared or extended
  - a keyword
  - a name brought in by an import

### Shape

#### Description

The same row and list, looking and behaving the same, wherever something sent before can be looked back on. Each use names what it lists, what the row counts, and what the row reads while expanded.

#### Row

A small row, always shown where it is used, with the tab bar's background colour. It reads "No …", "1 …", or "N …" followed by what it counts, beside a chevron, and does nothing until there is anything to list. Clicking it expands the list, and the row then reads what it says to go back; clicking it again closes the list.

#### List

A scrollable accordion of every item, oldest first, with a [ScrollbarScope](../scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope). Each time it is expanded, it opens scrolled to the bottom, with the most recent items in view, however it was scrolled when last closed, the first time as much as any other, and whether it takes the place of what it is shown over. Each is headed by its status and the first line of its prompt, with a Resend button at its right, when the use offers one, and opens onto the compiled prompt it was sent as and its [TaskTableScope](../task-table/index.md#task-table-scope). One item is open at a time. A use can say its tables collapse the steps leading up to the result; previous tasks show their tables whole.
An open item is exactly as wide as the list, however long the lines in its prompt or table, which wrap rather than running past the list's edge, and exactly as tall as what it shows: it ends a small margin below its table, like the margin above its prompt, with no empty space beneath it before the next item or the end of the list.
However long an open item's output, the list lays out only what is in

table's rows are drawn as the list scrolls to them, as each item's heading is.

The spec already said each previous task shows how long it took, but no time appeared because the history record never saved when a task started or ended. I fixed the record and spelled out how durations look in the previous tasks list. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files.
