**Durations** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#elapsed`)
- **Every previous task:** each heading shows how long the task took, whether it finished done, failed or cancelled. A task still running in the list counts up.
- **Chains:** a chain's parent row shows its total time, from when the first step was sent to when the last step ended. Each step shows its own time underneath.
- **Layout:** the times sit in their own right-aligned column just before each heading's buttons, so you can compare them at a glance and long ones stand out.
- **Older tasks:**
  - Tasks recorded before times were kept show an estimate, from the second their history file is named by to when their record was written, such as "≈ 4:12".
  - Their tooltip says the time is approximate.
  - Tasks where neither time can be worked out show nothing.

content.text:
I rewrote the default prompts so tasks read less before they start, write their constraints once, and end with a short reply. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 81 files.

## What changed in the spec

All edits are in `spec/scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.pi`, under `#defaults`.

- **Spec-reading default:** its last paragraph now tells a task to:
  - read the reference pages the prompt links to, then only the pages those link to that the change depends on;
  - not survey the spec, list its folders or search it first;
  - never read a page the prompt already gives it as a slice, or anything it has already read.
- **Understanding-file paragraph** (Code, Chain and Spec defaults): the file is written once, after reading and before the first change, and rewritten only when a constraint in it turns out to be wrong, never after each page read. It used to say to write it before changing anything and keep it current while reading.
- **Short final reply (new):** the Code, Chain, Spec and Ask defaults end by asking for "a reply of a few sentences saying what changed, or for a question, the answer, not a recap of the work or of what you read."
- **Summary sentence:** a sentence after the defaults states the goal: as few turns as possible before the work starts.

**Existing projects won't pick this up on their own.** The spec already says a project keeps its saved prompts when a default changes. Reset the prompts in Settings to get the new defaults; new projects get them automatically.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791485035-Prompt_81f60e02b63f82e2.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ModeSystemPromptsScope` `#defaults`: update `spec-reading.md`, `code.md`, `combined.md`, `spec.md` and `ask.md` in this repository's `.suspense/system-prompts`. The built-in defaults are taken from those files.

<task-instructions>
We're working on both the spec and the code, as a chain. This first step changes the spec only, located in ./spec; the code is changed in the next step.

Write the spec so it describes the application as it should be once the prompt is met, and constrains the code. Once you finish, the spec will be built and the same prompt sent to a coding agent, with your reply, to change the code to match it; so end your reply by saying what you changed in the spec and which anchors the code should follow.

When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read .suspense/suspense-fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.

Before creating or editing any .pi file, read .suspense/fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.

Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under .claude/reference, not by reading the source again. Never finish with a spec that `piton check` or `piton build` reports errors in.

Once you have read what the change depends on, and before your first change, write the constraints this task must meet to .suspense/history/1791485622-ImplementDebugInfoCollection.understanding.md, once. Rewrite it only when a constraint in it turns out to be wrong, never after each page you read. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.

End with a reply of a few sentences saying what changed, or for a question, the answer, not a recap of the work or of what you read.
</task-instructions>

Suspense keeps a debug log of what it does, so that a problem can be handed to an agent as files to investigate. It is `suspense.log` in Suspense's own data directory, beside `updates.log`, as the SelfUpdateScope keeps that one, one line per event, each with the time to the millisecond, the project it concerns, and what happened, keeping the last 20,000 lines across sessions.

It logs every child process the application starts, its command, working directory, how long it took, and its exit status, with its standard error when it failed; each task's and question's phases as they happen, queued, spec build, snapshot, preparing the container with its mounts and the podman command, harness started, its first event, each tool call, its result, and the closing snapshot, each with how long it took; each git status refresh, spec build, and language server start or restart, with how long it took; any time the window was unresponsive for more than 200 milliseconds; and every panic, with its backtrace, written before the application exits. It never logs environment variables, credentials, or prompt text. A task's history record also keeps the times of its phases.

The command palette has a "Collect debug info" command that writes a folder, named for the time, in Suspense's data directory and shows it in the file manager: the debug log, `updates.log`, the application's version, platform, and harness report, and the history records of the open project's last ten tasks and questions, with a short README saying what each file is. The palette also has "Open debug log", which opens `suspense.log` as the OpenFileScope opens a file.

use /lib
from /scope/open-file import OpenFileScope

export scope DebugLogScope:
    concept: {DebugLogConcept}

concept DebugLogConcept:
    pitch:
        A debug log of what Suspense does, so that a problem can be handed to
        an agent as files to investigate.

    shape: {DebugLogShape}

shape DebugLogShape:
    description:
        The log is `suspense.log` in Suspense's own data directory, beside
        `updates.log`, as the @{SelfUpdateScope} keeps that one. It is one
        line per event, each with the time to the millisecond, the project it
        concerns, by its folder, or none for the application's own, and what
        happened. It keeps the last 20,000 lines, across sessions: each launch
        appends to it, and the oldest lines go once there are more.

    logged:
        It logs:

        \\
        - every child process the application starts: its command, its working directory, how long it took, and its exit status, with its standard error when it failed
        - each task's and question's phases as they happen, each with how long it took: queued, spec build, snapshot, preparing the container, with its mounts and the podman command, harness started, the harness's first event, each tool call, its result, and the closing snapshot
        - each git status refresh, spec build, and language server start or restart, with how long it took
        - any time the window was unresponsive for more than 200 milliseconds, with how long
        - every panic, with its backtrace, written to the log before the application exits
        \\

    neverLogged:
        It never logs environment variables, credentials, or prompt text: a
        command is logged with its arguments but never the prompt given on its
        standard input, nor anything in its environment, and a tool call by
        its kind and the path or command it acted on, never what the harness
        replied.

    phases:
        A task's history record, as the @{ProjectDataScope} says, also keeps
        the times of its phases, as the log names them, when each began and
        ended, to the millisecond.

    collecting:
        The palette's "Collect debug info" writes a folder, named for the
        time, as `debug-2026-10-08-14-03-22`, in Suspense's data directory,
        and shows it in the file manager. It holds:

        \\
        - `suspense.log`, the debug log
        - `updates.log`
        - `about.txt`, the application's version and platform
        - `harness.json`, the open project's harness report
        - `history/`, the history records of the open project's last ten tasks and questions, each beside its hidden anchor's source
        - `README.md`, a short note saying what each file is
        \\

        With no project open, it holds what doesn't need one, and its README
        says no project was open. The palette's "Open debug log" opens
        `suspense.log` as the @{OpenFileScope} opens a file.
EOF

The "Containers" section is headed "Containers", with a muted line beneath saying that Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps, and questions always run in a container holding only what their mode may use, and that Code tasks always run on the host, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says.

Then a row for each harness, in the order of the Agent section: its name, and muted beside it whether it is logged in in its container, "Logged in" or "Not logged in", read from its volume each time the settings open, and a "Log in again" button, which runs its login in a container and shows the login view, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says, whether it is logged in or not. These are the user's, not the project's, so they are the same with or without a project open.

stands among the reply's markdown, as a prompt card: a box on the
        theme's raised surface, faintly tinted the mode's colour, with
        corners rounded 6 pixels, across the answer's full width. Along its
        top runs a small header, the mode's icon and name in the mode's
        colour, as "Code prompt", and beneath it the prompt's text as it was
        written, wrapped, in the body's text colour, not rendered as
        markdown. Along its bottom, at its right, is a row of small buttons,
        4 pixels apart, wrapping onto another line where the card is too
        narrow: Copy, with a copy icon, which puts the prompt's text on the
        clipboard; Edit, with a pencil icon, as below; and then "Send to
        Code", "Send to Chain", and "Send to Spec", in that order, each with
        an arrow icon and in its mode's colour, as the @{PromptModesScope}
        colours them. The send button for the card's own mode, where it is
        one of those three, is filled in its colour, and the others are ghost
        buttons in theirs, so the one the answer meant stands out while every
        task mode is a click away. A card for `ask` or `freeform` has, before
        the three, "Ask" or "Send to Freeform", filled in that mode's colour,
        the three after it as ghosts.

        Each send button sends the prompt's text at once, in its mode, as
        though it had been written in the @{ChatInputScope} on that tab and
        sent, as the @{PromptSendingScope} says, the Chain button sending it as
        a Chain prompt: a task is compiled anew, building the spec first,
        and queues while its lane is busy, and a question runs at once. It
        is sent with the Slice toggle as it stands, with nothing attached,
        and what is being written in the chat input, and attached to it, is
        left alone. The button then reads "Sent to Code", "Sent to Chain",
        "Sent to Spec", "Asked", or "Sent to Freeform", with a check, for 2
        seconds, and can be clicked again to send it again. The tooltip of
        each says what it does, as "Send this prompt as a Code task".

        Edit puts the prompt's text in the chat input's text input instead,
        and selects the card's mode's tab, Chain for Code and Spec selected
        together where the mode is `chain`, giving the input keyboard focus
        with the cursor at the end of the text. It never sends anything: the
        user reads, edits, and sends it as any prompt. Where the input
        already holds text, that text is set aside first as the chat input
        sets aside a prompt for editing a queued one, and comes back once the
        prompt from the card is sent or cleared, so nothing typed is lost.
        What is attached to the prompt being written stays attached. The
        button reads "Edited", with a check, for 2 seconds after.

        A block whose mode is missing or isn't one of those five is still a
        prompt card, headed "Prompt", in Ask's colour, with all three send
        buttons as ghosts, and Edit selects Chain, the tab the chat input
        starts on. While a block is
        still streaming in, its card is shown with what has come so far and
        its buttons disabled until the block closes. A block never closed by
        the end of a finished answer is a card all the same, holding what
        came. An answer may hold any number of cards, each in its place.

content.content:
#### Layout

Everything in the tab is laid out the same plain way, with no stray padding or margin anywhere. The header runs the tab's full width, 32 pixels tall, as tall as the body's tab bar, its contents centred up and down in it, with 12 pixels of padding at its left and 8 at its right, and a single 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour along its bottom, the only line in the tab. In it, from the left: the file's path, then 6 pixels after it the unsaved dot while there is one, then at the far right the Save button and the close button, 4 pixels apart. Both buttons are small ghost buttons 24 pixels tall, the close button an icon button 24 pixels square, neither with a border. The header has no margin of its own above, below, or beside it: it starts at the top of the tab, directly beneath the tab bar, and its left and right edges are the tab's.
Beneath the header, the file fills the rest of the tab edge to edge, with no margin, border, or rounded corner around it, and nothing between it and the header's line. Its text starts 12 pixels in from the tab's left edge, the same as the path in the header above it, so the two line up, and 8 pixels below the header's line. A message that the file can't be read, or can't be saved, is set in by the same 12 pixels, in a row as tall as its text needs with 8 pixels above and below it.

#### Ruler

A thin vertical line, in the theme's line colour, runs down the text at the 80th column, the width a line should keep within. Past it, the editor's background is a step darker than the well, as black laid over it, 25% in dark mode and 5% in light mode, so text running long stands out while staying as readable. The line and the shade scroll sideways with the text, are drawn behind it, and never take the mouse.

##### Session

At the far right of the bar, at the right end of the help text, sits how much context the selected tab's conversation holds, then a New conversation button. Each lane's tasks, and the questions of the Ask tab, have a conversation of their own, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, so the figure is the spec lane's on the Spec and Chain tabs, a Chain prompt starting in the spec lane, the code lane's on Code and Freeform, and the questions' on Ask.
The figure reads "Context", then the number of tokens, short and extra small, muted: "850", "42.1k", "123k", or "1.2M", to a decimal place below a hundred of a unit. It follows each reply as the harness reports it. While the next prompt would start a new conversation, as when the project has none yet or New conversation was just pressed, it reads "Context 0". Its tooltip says how many tokens the conversation the next prompt carries on holds, or that the next prompt starts a new conversation.
##### Slice

Just left of the context figure sits the Slice toggle: a small ghost button with a scissors icon, reading "Slice", which shows as selected while it is on. It starts off. Its tooltip says what the prompt is sent as: while off, the prompt written as a spec, its references linking to the spec they name; while on, the prompt with the `piton slice` of each spec it references. Clicking it turns it on or off, and it applies to every tab, Ask included. It stays as it is across sends, tab switches, and project switches, as the prompt being written does, and the help text gives way to it as it does to the session controls.

#### Hidden Anchor

While the user will be able to type plain text, behind the scenes, they'll be typing into a piton anchor with a userPrompt property, named after what the prompt asks for, as its naming says. It's this compiled anchor that will be send to the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope)

##### Naming

Each task and question is named by the harness, rather than at random, so its files, its snapshot refs, and its header say what it was for. When a prompt is sent or queued, the harness is asked for a short title for it with the prompt-title prompt of the [BakedSystemPromptsScope](../../harness-integration/baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts-scope), in a run of its own that keeps no session, as the notes and commit messages are, with a small model where the harness can be told one. A name already used by a task or question of the project, in its history, its questions, or its queue, is given the lowest number from 2 up that makes it unused, as in ChatTitlesFromTheAgent2.
Asking never holds a prompt up for long: it is asked while the spec builds ahead of a task, and a prompt is saved, queued, and compiled once it has its name. A title that hasn't come back within 10 seconds, that the harness fails to give, or that leaves no letter once cut down, is given up on, and the prompt is named as before, Prompt_ followed by 16 random hexadecimal digits. A task cancelled while it is being named is saved under that random name. Until a task has its name, its header shows no

content.text:
I added an effort-level picker to `ChatInputScope`, right beside the model picker we added last turn. `piton check` and `piton build` both ran clean.

**What's new** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#effort`): a small ghost button, just left of the model picker, naming the reasoning effort the next prompt will use — "Low", "Medium", "High", or "Default" (which tells the harness nothing, so it uses its own default). It works exactly like the model picker: applies to every tab but Freeform, is remembered per harness, and travels with a prompt through queuing, resending, and chain steps.

Only Codex actually takes a reasoning-effort setting (`--model-reasoning-effort`), so the picker is disabled for Claude Code and OpenCode with a tooltip explaining why — I didn't want to invent a capability those harnesses don't have. If either of them does support something equivalent, that's worth telling me so I can wire it in instead of disabling the control.

I also added a line to `UserPreferencesScope` so the per-harness effort choice persists, matching how the model choice is remembered.

content.content:
#### Wrap

The Wrap button, with a wrap-text icon, turns soft wrapping on and off, showing as selected while it is on. Its tooltip says whether long lines wrap or run past the edge, and that clicking does the other, with its shortcut, Alt+Z. It starts off. While it is on, a line longer than the editor is wide wraps at the editor's right edge, at a space where there is one and mid-word where there isn't, onto as many visual rows as it needs, each row after the first starting at the line's own indentation, so the text never scrolls sideways and the horizontal scrollbar goes. Only how the text shows changes: the file's text, its line numbers, the language server's positions, and what is saved are the same either way, and Home, End, and selecting by line act on visual rows while on, as in other editors, Home's smart indentation applying to the line's first row. The ruler and its shade stay at the 80th column, wrapped or not. Turning it on or off keeps the cursor's line in view where it was. The choice is remembered for the user, as the [UserPreferencesScope](../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences-scope) says, the same for every file and project, and holds for every file opened after.

    wrap:
        The Wrap button, with a wrap-text icon, hard wraps the text at 80
        columns, the ruler's, by Piton's rules, changing the file's text
        itself, as `piton format` changes it. It is an action, not a mode:
        clicking it, or pressing Alt+Z, wraps once, and the editor never
        wraps as it is typed in, nor shows a line any other way than as it
        is. It wraps the lines the selection touches, or, with nothing
        selected, the whole file. Its tooltip says it wraps long lines at 80
        columns, with its shortcut. It is shown only for a Piton file, and
        is disabled while the file can't be edited yet.

        Wrapping never changes what the file says: the file compiles to
        exactly what it did before, and only lines past the 80th column are
        touched. A line is broken only where Piton joins it back as it was,
        so each break is at a single space, which the break takes the place
        of, in the prose of a multi-line value, the lines after it taking
        the indentation of the line broken, as consecutive lines of a
        string block join with one space. Short lines are never joined, and
        a paragraph is never reflowed: only lines that run long are split,
        each at the last space it may break at before the 80th column, or,
        where there is none, at the first after it.

        Nothing is broken where Piton would read it otherwise. A line is
        never broken inside an expression in braces, whether written plain
        or after a dollar sign, a hash, or an at sign, nor inside an escape
        wrapper, nor at all inside an escape block or a code fence, whose
        text is kept exactly. No break is made where the line it starts
        would begin with `- `, `+ `, or `++ `, which make a list item or a
        composition line, with `//`, which makes a comment, with a
        backslash, or with a word followed by a colon and a space, which
        makes a key; the break moves to the space before or after instead.
        A line holding a key and its value, `name: value`, a list item, an
        import, or a declaration is never broken, since what follows it
        indented would be something else. A comment that runs long is
        broken the same way, its later lines comments of their own, each
        begun with `// ` at its indentation. A line with nowhere it may be
        broken is left as it is, however long.

        The wrap is one edit, undone in one step, and keeps the cursor and
        the selection on the same text. A file the language server reports
        errors in still wraps, by the same rules. Wrapping doesn't save the
        file; saving it formats it as ever.

EOF

content.text:
The editor's Wrap is now a hard wrap at 80 columns by Piton's rules, replacing the soft-wrap toggle. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 82 files.

- **How it works:** Wrap (or Alt+Z) is a one-off action that rewrites the file's text. It never wraps as you type. It wraps the selected lines, or the whole file when nothing is selected, and only appears for Piton files.
- **Never changes meaning:** the file must compile to exactly what it did before.
  - Only lines past column 80 are split, each at a single space, and the new line takes the broken line's indentation. Short lines are never joined.
  - Nothing is broken inside an expression, an escape wrapper, an escape block or a code fence.
  - A break never starts a line that Piton would read differently: one beginning with `- `, `+ `, `++ `, `//`, a backslash, or `word: `.
  - Lines holding a key and its value, list items, imports and declarations are never broken.
  - Long comments become several `// ` lines.
  - A line with nowhere safe to break is left as it is.
- **Editing:** one wrap is one undo step. The cursor and selection stay on the same text. Wrapping doesn't save the file.
- **Preference removed:** the remembered wrap setting is gone from `UserPreferencesScope`, since there's no longer a mode to remember.

**Anchors the code should follow:** `EditorScope` `#wrap` and `#layout`, and `UserPreferencesScope`, where the old preference was removed.

When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read .suspense/suspense-fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.

Before creating or editing any .pi file, read .suspense/fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.

Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under .claude/reference, not by reading the source again.         It is only there while a task is running: from the moment a task is
        sent from the Code, Chain, or Spec tab until its run is over. Questions
        from the Ask tab never show it, even when one is sent from the queue.

        When a task starts, it slides out from the right edge of the message
        list and the chat input, growing from nothing to its width, its
        contents sliding into view from behind that edge as it does. When the
        run is over, it slides back the same way. The slide is quick and
        settles without bouncing. It pushes rather than covers: from the
        first frame of the slide to the last, the body's tab bar, the message
        list or open file beneath it, and the chat input end exactly at the
        sidebar's left edge, narrowing as it grows and widening as it
        shrinks, laid out again each frame, as the @{BodyScope} says. Nothing
        runs beneath the sliding sidebar, nothing is clipped by it, and
        nothing jumps to a new width once the slide settles.


    basicDesignAndLayout:
        The @{MessageList} fills the body's Chat tab: all the space between
        the body's tab bar and the @{ChatInputScope} along the bottom. From top to bottom it holds the
        previous tasks row, the header, holding the latest task and every
        other task under way, one of them selected and shown in full and the
        rest as compact rows, as the @{MessageList} says, the selected task's
        output, and the queue.

        Before any task has been sent, the space shows a hint instead, which
        wraps when the view is narrow. It reads
        "Write a prompt below. Enter adds a line; Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it."
        or, while no project is open, as the @{NoProjectStateScope} says,
        "Open a project to start prompting."

    chatHistory: @{MessageList}

    previousTasks:
        Previous tasks are a @{HistoryListScope} along the top of the view,
        listing every task sent. Its row counts every task but those the
        header shows, the latest, which heads the view, and any other under
        way: "No previous tasks", "1 previous task", or
        "N previous tasks", and each offers Resend. Expanded, the list takes the place of the latest
        task and its output, and the row reads "Back to the latest task".

        Every task in the list has a checkbox at the left of its heading,
    placement:
        The queue sits along the bottom of the view, below the output and
        directly above the chat input, with a border along its top. It is not
        part of the header. A row saying how many prompts are queued, with a
        chevron, expands to list each queued prompt in order, one line each,
        with a button to cancel it. Each prompt in the list is numbered, with
        its number, text, and cancel button vertically centred in its row,
    scrollingPast:
        Scrolling carries on past either end of the latest task and the
        previous tasks, from one to the other, through an elastic stretch at
        that end. A scroll that reaches an end doesn't stop dead there: the
        same scroll keeps going, with no pause needed, into the stretch, which
        resists it, and it crosses over only once it has pushed far enough

use /lib

from /scope/prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/message-list import MessageList
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope

from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /ui/components/growing-text-input import GrowingTextInputScope
from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope

export ui-component TasksTabScope:
    concept: {TasksTabConcept}

concept TasksTabConcept:
    pitch:
        The right sidebar's Tasks tab: every task of the project at a glance,
        what has run, what is running, and what is queued, where any of them
        can be looked into, edited, and adjusted, and a chain given more
        steps.

    shape: {TasksTabShape}

shape TasksTabShape:
    description:
        The tab is one scrolling column, with a @{ScrollbarScope}, read top to
        bottom as a timeline, in three groups, each headed by a small muted
        label with its count: "Previous", every task that has run, oldest at
        the top, as the @{PromptEditor}'s previous tasks are, with their
        filters and batch actions along the group's heading; "Running", every
        task under way, in either lane; and "Queued", the queue, in its order,
        as the @{QueueListScope} says, reordered by dragging, its auto-send
        switch and "Send next" button along its heading. A group with nothing
        in it shows its heading alone, muted, "No queued prompts" and the
        like. Each time the tab is shown, it is scrolled so the Running
        group, or the start of the Queued one when nothing runs, is in view.

    rows:
        Every task is one row, 28 pixels tall, as a queued prompt's is: a bar
        2 pixels wide down its left edge in its mode's colour, as the
        @{PromptModesScope} colours it, then its status, a spinner while it
        is under way, a tick, cross, or dash once it has ended, or, queued,
        its place in the queue, then the first line of its prompt, cut off
        with an ellipsis, then, at its right, muted, how long it took, or has
        been running, as the @{MessageList} writes it. A chain is one row,
        its steps as rows indented beneath it, collapsed to start with, as
        the previous tasks group a chain. Clicking a row opens it, as below,
        and the row stays highlighted while it is open. Hovering a row shows
        its prompt's first lines in its tooltip.

    details:
        An open task takes the tab's place, with a back arrow and the task's
        mode and name along its top, the arrow and <Escape> going back to the
        list as it was left. Opening a task that has run or is running also
        shows its output in the @{MessageList}, as it shows the selected
        task, with a bar above it reading "Back to the latest task" while it
        isn't the latest. What the open task shows, top to bottom:

        \\
        - At a glance: its status and how long it took, its lane, its place in the queue while it waits, the conversation it carries on or that it starts a new one, its model and effort, and once it has run, how many tool calls it made, its errors, its tokens and their cost, and how many files it changed, each a labelled figure, those that don't apply left out
        - Its prompt, as it was typed, in a GrowingTextInputScope, and beneath it what is attached to it
        - Its parameters: its mode, its model and effort, its Slice toggle, and whether it starts a new conversation, each as the chat input shows it
        - Its actions: Resend, Send to Spec or Send to Code, Cancel while it is under way or queued, and Open output, as the PromptSendingScope gives them
        \\

        A queued task is edited right there: its prompt can be typed in, its
        attachments removed, and its parameters changed, its mode among
        those of the tabs, a change of lane moving it to that lane's queue in
        its place. Each change is saved with the project as it is made, as
        saving a queued prompt's edit is, and while it is being changed the
        task is held, never sent, as a queued prompt being edited is; going
        back, or opening another, lets it go. A task that has run, or is
        running, can't be changed: its prompt and parameters read as they
        were sent, and "Edit and resend" puts them in the open task as a new
        queued prompt, ready to change, sent once "Send" is clicked. The
        chat input's own <Up> editing still works as the @{ChatInputScope}
        says, and opens the same task here.

    chainSteps:
        An open Chain task lists its steps beneath its parameters, in the
        order they run, each a row as in the list, with its status: its spec
        step, its code step, and its spec follow-up when it has one. An "Add
        step" button beneath them adds a step of its own after the last: a
        Code or a Spec step, chosen from a small menu, with a prompt of its
        own, typed in the step's row as it expands, its model and effort
        those of the chain until changed. An added step runs once the step
        before it finishes, in its own mode's lane and place, as every step
        of a chain does, told its own prompt, the chain's prompt as typed,
        and what the step before it replied, as the spec-to-code prompt
        tells a code step, so a chain can be carried on, as a further code
        change once the spec is built, or a spec tidy-up after the code. A
        step not yet sent can be edited, moved among the others not yet
        sent, or removed; one sent reads as it was. Steps are saved with the
        chain, in its hidden anchor, as the @{PromptSendingScope} keeps a
        queued prompt, so a chain keeps its added steps across restarts, and
        a step whose step before it failed or was cancelled is never sent, as
        none of a chain's are.

use /lib
use /ui
from /scope/prompt-mode import PromptEditor
from /scope/prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/message-list import MessageList
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/queue-list import QueueListScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from /ui/components/growing-text-input import GrowingTextInputScope
from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope

export ui-component TasksTabScope:
    concept: {TasksTabConcept}

concept TasksTabConcept:
    pitch:
        The right sidebar's Tasks tab: every task of the project at a glance,
        what has run, what is running, and what is queued, where any of them
        can be looked into, edited, and adjusted, and a chain given more
        steps.

    shape: {TasksTabShape}

shape TasksTabShape:
    description:
        The tab is one scrolling column, with a @{ScrollbarScope}, read top to
        bottom as a timeline, in three groups, each headed by a small muted
        label with its count: "Previous", every task that has run, oldest at
        the top, as the @{PromptEditor}'s previous tasks are, with their
        filters and batch actions along the group's heading; "Running", every
        task under way, in either lane; and "Queued", the queue, in its order,
        as the @{QueueListScope} says, reordered by dragging, its auto-send
        switch and "Send next" button along its heading. A group with nothing
        in it shows its heading alone, muted, "No queued prompts" and the
        like. Each time the tab is shown, it is scrolled so the Running
        group, or the start of the Queued one when nothing runs, is in view.

    rows:
        Every task is one row, 28 pixels tall, as a queued prompt's is: a bar
        2 pixels wide down its left edge in its mode's colour, as the
        @{PromptModesScope} colours it, then its status, a spinner while it
        is under way, a tick, cross, or dash once it has ended, or, queued,
        its place in the queue, then the first line of its prompt, cut off
        with an ellipsis, then, at its right, muted, how long it took, or has
        been running, as the @{MessageList} writes it. A chain is one row,
        its steps as rows indented beneath it, collapsed to start with, as
        the previous tasks group a chain. Clicking a row opens it, as below,
        and the row stays highlighted while it is open. Hovering a row shows
        its prompt's first lines in its tooltip.

    details:
        An open task takes the tab's place, with a back arrow and the task's
        mode and name along its top, the arrow and <Escape> going back to the
        list as it was left. Opening a task that has run or is running also
        shows its output in the @{MessageList}, as it shows the selected
        task, with a bar above it reading "Back to the latest task" while it
        isn't the latest. What the open task shows, top to bottom:

        \\
        - At a glance: its status and how long it took, its lane, its place in the queue while it waits, the conversation it carries on or that it starts a new one, its model and effort, and once it has run, how many tool calls it made, its errors, its tokens and their cost, and how many files it changed, each a labelled figure, those that don't apply left out
        - Its prompt, as it was typed, in a GrowingTextInputScope, and beneath it what is attached to it
        - Its parameters: its mode, its model and effort, its Slice toggle, and whether it starts a new conversation, each as the chat input shows it
        - Its actions: Resend, Send to Spec or Send to Code, Cancel while it is under way or queued, and Open output, as the PromptSendingScope gives them
        \\

        A queued task is edited right there: its prompt can be typed in, its
        attachments removed, and its parameters changed, its mode among
        those of the tabs, a change of lane moving it to that lane's queue in
        its place. Each change is saved with the project as it is made, as
        saving a queued prompt's edit is, and while it is being changed the
        task is held, never sent, as a queued prompt being edited is; going
        back, or opening another, lets it go. A task that has run, or is
        running, can't be changed: its prompt and parameters read as they
        were sent, and "Edit and resend" puts them in the open task as a new
        queued prompt, ready to change, sent once "Send" is clicked. The
        chat input's own <Up> editing still works as the @{ChatInputScope}
        says, and opens the same task here.

    chainSteps:
        An open Chain task lists its steps beneath its parameters, in the
        order they run, each a row as in the list, with its status: its spec
        step, its code step, and its spec follow-up when it has one. An "Add
        step" button beneath them adds a step of its own after the last: a
        Code or a Spec step, chosen from a small menu, with a prompt of its
        own, typed in the step's row as it expands, its model and effort
        those of the chain until changed. An added step runs once the step
        before it finishes, in its own mode's lane and place, as every step
        of a chain does, told its own prompt, the chain's prompt as typed,
        and what the step before it replied, as the spec-to-code prompt
        tells a code step, so a chain can be carried on, as a further code
        change once the spec is built, or a spec tidy-up after the code. A
        step not yet sent can be edited, moved among the others not yet
        sent, or removed; one sent reads as it was. Steps are saved with the
        chain, in its hidden anchor, as the @{PromptSendingScope} keeps a
        queued prompt, so a chain keeps its added steps across restarts, and
        a step whose step before it failed or was cancelled is never sent, as
        none of a chain's are.
EOF

content.text:
I rewrote the editor's hover rule so that resting on a symbol or an error opens a proper popover filled from the language server. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 82 files.

**How the popover behaves:**
- **When it opens:** after the pointer rests on a symbol or an error for 500ms. It sits just below the hovered text, or above it if there's no room below.
- **Size:** at most 480×320px, scrolling beyond that.
- **Staying open:** you can move the pointer into it to select text or click links. It closes when the pointer leaves both the popover and the text, on Escape, or when the editor scrolls.
- **Symbols:**
  - Names, keys, keywords, imported names and names inside expressions send `textDocument/hover` to the server. The editor's unsaved text is sent first.
  - The answer shows as markdown with Piton highlighting in its code blocks.
  - An answer that arrives after the pointer has left is dropped. Prose, numbers, comments, and empty or repeat-the-text answers still open nothing.
- **Errors:** anywhere along an error's underline, the popover shows the message first: a severity icon and colour, the message, its code and any related notes as links. If the error is on a symbol, the symbol's hover follows. If the server offers fixes, a "Quick fix (Ctrl+.)" link lists them.
- **Underlines:** errors, warnings and info are wavy underlines in their severity's colour.
- **Typing:** typing closes the popover until the pointer moves again.

**Anchors the code should follow:** `EditorScope` `#language-support`, its `hover` and `diagnostics` entries, and `LSP` for the hover request and the published diagnostics.

content.content:
#### Previous Task Filters

A filter bar sits beneath the Previous group's heading in the Tasks tab, above its first row, on the tab bar's background with the theme's line beneath it, shown while the group holds a task. It holds two groups of small toggle chips, the second set 12 pixels apart from the first, wrapping onto another line when the bar is too narrow. Each chip reads its label and, muted after it, how many previous tasks match it on its own, whatever other chips are on; the latest task, heading the view, is never counted.
The first group filters by the mode each task was sent in, one chip per task mode in the [PromptModesScope](./modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope)'s order, "Code", "Chain", "Spec", and "Freeform", each tinted its mode's colour while on, its border in that colour and its background a faint tint of it. The second group's chips take the theme's accent the same way while on. The second filters by where a task stands with the other mode, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says, with "Can send to Spec" for tasks that offer Send to Spec, "Can send to Code" for those that offer Send to Code, "Sent" for those already sent to the other mode or being sent there, and "Marked done" for those marked done by hand.
With no chip on, which is how the list starts, every previous task shows. Within a group, the chips on combine as either, so a task shows when it matches any of them, and the two groups combine as both, so with chips on in each, a task shows only when it matches one in each. Clicking a chip turns it on or off, and a "Clear" button at the bar's right end, shown only while any chip is on, turns them all off. A chip that would show no tasks is still shown, its count 0, and can still be turned on.
Filtering only hides tasks from the list; it changes nothing about them. A chain whose steps are hidden in part keeps its parent row above the steps still shown, and is hidden with its parent only when none of its steps shows. Session dividers show only above a session with a task shown. The row's count still counts every previous task, and while any chip is on, what the row reads, the count, or "Back to the latest task" while the list is expanded, is followed by " · N shown", N counting the previous tasks the filters show. A hidden task stays selected if it was, and is still counted in "N selected" and sent by the batch actions; an open task that is filtered out closes. With every task filtered out, the list reads "No previous tasks match these filters", muted, centred. The filters are kept while the list is closed and opened again, and each open project keeps its own, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says, but they are not saved with the project.

#### Chained Tasks

content.text:
Suspense almost certainly looks for `codex` in a narrower set of places than your terminal does. Codex is usually installed with npm, which puts it somewhere only your shell's PATH points to, such as npm's global folder or nvm's `bin`. An app started from the dock, Finder or the Start menu doesn't get that PATH. On Windows npm installs it as `codex.cmd`, which isn't found if Suspense only looks for an exact `codex` executable. I can't see the code from this step, so that's the likely cause rather than a confirmed one. I added a "Finding Programs" section to `ApplicationScope` so programs are found the way your terminal finds them. `piton check` and `piton build` ran clean.

- **macOS and Linux:**
  - At launch, Suspense reads the PATH your login shell sets up, giving it up after 5 seconds.
  - It also searches the usual places tools get installed for you: `~/.local/bin`, `~/.cargo/bin`, npm's global bin, nvm, fnm, asdf, Volta, Bun, Homebrew and `/usr/local/bin`.
- **Windows:**
  - It reads the current user and machine PATH from the registry, plus `%APPDATA%\npm`.
  - It tries each extension Windows lists, so `codex.cmd`, `.bat` and `.ps1` shims are found.
  - It runs those through `cmd.exe` or PowerShell, still without a console window.
- **Clearer messages:**
  - A program only counts as installed once its `--version` succeeds.
  - "Found but won't run" is reported separately from "not found", with what the program printed.
  - "Not found" lists every folder that was searched.
- **Welcome page:** it shows the path each program was found at. Check again searches again, so you don't need to restart Suspense after installing something.

**Anchors the code should follow:** `ApplicationScope` `#finding-programs` and `#child-processes`, `WelcomeScope`'s Harness check, and `HarnessIntegrationScope` `#harnesses` and `#failures`.

grep -c "it is the project's" $f; grep -c "saved with the project straight away" $f; grep -n "^from /scope/project-data" $f

content.content:
#### Attachments

What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.
Images can be attached too: pasted from the clipboard while the chat input has focus, dropped onto the chat input from the file manager, or chosen with a small ghost button with an image icon, whose tooltip says "Attach images", on the tab row between the last tab and the help text, which opens the platform's file picker for any files, several at once, since the picker can't be limited to images. Pasting an image attaches it rather than putting anything in the text, even when the clipboard holds text as well; every image on the clipboard is attached, and a clipboard with no image pastes its text as usual. Several files dropped or chosen at once are attached in their order, each on its own merits. An image is known by its content, not its name, and only PNG, JPEG, GIF, and WebP are taken: anything else pasted, dropped, or chosen, BMP, TIFF, and SVG included, is not attached, and a warning notification titled "Not attached" says it isn't an image. An image larger than 5 MB is not attached either, and the same notification says it is too large. A folder dropped or chosen isn't an image either, and a file that can't be read is not attached, the same notification saying it couldn't be read, and why. Each file left out has its own notification, and the others are still attached.
Files can be dropped only on the chat input itself, its tabs, the attachments, and the text input; dropping them on the message list above it does nothing. While files are dragged over the chat input, its background is highlighted with the accent's fill, laid about a quarter of the way over it.
An attached image's row shows a small thumbnail, its file name, or "Pasted image" for one pasted, and its size in pixels, muted, with the same remove button; hovering the thumbnail shows the image larger, at most 320 pixels. Images and text are listed together in the order they were attached while the prompt is written. A prompt taken back into the input, as when a queued prompt is edited, lists its text first, then its images, each image named by its saved file, a pasted one included.
Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps the attachments it was sent with.

#### Projects
##### Attached Images

Each attached image is saved in the project's data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, once the prompt is sent or queued, and a prompt with images gives the hidden anchor an attachedImages

###### Property

a list of the saved images' paths, from the project

directory, in the order they were attached, keyed image1, image2, and so on, each written as an escape block as attached text is. The same image attached twice is saved once but listed, and given to the harness, twice. The images themselves are never put into the compiled prompt as text. The preview draws its thumbnails from the images in memory, saving nothing.
The harness is given the images alongside the compiled prompt, in the way it takes images, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, in the order they were attached. A message sent to a running task can carry images the same way, and so can a question. A saved image that can't be found when the run starts fails it saying so, before anything is run.
Wherever an attached prompt is shown, in the latest task's header, among the previous tasks, in the questions of the Ask conversation, in the queue, and in the preview, its images are shown as thumbnails beneath the prompt as typed, between it and any slices, except in the latest task's header, where they come beneath the whole prompt, slices included. A message sent to a running task shows none in the task's output. The raw prompt lists their paths, as the [PromptEditor](../index.md#prompt-editor) says. Clicking a thumbnail opens the image full size, in the platform's image viewer. Resending, sending to the other mode, and editing a queued prompt keep its images, and a Freeform prompt sends them as any other does.
What the harness receives is the compiled userPrompt followed by the attached text: a line reading "Attached text:", then each piece as a fenced code block, whose fence is longer than any run of backticks in the text itself. This is also the compiled prompt shown in the task's header.

##### New Conversation

content.text:
Any file can now be attached to a prompt, not just images. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 82 files.

- **Attaching:** paste, drop or pick files the same way as images. The button is now a paperclip, "Attach files", and files copied in your file manager paste as attachments.
- **Images vs files:**
  - PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP up to 5 MB still go to the harness as images.
  - Anything else up to 25 MB is attached as a file, including other image formats and images over 5 MB, which used to be refused.
  - Folders and files over 25 MB are refused with a notification.
- **Rows:** each file shows a kind icon, its name and its size.
- **Saving:** files are saved in a new `.suspense/attachments/` folder, in subfolders named by time and content hash. Each prompt's hidden anchor lists them in a new `attachedFiles` property.
- **What the harness gets:** an "Attached files:" list of paths, names and sizes after any attached text, never the files' contents. The harness reads them with its own tools.
- **Containers:** container runs get each attached file mounted read only on its own, never the whole folder.
- **Showing and carrying:** wherever a prompt is shown, its files are listed, and clicking one opens it. Files travel with resends, sends to the other mode, edits of queued prompts, chain steps, questions and messages sent to a running task.

The 25 MB limit is my choice; I can change it.

**Anchors the code should follow:** `ChatInputScope` `#attachments` and `#attached-files`, `ProjectDataScope` `#contents`, and `ContainerEnvironmentScope` `#mounts`.

content.content:
#### Chained Tasks

A prompt sent in Chain runs as steps, each saved in the history as a task of its own: first the Chain task itself, which writes the spec; then the same prompt sent to Code, told what the spec step did; and, when the chain asks for a post-build spec update, the same prompt sent to Spec once more, told what the code step did. Each step knows the one it was sent from, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. Only the steps the chain sends itself belong to it; a task sent to the other mode by hand, or resent, from one of its steps is a task of its own.
Each step runs in the lane of the work it does, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says: the Chain task and its spec follow-up in the spec lane, the code step in the code lane. A step is sent once the step before it finishes, never before, and takes its place in its lane's queue by when its chain was sent, not when the step itself was: behind every prompt waiting there that was sent before its chain, earlier chains' steps included, and ahead of every prompt sent after it. So a chain's code step never jumps ahead of a Code prompt, or another chain's code step, sent before the chain was, and a Code prompt sent while the chain's spec step ran waits for the chain's code step rather than coming between the chain's steps. Two steps whose chains were sent in the same order run in that order, whichever spec step finished first. Where nothing sent before its chain is waiting, it runs as soon as its lane is free, and straight away if it already is. Its place holds however it came to be queued, so a restart, with the queue read back from the project, keeps it there. The lane it leaves is free for its own queue meanwhile, so a Spec task sent while a chain's co
Each step also runs where the work of its lane runs, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says: the spec steps in a container holding the spec and no code, the code step always on the host, with its protected locations. Each carries on its own lane's conversation, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, so a step is told what the step before it did only through its prompt: the Chain prompt as typed and that step's final output, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](./mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says.
In the previous tasks list, a chain's steps are grouped under one parent item, so they read as parts of a single chain. The parent is a heading row in the list, tinted the Chain colour, as the [PromptModesScope](./modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it, a little more strongly than a single task's tint: a joined chain icon, the first line of the prompt, and at its right how many steps it has, "2 steps" or "3 steps". Its status is the chain's as a whole: Running while any step runs, Failed or Cancelled if a step was, and otherwise that of its last step. It has no checkbox, Resend, or Send to the other mode of its own, and clicking it doesn't open anything.
Beneath it, each step stays an item of its own, exactly as any previous task is, with its checkbox, status, Resend, and whatever else a task offers, opening onto its own prompt, table, and changed files. The steps are indented from the parent, joined to it by a thin line in the Chain colour down their left, from the parent's heading to the last step, and each is labelled by what it did, "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", in that step's mode colour, before its prompt, which leaves out the prompt's first line when it is the parent's. They are listed in the order they ran.
A chain is listed where its first step was sent, oldest first like every other item; tasks sent while it ran, such as questions or tasks of the other lane run between its steps, are never listed within it, and are listed after the chain, in the order they were sent. A chain's steps are found by which step each was sent from, not by being next to each other in the history. A chain still running, or one whose later steps haven't been sent yet, shows as many steps as have been, and a step still running shows as it would anywhere. When the latest task, heading the view, is a step of a chain, that chain's earlier steps are still grouped under its parent in the list, the parent saying the rest is the latest task. A session divider never falls between a chain's steps: it goes above the chain's parent. A step from the history whose chain can't be worked out, as when the step it was sent from is missing, is listed as a task of its own.

content.content:
### Shape

#### Description

Beneath the [RibbonScope](../../ui/components/ribbon/index.md#ribbon-scope), to the right of the [ProjectSidebarScope](../../ui/components/project-sidebar/index.md#project-sidebar-scope), which runs the full height beside it, and reaching the window's right edge. It is part of the [PromptEditor](../prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor).
The [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) lives within the body, along its bottom: its left edge against the project sidebar, and above it, beneath the body's tab bar, the selected tab's contents: the message list, or an open file. While a task runs, the [RightSidebarScope](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope) runs the body's full height at its right, beside the tab bar, the selected tab's contents, and the chat input, and the chat input's right edge is against it: the chat input never runs beneath the right sidebar. While that sidebar isn't there, the chat input reaches the window's right edge.
The body is flat and quiet: the selected tab's contents, the message list or an open file, sit on the theme's base surface, #444444 in dark mode, running edge to edge with no border, and the chat input along the bottom is set apart from them only by its own darker tab strip, as the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says, with no line between them.

#### Sliding

content.content:
#### Tabs

Along the top of the body runs a tab bar, in gpui-kit's default tab styling, across the width the message list takes: from the project sidebar to the right sidebar while a task runs, and to the window's right edge otherwise, or, while the body is split for Ask, to the edge between it and the Ask conversation. Its first tab, Chat, shows the message list, and is always there: it can't be closed or moved. After it comes a tab for each open file, in the order they were opened unless they have been dragged since, scrolling sideways once there are more than fit.
Just one tab's contents show at a time, filling the space between the tab bar and the chat input. The chat input stays along the bottom whichever tab is selected, so a prompt can be written while a file shows. The body starts with Chat selected, and clicking a tab selects it.
Every tab in the bar, Chat and each file's alike, is laid out the same plain way, with nothing extra around it: the bar's full height, 32 pixels, its contents centred up and down in it, 12 pixels of padding at its left, and 12 at its right, and no margin of its own above, below, or beside it, so one tab ends where the next begins, with only the tab styling's own line between them. Nothing is inset from the bar's top or bottom, and the first tab starts at the bar's left edge.
A file's tab shows the file's name, then, while it has unsaved changes, a dot, and then a small close button, an icon button 16 pixels square, set close beside the name, 4 pixels from it or from the dot, with no more room between them however long or short the name is. Since the button has room of its own around its icon, a file tab's right padding is 6 pixels rather than 12, so the icon sits as far from the tab's right edge as the name does from its left; the tab is only as wide as its padding, name, dot, and close button need. Chat's spinner, while something runs, sits 6 pixels after its label, inside the same padding. Hovering a file's tab shows the file's path in the project as its tooltip.
A file's tab can be dragged along the tab bar to reorder the files, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, a vertical line showing the gap between two tabs it will land in, and the tab dragged following the pointer as the file's name. Chat stays first: no gap before a file's first tab, between Chat and it, shows the indicator, and Chat itself can't be dragged. Dragging a tab selects it, as clicking it does, and the selection follows the tab to its new place; nothing else about its editor changes. A press on a tab's close button closes it rather than starting a drag. A file opened afterwards still gets its new tab just after the one selected.

#### Open File

A file opened, from the [FileTreeScope](../../ui/components/file-tree/index.md#file-tree-scope) or anywhere else the [OpenFileScope](../open-file/index.md#open-file-scope) says, shows in an [EditorScope](../editor/index.md#editor-scope) in a tab of its own, as many files open at once as are opened. A file not open yet gets a new tab, just after the one selected, and is selected. Opening a file that already has a tab selects that tab instead, leaving its editor as it was, unsaved changes and all.
Nothing slides: a file's tab is selected, and its editor shows, at once, and closing it takes it away at once too. Files never split the body among themselves; the file takes the tab bar's full width above the chat input, beside the Ask conversation while the body is split for Ask.

content.content:
#### Logging In

When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the command prints. The login URL the command prints opens in the host's browser, once, and nothing else ever opens one.
Only the login command's own output is read for it, from when the command starts, never what the image build prints before it, nor anything Podman prints while it pulls, builds, or starts the container, all of which is shown as text and never opened, its URLs at most clickable links. And only a URL that is the harness's login is opened: the first one the login command prints that leads to its sign-in, as Claude Code's to claude.ai or console.anthropic.com, Codex's to auth.openai.com, or OpenCode's to the provider it is logging in with, or a localhost callback it asks to be visited. Any other URL it prints, as a link to documentation, release notes, or a package's homepage, is only shown. A l
Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is cancelled or fails.
A login needs the image, as any run in a container does, and the first login on a machine is most often the first thing to need it. So the login view builds it first where it isn't there or is out of date, showing "Preparing environment" and what the build prints as it goes, and starts the login command only once the build has succeeded. A build that fails shows why in the login view, as a failed build says it, with a "Try again" button that builds it again, and starts no login.
The harness's volume is ready for it before its first login: created by the application with `podman volume create` where it isn't there, and mounted so that the user the container runs as owns it and can write it, as with Podman's `:U` option, never left owned by root where the harness runs as the user. The container's HOME, where the volume is mounted beneath it, as ~/.claude, is a directory that user owns, as is the volume, so the login command can write its credentials there on the first login as on any other.
The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every run. The [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) shows whether each harness is logged in in its container, and can log it in again.

#### Guards
33:- "Harness login", required, passing while the harness in use is logged in in its container, read from its volume. Not logged in, its guidance offers "Log in", which shows the login view, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says. It is checked only once "Containers" passes.

project's runs use the default image.

        While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows
        "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes
        to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.

        The image is a Linux image, whatever the host is, so what it holds is
        installed in it for Linux, for the architecture Podman runs: each
        harness and piton at the version found on the host, from its own
        Linux release or package, never a binary copied from the host, which
        on macOS or Windows can't run in it. The build is given only the
        Containerfile the application writes for it, in a build context of
        its own, a fresh temporary directory holding nothing else, never the
        project or the user's home, and needs nothing from the host but the
        network. A version that can't be found on the host, or isn't
        published for Linux, is installed at its latest.

        Only one build of an image runs at a time. A run, a login, or a
        welcome or settings check that needs an image already being built
        waits for that build and shares how it ended, rather than starting
        another, so two builds never race to tag the same image. A build is
        tagged only once it has succeeded, so a build that fails or is
        interrupted never leaves an image that is taken for a good one, and
        the next need of it builds it again.

        A build that fails says why in Podman's own words: the step it
        failed at and everything the build printed, as written, never only
        that the image couldn't be created, and the same is kept in the log
        the application writes for its builds, beside its preferences.

The build is failing because the image pins OpenCode to `opencode-ai@2.0.14`, the version read from your machine. npm doesn't have that version, so the whole install step fails, taking Claude Code and Codex down with it. I changed the spec so a bad version can't break the image, and so failures guide you instead of dumping Podman's output. `piton check` and `piton build` ran clean.

- **Versions are checked first:** each harness version taken from your machine is used only if npm confirms it exists. Otherwise that harness gets its latest version. Only a plain version number is read from the host's output.
- **One harness can't break the others:** each harness installs in its own step. One that can't install is left out and the image still builds; only runs that need it fail.
- **Version differences:** if a harness runs a different version in its container than on your machine, Welcome and Settings note it quietly, not as an error.
- **Guidance instead of walls of output:** a failure shows a short warning in plain words with fix buttons. Podman's output is collapsed under "Details" and kept in the debug log.
  - "OpenCode 2.0.14 isn't available to install", with "Use the latest OpenCode"
  - a network problem, with "Try again"
  - Podman out of disk space, with "Free up space", which runs `podman system prune` after confirming
  - anything else, with "Try again" and "Copy details"
- **Welcome uses the project's harness:** the Harness and Harness login rows name the open project's harness, so they won't say Claude Code when your project uses Codex. They re-check whenever you switch projects or change the harness.

**Anchors the code should follow:** `ContainerEnvironmentScope` `#image` and `#logging-in`; `WelcomeScope`'s Harness and Harness login checks and Check again; and `HarnessIntegrationScope` `#harnesses`.

content.text:
You're right, and the earlier rule was mine. I wrote that a chain stays "Running" until every step it might send is done. So any chain whose code step was never sent, like old ones or ones interrupted by closing the app, was stuck Running for good. I replaced that rule. `piton check` and `piton build` ran clean.

- **Running only when a step is running now:** a chain reads Running exactly while one of its steps is building, compiling or running in the app at that moment, never otherwise.
- **Queued:** if no step is running but one is waiting in the queue, the chain reads Queued and sits in the Queued group.
- **Otherwise it's over:**
  - It reads Failed or Cancelled if a step was. Otherwise it takes its last step's own status: Done, or Not recorded if that step has no record of its run.
  - A chain whose code step was never sent shows that as a muted note on its parent row, never as Running.
- **Reading state correctly:**
  - Each step's state comes from where it actually is. It's running only while the app has its run going, which no step from the history can be after a restart. It's queued only while its prompt is in the queue. Otherwise it comes from its own history record.
  - Steps are joined to a chain only by which step each was sent from, so a task never picks up another chain's state.

**Anchors the code should follow:** `PromptEditor` `#chained-tasks`, `TasksTabScope` `#description` and `#rows` for which group a chain sits in, and `MessageList` `#status`.

content.content:
#### Description

The tab is one scrolling column, with a [ScrollbarScope](../../scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope), read top to bottom as a timeline, in three groups, each headed by a small muted label with its count: "Previous", every task that has run, oldest at the top, as the [PromptEditor](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor)'s previous tasks are, with their filters and batch actions along the group's heading; "Running", every task under way, in either lane; and "Queued", the queue, in its order, as the [QueueListScope](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/queue-list/index.md#queue-list-scope) says, reordered by dragging, its auto-send switch and "Send next" button along its heading. A group with nothing in it shows its heading alone, muted, "No queued prompts" and the like. Each time the tab is shown, it is scrolled so the Running group, or the start of the Queued one when nothing runs, is in view.
The Previous group starts collapsed: its heading alone shows, with its count and a right chevron, and none of its rows. Clicking the heading, anywhere but its filter and batch actions, expands it, the chevron turning down, its rows showing above Running, the newest nearest it, and clicking again collapses it. It is collapsed each time a project is opened, and otherwise stays as it was left while the application runs, each open project keeping its own. While it is collapsed, its filters and batch actions still work and its count still follows them, and opening a previous task from elsewhere, as from the running activity list, expands it to show that task.

#### Rows

Every task is one row, 28 pixels tall, as a queued prompt's is: a bar 2 pixels wide down its left edge in its mode's colour, as the [PromptModesScope](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it, then its status, a spinner while it is under way, a tick, cross, or dash once it has ended, or, queued, its place in the queue, then the first line of its prompt, cut off with an ellipsis, then, at its right, muted, how long it took, or has been running, as the [MessageList](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list) writes it. A chain is one row, its steps as rows indented beneath it, collapsed to start with, as the previous tasks group a chain. Clicking a row opens it, as below, and the row stays highlighted while it is open. Hovering a row shows its prompt's first lines in its tooltip.

#### Virtualized

The list is virtualized: however many tasks the project has run, it lays out and draws only the rows in view, and a few rows either side of it, never every row, so opening the tab, scrolling it, resizing the sidebar, filtering, and new tasks arriving cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks as with ten. Every row is 28 pixels tall, group headings and a chain's expanded steps included, so where each row lies is known from its place in the list alone, without laying out the rows before it, and the scrollbar's thumb is sized and placed from the whole list's height, as though every row were drawn.
A row is drawn only from what its row shows, its mode, status, first line, and time, read from each task's history record once and kept, never by reading a record's output, lines, or snapshots while scrolling; those are read only when a task is opened. Running rows update their time and spinner in place, redrawing only what is in view. Scrolling to a row, as when the tab opens on Running, a filter changes, or a queued row is dragged past the edge, jumps straight to its place without drawing the rows between. A row scrolled out of view and back is the same as it was, its chain expanded or not, its selection and highlight kept.
Scrolling past either end does nothing: with the list at its top or its bottom, a wheel, trackpad, or drag that goes further leaves every row exactly where it is, frame after frame, with no stretch, bounce, or nudge of even a pixel and back, and draws nothing anew, since nothing moved. Its scroll position is clamped to its ends before a frame is drawn, never drawn past an end and corrected the frame after, and kept in whole device pixels, so a row never shimmers between two places. What lies at an end stays at it: a running row's time ticking, a task finishing, a row added or removed elsewhere in the list, or the tab being resized never makes the rows in view jump and settle. A list scrolled to its bottom stays at its bottom as rows are added, and one at its top stays at its top. The list counts as taller than the tab only once it overflows it by a whole pixel, as the right sidebar's panels do, so a list that fits never scrolls at all.

#### Details

content.text:
The Tasks tab is now three collapsible accordion sections with sticky headings, every row lines up in the same columns, and chains no longer expand inline. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 82 files.

- **Accordion sections:** Previous, Running and Queued each collapse on their own.
  - Each heading is a 28px raised row: a chevron, the title and count, then its controls at the right.
  - Clicking a heading toggles only that section, and any number can be open at once.
  - Previous starts collapsed and the other two expanded whenever a project opens. Otherwise each project keeps them as you left them.
- **Sticky headings:** a section's heading stays pinned at the top while you scroll its rows, until the next section's heading pushes it out. Pinned headings never let rows show through and never move any row.
- **Aligned columns:** every row in every section uses the same columns:
  - the mode bar;
  - a 20px lead column: a checkbox in Previous, a drag grip in Queued, kept empty in Running;
  - a 20px status column;
  - the prompt;
  - a right-aligned time.

  So status and text start at the same place whatever the row has, and the headings' titles line up with the rows' text.
- **Chains:** a chain is one row with its overall status and its step count. Its steps show only once you open it, and selecting the row selects its steps for batch actions.
